decls.name: no_four_close
decls.docstring:
Four distinct positions on a cycle of length at least six cannot all be within cyclic
distance two of one another.

decls.name: far_edges_anticomplete
decls.docstring: Positions farther than two apart index anticomplete rim edges.

decls.name: four_yEdges_give_anticomplete_pair
decls.docstring:
If a hole has at least four `Y`-complete edges, two of them have no edge between their
endpoint pairs.  This is the elementary selection made in the last paragraph of claim (4).

links.rationale: If a hole has at least four Y-complete edges, two of them have no edge between their endpoint pairs -- the elementary selection made in the last paragraph of claim (4) of 16.2, but stated as reusable combinatorial fact rather than a quoted sentence.

decls.name: no_square_on_long_hole
decls.docstring:
Four pairwise distinct rim vertices cannot carry the four edges of a square when the
ambient hole has length at least six.

links.rationale: Four pairwise distinct rim vertices cannot carry all four edges of a square once the ambient hole has length at least six; combinatorial fact about holes, no direct paper quote.

decls.name: second_complete_of_pair
decls.docstring:
If the head of a path is one end of its unique complete edge, the next path vertex is the
other end.

decls.name: same_side_tracks_false
decls.docstring:
The two same-side bridges force a long prism.  If only one were present, the two track
parities close it into an odd hole; if neither were present, 15.3 gives the paper's
`nobanister` contradiction.

links.rationale: The two same-side bridges force a long prism.

decls.name: opposite_tracks_oriented_false
decls.docstring:
The crossed-bridge case, in the orientation in which `q₁r₂` is present.  The short
holes force both tracks to have odd edge length and `S` to have even vertex length.  Deleting
the complete outer ends gives the odd path used in 13.6; its forced length three reduces to
the four-vertex path used in 2.2.

links.rationale: The crossed-bridge case, in the orientation in which q₁r₂ is present.

decls.name: opposite_tracks_false
decls.docstring:
The orientation-independent crossed-bridge argument.  If neither possible bridge exists,
the three tracks form the forbidden banister configuration.  Otherwise reverse the roles of
the two rim tracks, if necessary, and apply `opposite_tracks_oriented_false`.

links.rationale: The orientation-independent crossed-bridge argument.

decls.name: odd_path_endgame
decls.docstring:
The final 13.6/2.2 move in claim (3).  Unlike the shared claim-(5) version, `f₁` may
also see `p₂`; this harmless second possibility has wheel parity opposite to `p₁`.

links.rationale: Proves the contrapositive of claim (3) of 16.2: under the configuration following claim (1), X1 does not have members of opposite wheel-parity, via the triangle case and the R1/R2/Q1/Q2 computation ending in 13.6.

decls.name: endgame_contradiction

Here `y` has no neighbour in `F₁`, as supplied by the first outcome of
17.2 applied to `F₁`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the sub-case of the proof where y has a neighbour in F2: b can be linked onto the triangle {y, a0, b0}, contradicting 2.4.

decls.name: outsideNeighborContradictsCatch
decls.docstring:
PAPER (proof of 17.3, printed p. 104):

> *"If `y₁` has neighbours in `F₂` then `(F \ {a}) ∪ {y₂}` catches
> the triangle `{a,a₀,y₁}`; ... there is no reflection ... contrary to
> 17.1. So `y₁` has no neighbours in `F₂`."*

links.rationale: Formalizes the sub-case of the proof where y1 has a neighbour in F2: (F \ {a}) union {y2} catches the triangle {a, a0, y1} with no reflection, contrary to 17.1.

decls.name: disconnectedCase
decls.docstring:
The disconnected branch of 17.3, assembled from the three printed
sentences isolated above and 17.2 on the block `F₁`.

links.rationale: Handles the proof's case split when F \ {b} is disconnected, assembling the component-split facts with 17.2 applied to F1.

decls.name: main
decls.docstring: The full conclusion of 17.3.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.3.
The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.4, concluding that p_{n-1} is nonadjacent to x1.

decls.name: misses_deleted
decls.docstring: Completing `X \ {x}` but not `X` means missing `x`.

links.rationale: Pure set-theoretic fact used throughout claim (2): a vertex that completes X\{x} but not all of X must be missing exactly x.

decls.name: cross_pair_parity
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Since `pᵢ-x₁-Q-x₂-pⱼ-pᵢ` is an antihole it follows that
`Q` is odd." For adjacent `pᵢ,pⱼ`, the extra vertex `z` instead makes
`z-pᵢ-x₁-Q-x₂-pⱼ-z` an antihole, forcing the opposite parity.

links.rationale: Shows the antipath Q between x1 and x2 has opposite parity depending on whether the two path vertices completing X\{x1} and X\{x2} are adjacent: this is the antihole/parity mechanism the paper uses to show Q is odd in claim (2) of 17.5's proof.

decls.name: Marked
decls.docstring: The indexed set of complete vertices used as `Wᵢ` in claim (2).

links.rationale: Formalizes the paper's indexed sets Wi = the set of vertices of P complete to X\{xi} (i=1,2), used throughout claim (2)'s proof; instantiated generically here to any set X and index i on the path.

decls.name: Line
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Let us say a line is a minimal subpath of `P \ p₁` meeting
both `W₁` and `W₂`." Indices are zero-based.

links.rationale: Formalizes the paper's ad hoc definition of a 'line': a minimal subpath of P\p1 (given here by zero-based indices a<b) with one end marked by A and the other by B, and no marked vertex strictly between.

decls.name: edges_empty_of_unique
decls.docstring: A path with just one complete vertex has no complete edge.

links.rationale: Combinatorial fact: if at most one path vertex is X-complete, no pair of path vertices can form an X-complete edge.

decls.name: shorter_unique_not_odd
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "The triple `L, X \ {x₁}, X \ {x₂}` is another
counterexample ... contrary to the optimality of `P,X,Y`."
The same construction applies to the final suffix in the proof.

links.rationale: Formalizes the optimality-contradiction schema reused throughout claim (2): a shorter subpath, together with two anticonnected sets whose union is anticonnected and which the subpath's ends uniquely complete, cannot itself be odd, since it would be a smaller counterexample to 17.5.

decls.name: clean_interval_even
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "But this path has length at least 2, and `z` has no
neighbour in it, so by 2.2 it is even." This form applies to every interval
with complete ends and no complete internal vertex.

links.rationale: Formalizes the '2.2' parity step used repeatedly in claim (2): an interval of P whose only X-complete vertices are its two named endpoints has even length, since the X-complete vertex z has no neighbour on the path.

decls.name: exists_edge_index
decls.docstring: A positive complete-edge count supplies an indexed complete edge.

links.rationale: Extracts a concrete pair of consecutive path indices realizing an X-complete edge from the hypothesis that the path carries an odd (hence positive) number of X-complete edges.

decls.name: line_argument_absurd
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "So we may assume that `(X \ {xᵢ}) ∪ Y` is anticonnected
for `i = 1,2`. ... This proves (2)."
Both deleted sides have odd complete-edge counts. The antihole argument
excludes one-edge lines, and optimality excludes longer odd lines. The
complete-interval and suffix parity rules then give the index contradiction.

links.rationale: Formalizes the line-counting contradiction closing claim (2) of 17.5's proof, once (X \ {xi}) union Y is assumed anticonnected for both i.

decls.name: marks_disjoint
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "So `W₁ ∩ W₂ = {p₁}`." Away from index zero, a vertex
cannot complete both deleted sets, since their union is `X`.

links.rationale: Formalizes 'W1 ∩ W2 = {p1}': away from index 0 no path vertex can be complete to both X\{x1} and X\{x2}, since together these two sets cover all of X, and p1 is the only X-complete vertex on P by claim (1).

decls.name: cross_nonadjacent
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "We claim that `Q` is odd. ... If some line has length 1,
... `z-pᵢ-x₁-Q-x₂-pᵢ₊₁-z` is an odd antihole, a contradiction."
In fact every pair of differently marked vertices after `p₁` is nonadjacent.
The two odd edge counts supply nonadjacent differently marked vertices first,
which fixes the parity of the antipath in `X`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the key nonadjacency fact behind claim (2): any positive-index vertex of P completing X\{x1} is nonadjacent to any positive-index vertex completing X\{x2}, since an adjacent such pair together with z and the antipath Q between x1,x2 would build the one-edge-line antihole z-pi-x1-Q-x2-pi+1-z, contradicting the parity forced by cross_pair_parity.

decls.name: line_swap
decls.docstring: Exchanging the two sets does not change the lines.

links.rationale: Trivial symmetry lemma: a line for the pair (A,B) is also a line for the swapped pair (B,A) with its endpoint markings exchanged.

decls.name: exists_line_between
decls.docstring:
Between differently marked vertices there is a line: take the first
vertex of the second kind, then the last vertex of the first kind before it.

links.rationale: Combinatorial extraction lemma: between two differently-marked path positions there is always a 'line', obtained as the last A-marked index before the first B-marked index following it.

decls.name: even_line_ends
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "If there is a line contained in the path `p_r-⋯-p_s`, ...
one of the paths `p_r-⋯-p_h` and `p_k-⋯-p_s` is odd, contrary to the
minimality of `s-r`."
This is the same parity argument as induction on the right endpoint of a
line. The previous vertex of the right endpoint's kind is either index zero
or the start of an earlier line.

links.rationale: Formalizes the induction showing both ends of every 'line' occur at an even index: peeling off the line with maximal left end and applying the interior-parity facts and the minimality of s-r inductively forces evenness at each step.

decls.name: even_lines_absurd
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Choose `j` ... maximum such that `{p_j,…,p_n}` includes a
line. ... `W_k ∩ {p_j,…,p_n} = {p_j}`. ... So `n-j` is even."
Together with the parity of all line ends, this contradicts the odd path
length. This is the final index argument of claim (2).

links.rationale: Derives the final contradiction of claim (2) purely from the abstract parity constraints: the maximal-index line forces its own start to be even while the tail from that start to the odd path length n must also be even, which is impossible; the printed proof reaches this via a longer chain of concrete vertex choices (q,t,r,s,...) that this lemma abstracts away, so no single paper sentence corresponds to it directly.

decls.name: even_short_slice
decls.docstring:
The slice form of the smaller-counterexample argument in claim (2).
The slice starts after `p₁`, and its unique complete vertices are its ends.

links.rationale: Generic slice form of the optimality-contradiction schema (shorter_unique_not_odd), specialized to a subpath of P starting strictly after p1 whose only A-complete and B-complete vertices are its own two named endpoints; instantiated below for both the 'line' case and the 'tail' case, so it has no single paper sentence of its own.

decls.name: tail_even
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "If the path `p_j-⋯-p_n` has odd length, then
`p_j,…,p_n, X \ {x_k}, Y` is a counterexample ... So `n-j` is even."
Here `i` is the last complete index for the first side.

links.rationale: Formalizes the parity deduction that n - j is even (hence j even) in claim (2) of 17.5's proof, from the optimality of P, X, Y ruling out the path p_j-...-p_n as a shorter counterexample.

decls.name: oriented_line_even
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "If some line `L` has odd length greater than 1, then the
triple `L, X \ {x₁}, X \ {x₂}` is another counterexample ... Hence
every line is even." The antihole argument supplies the nonadjacent ends.

links.rationale: Formalizes 'every line is even' from claim (2): applying the optimality-contradiction slice argument to a line with nonadjacent ends shows an odd line of length > 1 would give a strictly smaller counterexample to 17.5, so every line must have even length.

decls.name: blocks
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "There is an antipath `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_t` such that
`s,t > 1` and `X = {x₁,…,x_s}`, and `Y = {y₁,…,y_t}`."
This assembles the size argument, the two non-cut arguments, and the unique
cross-pair. Its list conclusion avoids an import cycle with `Thm175Claims`.

links.rationale: Formalizes claim (3) of 17.5's proof in full: X and Y are exactly the vertex sets of a single antipath x1-...-xs-y1-...-yt with s,t>1, assembled from the size bound |X|,|Y|≥2, the two antipath constructions from non-cut vertices, and the unique cross-nonadjacent pair joining their distinguished ends.

decls.name: not_subsingleton
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "For if `|X| = 1`, `X = {x}` say, then
`z-x-p₁-⋯-pₙ` is an odd path of length at least 5 between `Y`-complete
vertices, and none of its internal vertices are `Y`-complete, contrary to
13.6. So `|X| ≥ 2`." The empty case is excluded by claim (1).

links.rationale: Formalizes the |X| >= 2 (and symmetrically |Y| >= 2) step opening claim (3) of 17.5's proof: a singleton X would give an odd path of length >= 5 between Y-complete vertices, contrary to 13.6.

decls.name: path_of_two_noncut
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "By (2), there do not exist two vertices `x₀ ∈ X \ {x}` such
that `X \ {x₀}` is anticonnected; and therefore `X` is an antipath."
An induced path between the only two possible non-cut vertices covers the
connected set: otherwise there is a non-cut vertex outside that path.

links.rationale: General graph fact underlying claim (3)'s antipath constructions: if a connected set S has exactly two vertices a,b whose individual removal keeps S connected, the induced path between a and b already covers all of S, since any vertex outside that path would give a third non-cut vertex.

decls.name: one_block
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Hence there are at least two vertices `x ∈ X` such that
`X \ {x}` is anticonnected, and from (2), `X ∩ Y = ∅`, and there is a
unique vertex `x ∈ X` with nonneighbours in `Y`."
The same application of (2) locates the two ends of the first block.

links.rationale: Formalizes the construction of one antipath block of claim (3): from |X|≥2 there are two non-anticut vertices a,b of X, and applying (2) to them gives X∩Y=∅ and a unique vertex of X (WLOG b) with a non-neighbour in Y, from which path_of_two_noncut builds the antipath covering X with b as its distinguished end.

decls.name: join_blocks
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Because of the symmetry between `X,Y`, the same applies for
`Y`, and this proves (3)." The unique missing cross-pair joins the two
antipaths at their distinguished ends.

links.rationale: Formalizes the gluing step completing claim (3): concatenating the X-antipath (ending at its unique vertex x with a non-neighbour in Y) with the reversed Y-antipath (starting at the corresponding unique vertex y of Y) produces one long antipath, since x and y are precisely the unique nonadjacent cross-pair between X and Y.

Builds the path z-x1-R from a subpath R of P whose only neighbour of x1 is R's starting vertex, used to attach z and x1 onto each half of the interval split around the exceptional pair pi,pi+1 in claim (4).
Case-splits the interior of the constructed path z::x1::R into 'the vertex is x1' or 'the vertex lies in R and is not R's far endpoint'.
Technical helper: the path z::x1::R (for a subpath R of P) has no interior wSet-complete vertex other than R's own far endpoint, given that R itself has none.
Shows z, x1, and every vertex of a subpath R of P lie outside wSet, so the constructed path z::x1::R avoids wSet entirely.

decls.name: restricted_complete_vertices
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "... so `k=j+1` ... every `W`-complete vertex in `P\p₁` is
adjacent to `p_k` ... `i=1`, and so `j=2,k=3`, and the `W`-complete vertices
in `P` are `p₁,p₂` and possibly `p₄`."

links.rationale: Formalizes the culmination of the first paragraph of claim (4): once the two consecutive W-complete vertices pi,pi+1 are located inside [a,d], the clean-path parity arguments pin i down to 0 and d down to 2, so every W-complete vertex of P is one of p1 (index 0), p2 (index 1), or p4 (index 3).

If a path's only possible A-complete vertices are its two named ends, those ends must be nonadjacent (a shorter path could not carry two distinct such ends), so no pair of the path's vertices forms an A-complete edge.

decls.name: even
decls.docstring: A complete vertex avoiding the interior excludes an odd clean path by 2.2.

links.rationale: Instantiates 2.2 for a 'clean' path (A-complete only at its two named ends, with z complete to A and anticomplete to the path): an odd such path would force 2.2 to give an A-complete edge or an interior vertex adjacent to z, both excluded, so the path must be even.

decls.name: length_three
decls.docstring: An odd clean path has length three by 13.6.

links.rationale: Instantiates 13.6 for a clean odd path between A-complete ends: since noedge rules out the theorem's A-complete-edge alternative, 13.6 forces the path to have length exactly 3.

decls.name: adjacent_complete_contradiction
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Then `z-p_b-x₁-⋯-x_s-p_c-z` is an antihole, so `s` is odd.
But then `p₂-x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-p₂` is an odd antihole, a contradiction."
The two antiholes differ in length by one.

links.rationale: Formalizes the closing contradiction of claim (4): given an edge uv with u complete to wSet=X\{x1} and v complete to X\{xs}, Bergeness applied to the antihole z-u-x1-...-xs-v-z and, separately, to the antihole p2-x1-...-xs-y1-p2 (valid since t0=0 and p2 is W-complete) forces incompatible parities on s, a contradiction.
x1 itself is never wSet-complete, since its second neighbour along the antipath qX is a wSet vertex that is adjacent to x1 in G (nonadjacent in the complement).

decls.name: two_consecutive
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "By 2.3 it contains exactly one, and only two `W`-complete
vertices; so `j=i+1`."  This extracts the two consecutive vertices from the
hole formed by an interval with no internal neighbour of `x₁`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the extraction of the two consecutive W-complete vertices of claim (4): applying 2.3 to the hole x1-ph-...-pk-x1 (built from an interval whose only interior neighbour of x1 is impossible) shows it has exactly one W-complete edge, giving indices i,j=i+1 as exactly the interval's W-complete vertices.

decls.name: missed_not_complete
decls.docstring: The last vertex of the antipath prefix misses its predecessor in `W`.

links.rationale: The second-to-last vertex of the antipath prefix x1-...-xs-y1-...-y_t0 is adjacent in G to y_t0 (its complement-predecessor), so y_t0 cannot be wSet-complete.

decls.name: first_miss_zero
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "... so the other end `y_{t₀}` is not [X-complete]; and hence
`t₀=1`, since all other vertices of `Y` are `X`-complete."

links.rationale: Formalizes the deduction that t0=1 in the paper's 1-based indexing (s.t0=0 here) closing the first paragraph of claim (4): the path p1-...-pd-y_t0 is odd with p1 its only X-complete end, so y_t0 is not X-complete, forcing y_t0 to be y1, the antipath's first Y-vertex.

decls.name: main
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "For every subpath `P'` of `P`, if the ends of `P'` are adjacent
to `x₁`, then there are an even number of `W`-complete edges in `P'`."

links.rationale: Formalizes claim (4) itself: for every subpath P' of P whose two ends are adjacent to x1, the number of wSet-complete edges inside P' is even, proved by deriving a contradiction from an odd count using the exceptional-pair, restricted-complete-vertex, first-miss and closing-antihole lemmas.

decls.name: second_misses
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "By 17.4 (with `X` and `Y` exchanged), `p₂` is nonadjacent to
`y_{t₀}`."  Apply 17.4 to the reversed original path and to the reversed
antipath `x_s-y₁-⋯-y_{t₀}-p₁`.

links.rationale: Formalizes 'p2 is nonadjacent to y_t0' via 17.4 applied with X and Y exchanged (to the reversed path and reversed antipath xs-...-y_t0-p1), needed to build the second antihole in the closing contradiction of claim (4).

decls.name: first_other_complete
decls.docstring:
The first `V`-complete vertex after `p₁` has positive even zero-based
index, where `V=X\{x_s}`.  This is the choice of `c` in printed claim (4).

links.rationale: Locates the first V-complete vertex after p1 (V=X\{xs}) at a positive even zero-based index: this is the choice of index c in the second paragraph of claim (4)'s proof, reached by the same clean-path parity technique used for the W-complete case.
Technical monotonicity lemma: the complete edges counted on a sub-interval of the path are a subset of those counted on any interval containing it.

decls.name: slice_edges_split
decls.docstring: Cutting an induced path at a vertex partitions its complete edges.

links.rationale: Technical additivity lemma: splitting an induced path interval at an interior vertex partitions its complete-edge count as the sum of the two halves' counts.

decls.name: parity_of_intervals_without_internal_neighbor
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "For suppose not; then we may choose `P'` such that no internal
vertex of `P'` is adjacent to `x₁`."  Add the two edge counts when an internal
neighbour splits an interval.

links.rationale: Formalizes the case-split sentence opening the derivation of claim (4): if a W-complete-edge parity fails on a subpath P' whose ends are adjacent to x1, take P' with no internal vertex adjacent to x1, then combine the parities of the two halves split at an internal neighbour of x1 by induction on the subpath length.

decls.name: gap_first_other_complete
decls.docstring:
**17.5 (4), printed pp. 107--108.**
PAPER: "Choose `c` with `2≤c≤d` minimum such that `p_c` is `V`-complete.
Since `p₂` is nonadjacent to `x₁` it follows that `c≥3`. Since `p₁-⋯-p_c`
is between `V`-complete vertices and its internal vertices are not
`V`-complete and `z` has no neighbour in it, it is even by 2.2, and so `c`
is odd."
Here `V=X\{x_s}`. The returned index is zero-based. The existence of a
`V`-complete vertex uses 2.2 on `p₁-⋯-p_d-y₁`, as in the preceding sentence.

links.rationale: Formalizes the choice of the first V-complete vertex p_c after p1 (V=X\{x_s}) and the parity argument via 2.2 showing the index c is odd.

decls.name: adjacent_completions
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "If `c-b>1` then `p_b-⋯-p_c,W,V` is a counterexample ...
contradicting the optimality of `X,Y,P`. So `c=b+1`."
The finite maximum chooses `b`, and the shorter counterexample proves the
adjacency needed in the two-antihole argument.

links.rationale: Formalizes the optimality step ruling out c-b>1: since p_b-...-p_c together with W,V would otherwise give a shorter counterexample, the finite maximum b chosen just below c must satisfy c=b+1, giving the adjacent W- and V-complete vertices used in the closing antihole argument.

decls.name: Setup
decls.docstring:
The antipath blocks and first missed vertex chosen just before (4).
PAPER: "So `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_{t₀}-p₁` is an antipath."
The integer `t₀` is zero-based.

links.rationale: Bundles the two antipath blocks qX, qY, their endpoints, and the first Y-vertex y_{t0} missed by p1 into one record, used throughout the formalization of claims (4) and (5).

decls.name: wSet
decls.docstring: The set `W=(X\{x₁})∪{y₁,…,y_{t₀-1}}` in the printed proof.

links.rationale: Defines the paper's set W=(X\{x1})∪{y1,...,y_{t0-1}} used throughout claims (4) and (5), with the list indices taken zero-based.

decls.name: edges
decls.docstring: The complete edges of a list, each counted once as an unordered pair.

links.rationale: Defines the set of A-complete edges of a vertex list, each unordered pair counted once, used to state the odd/even complete-edge-count parity claims.
x1 (the head of the antipath block qX) belongs to X.
x1 does not lie on the path P, since P is disjoint from X and x1 ∈ X.
Derives that X and Y are disjoint from the antipath qX++qY having no repeated vertex.
x1 is not itself a member of W=(X\{x1})∪{y1,...,y_{t0-1}}, since it is excluded from the first part and X, Y are disjoint.
W is contained in X∪Y, since it is built from a subset of X and a subset of Y.
No vertex of the path P lies in W, since W is built only from vertices of X and Y, which are disjoint from P by hypothesis.
p1 is complete to W, since it is X-complete and (by the choice of t0) adjacent to every yj with j<t0.
z is complete to W, since z is complete to X∪Y and W⊆X∪Y.

decls.name: complete_X_of_complete_wSet
decls.docstring: On `P`, adjacency to `x₁` and completeness to `W` imply completeness to `X`.

links.rationale: On the path, a vertex adjacent to x1 and complete to W=(X\{x1})∪{y1,...,y_{t0-1}} is complete to all of X.
Rewrites the set W as exactly the vertices of the list qX.tail ++ qY.take t0, connecting the set- and list-based descriptions of W.
W is anticonnected, since it is (up to reindexing) an initial segment of the induced antipath qX++qY with x1 removed.
W∪Y equals the set of vertices of the antipath qX++qY with its head x1 removed.
W∪Y is anticonnected, being the tail of the induced antipath qX++qY with x1 deleted.

decls.name: odd_edges_wSet
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "From the optimality of `P,X,Y`, it follows that `P,W,Y` is not a
counterexample ... and so there are an odd number of `W`-complete edges in `P`."
The union loses `x₁`, so the second optimality clause suffices.

links.rationale: Formalizes the parity conclusion used to start claim (4): since P,W,Y cannot itself be a smaller counterexample (W loses x1 from X), the number of W-complete edges of P is odd.

decls.name: antiPrefix
decls.docstring: The antipath prefix ending at the first vertex of `Y` missed by `p₁`.

links.rationale: Names the list x1,...,xs,y1,...,y_{t0} (the antipath prefix up to and including the first vertex of Y missed by p1).
Reindexes the antipath prefix antiPrefix as an initial segment (take) of the concatenated list qX++qY, for use with generic path-slicing lemmas.
The antipath prefix x1,...,xs,y1,...,y_{t0} is itself a genuine antipath from x1 to y_{t0}, obtained by slicing the full antipath qX++qY.
Every vertex of the antipath prefix lies in X or in Y.

decls.name: first_miss_antipath
decls.docstring: PAPER: "So `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_{t₀}-p₁` is an antipath."

links.rationale: Formalizes the unnumbered construction just before claim (4): extending the antipath x1-...-xs-y1-...-y_{t0} by p1 gives an antipath, using that p1 is not Y-complete so some y_{t0} is nonadjacent to it.
Technical list lemma: characterizes membership in a dropped suffix by an index bound on the original list.

decls.name: complete_index_eq_one
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "By 13.6 applied in [the complement], ... `S` has odd length. ...
so by 2.2 applied in [the complement], some internal vertex of `S` has no
neighbour in `P\{p₁,p₂}`. But they are all adjacent to `p_j` or to `p_n`,
so `j=2`."  Here `j` is zero-based.

links.rationale: Formalizes the two complement-graph applications (13.6 to get S odd, then 2.2 to pin down an internal vertex of S with no neighbour outside {p1,p2}) that force the index j to equal 2 in the paper's one-based numbering (j=1 here, zero-based).

decls.name: exists_first_neighbor
decls.docstring: The first neighbour of `y_{t₀}` on `P` is at or after `p₃`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the choice of d, the first path vertex adjacent to the missed vertex y_{t0}, together with the derived lower bound d>=3 (here: 2<=d in zero-based indexing).
x1 is adjacent to the missed vertex y_{t0}, from the general fact that the two ends of an antipath of length at least 3 are adjacent in G, applied to the antipath prefix x1,...,y_{t0}.

decls.name: first_neighbor_hole
decls.docstring: PAPER: "`x₁-p₁-⋯-p_d-y_{t₀}-x₁` is a hole of length at least 6."

links.rationale: Formalizes the construction of the hole x1-p1-...-pd-y_{t0}-x1, later shown to share three vertices with the antihole D.

decls.name: four_of_three_shared
decls.docstring: The three shared vertices force the antihole to have length four, by 15.7.

links.rationale: Formalizes the application of 15.7 to a hole and antihole sharing three named vertices, forcing the antihole D's length to be exactly 4.

decls.name: not_unique_neighbor
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "For assume `h=1`; so `p₁` is the only neighbour of `x₁` in `P`."
The two complement arguments, 17.4, 15.7, and the final long prism contradict
this assumption.

links.rationale: Formalizes claim (5)'s case analysis: assuming h=1 (p1 the only path-neighbour of x1), the chain of complement-graph and 15.7/13.6 applications forces s=2, t0=1, and finally a long prism, contradicting InF5's exclusion of long prisms.

decls.name: contradiction
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "But then the three paths `p₁-x₁`, `x₂-z`, `p₂-⋯-p_d-y₁`
form a long prism, a contradiction."

links.rationale: Formalizes the closing sentence of claim (5)'s case h=1: the three named paths assemble into a long prism, which is impossible for a graph in F5, giving the desired contradiction.
Numeric consequence of P having odd length greater than 1: P has at least 4 vertices.

decls.name: last_complete_is_second
decls.docstring: The conclusion `j=2` in the paper, including its maximality clause.

links.rationale: Formalizes the conclusion j=2 (here: index 1, zero-based) reached in the middle of claim (4)'s proof: p2 is W-complete, and no later path vertex besides possibly p4 is.

decls.name: prefix_interior_wSet
decls.docstring: The interior of `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_{t₀}` is contained in `W`.

links.rationale: Every internal vertex of the antipath prefix x1,...,y_{t0} lies in W, connecting the antipath's interior to the set W used in claim (4).

decls.name: second_prefix_antihole
decls.docstring: PAPER: "Therefore `p₂-x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_{t₀}-p₂` is an antihole `D`."

links.rationale: Formalizes the construction of the antihole D=p2-x1-...-xs-y1-...-y_{t0}-p2, using that p2 is nonadjacent to both x1 and the missed vertex y_{t0}.

decls.name: HasNonneighborIn
decls.docstring: A vertex has a nonneighbour in a set.

links.rationale: Auxiliary predicate: a vertex has some nonneighbour inside a given set, used to state claim (2)'s conclusion about the unique vertex of X with a nonneighbour in Y.

decls.name: completePathEdges
decls.docstring: The set of complete edges counted on a path list.

links.rationale: Defines the set of A-complete edges counted on a path list, each unordered pair of path vertices counted once.

decls.name: Claim2Conclusion
decls.docstring: The conclusion of printed claim (2).

links.rationale: States the conclusion of printed claim (2) as a Prop: whenever deleting either of two vertices x1,x2 from X keeps it anticonnected, X and Y are disjoint and one of x1,x2 is the unique vertex of X with a nonneighbour in Y.

decls.name: disjoint_complete_of_not_anticonnected_union
decls.docstring:
If two anticonnected sets have a union that is not anticonnected, they are
disjoint and complete to each other.  This is the elementary first step of
claim (2), applied in the complement graph.

decls.name: claim2_bad_union
decls.docstring:
The first paragraph of claim (2): if deleting `xᵢ` makes the union with
`Y` non-anticonnected, then `xᵢ` is the unique vertex of `X` with a
nonneighbour in `Y`.

decls.name: odd_edges_after_delete
decls.docstring:
Removing one of the two non-cut vertices gives an odd complete-edge count.
Otherwise it would be a counterexample with the same path and a smaller union,
or with the same union and smaller total side size.

decls.name: claim2_line_argument
decls.docstring:
The remaining line argument in printed claim (2), after both
`(X\{xᵢ})∪Y` have been shown anticonnected and optimality has supplied the two
odd complete-edge counts.

PAPER: *"So we may assume that `(X\{xᵢ})∪Y` is anticonnected for
`i=1,2`. … This proves (2)."*

links.rationale: Formalizes the remaining line/antihole argument of claim (2), invoked after both (X\{xi})∪Y have been shown anticonnected and optimality has supplied the two odd complete-edge counts.

decls.name: claim2
decls.docstring:
**17.5, claim (2).**

PAPER: *"Suppose that `x₁,x₂ ∈ X` are distinct and such that
`X \ {xᵢ}` is anticonnected for `i=1,2`. Then `X ∩ Y = ∅`, and one of
`x₁,x₂` is the unique vertex of `X` with a nonneighbour in `Y`."*

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (2) in full: given two distinct vertices whose individual removal keeps X anticonnected, X and Y are disjoint and one of them is the unique X-vertex with a nonneighbour in Y.

decls.name: AntipathBlocks
decls.docstring:
The block form of printed claim (3).  The concatenation `qX ++ qY` is the
paper's antipath `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_t`; the two list vertex sets are exactly
`X` and `Y`, and both blocks contain at least two vertices.

links.rationale: The block form of printed claim (3): a structure recording the antipath x1,...,xs,y1,...,yt as two list blocks whose vertex sets are exactly X and Y, each of length at least two.

decls.name: claim3_from_symmetric_claim2
decls.docstring:
The structural part of claim (3), after claim (2) has been applied on both
sides using the `X,Y` symmetry.

PAPER: *"There is an antipath `x₁-⋯-x_s-y₁-⋯-y_t` such that
`s,t>1` and `X={x₁,…,x_s}`, and `Y={y₁,…,y_t}`."*

links.rationale: Internal step of claim (3): once claim (2) is available for both the counterexample and its X/Y-swap, extracts the antipath-block structure witnessing X={x1,...,xs}, Y={y1,...,yt}.

decls.name: claim3
decls.docstring:
**17.5, claim (3).**  Claim (1) makes the counterexample symmetric under
reversing its path and exchanging `X,Y`; claim (2) is therefore available on
both sides before the structural conclusion is invoked.

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (3) in full, obtaining it by applying claim (2) to both the original and the X/Y-swapped optimal counterexample (using the symmetry from claim (1)).

decls.name: FirstMissContext
decls.docstring:
The first vertex `y_{t₀}` in the second block missed by `p₁`.  Indices in
this structure are zero-based.

links.rationale: Records the first vertex y_{t0} of the Y-block nonadjacent to p1, together with the fact that every earlier y-vertex is adjacent to p1.

decls.name: W
decls.docstring:
The paper's set
`W=(X\{x₁})∪{y₁,…,y_{t₀-1}}`, using zero-based list operations.

links.rationale: Restates the paper's set W=(X\{x1})∪{y1,...,y_{t0-1}} in terms of the AntipathBlocks/FirstMissContext data, using zero-based list operations.

decls.name: exists_first_miss
decls.docstring:
The unnumbered choice immediately before claim (4): take the first vertex
of the `Y` block that is nonadjacent to `p₁`.

links.rationale: Existence lemma for the unnumbered choice just before claim (4): among the Y-block vertices there is a first one nonadjacent to p1, since p1 is not Y-complete.

decls.name: Claim4Conclusion
decls.docstring:
The exact universal parity assertion in printed claim (4), with a subpath
represented by its two inclusive indices in `c.core.p`.

links.rationale: States the universal parity conclusion of printed claim (4) as a Prop, with a subpath P' represented by its two inclusive endpoint indices in c.core.p.

decls.name: claim4
decls.docstring:
**17.5, claim (4).**

PAPER: *"For every subpath `P'` of `P`, if the ends of `P'` are
adjacent to `x₁`, then there are an even number of `W`-complete edges in
`P'`."*

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (4) in full: any subpath of P whose two ends are adjacent to x1 contains an even number of W-complete edges.

decls.name: LastNeighborContext
decls.docstring: The maximum-indexed neighbour of `x₁` on `P`.

links.rationale: Records the maximum-indexed path vertex adjacent to x1, i.e. the paper's h, together with its maximality.

decls.name: exists_last_neighbor
decls.docstring:
The unnumbered choice after claim (4): choose the last neighbour of `x₁`
on `P`.

links.rationale: Existence lemma for the unnumbered choice after claim (4): the finite set of path indices adjacent to x1 is nonempty (p1 is adjacent to x1), so it has a maximum, giving h.

decls.name: claim5

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (5), h>1 (here 0<h in zero-based indexing), by ruling out h=1 via the complement-graph/prism contradiction packaged in not_unique_neighbor.

decls.name: FinalSetup
decls.docstring:
The data used in the final invocation of 17.3.  The letters match the
statement of 17.3.  The last field says that every vertex in `T` does have a
neighbour in `F \ {a}`, which will contradict the vertex returned by 17.3.

links.rationale: Bundles the connected set F, anticonnected set T, and the four named vertices with all hypotheses needed for the closing application of 17.3; the hhit field records that every vertex of T has a neighbour in F\{a}, which will contradict 17.3's conclusion.

decls.name: final_setup
decls.docstring:
The final paragraph after claim (5), packaged up to the application of
17.3.

PAPER: *"The set `F={x₂,p_h,…,p_n}` is connected; the only neighbour of
`x₁` in `F` is `p_h`; the only neighbour of `z` in `F` is `x₂`. Since
`x₁,z` are `(X\{x₁,x₂})∪Y`-complete, and `p_h,x₂` are not, it follows from
17.2 that there is a vertex in `(X\{x₁,x₂})∪Y` with no neighbour in `F`
except possibly `x₂`. But every vertex in `(X\{x₁,x₂})∪Y` is adjacent to
either `p_j` or to `p_n`, a contradiction."*

The formal closing below uses 17.3, whose asymmetric conclusion is exactly
the "except possibly `x₂`" form needed here.

links.rationale: Formalizes the closing paragraph of the proof, constructing the connected set F={x2,ph,...,pn} and anticonnected set T=(X\{x1,x2})∪Y with the neighbour data needed for the final application of 17.3.

decls.name: finalSetup_absurd
decls.docstring:
Once the last paragraph has supplied `FinalSetup`, 17.3 gives the desired
contradiction.

links.rationale: Once FinalSetup's data is supplied, applies 17.3 to obtain a vertex of T with no neighbour in F except possibly one endpoint, then derives False from the FinalSetup.hhit field, which says every vertex of T does have such a neighbour.

decls.name: optimal_counterexample_absurd
decls.docstring:
An optimal counterexample is impossible.  This follows by invoking the
numbered claims in their printed order and then applying 17.3.

links.rationale: Assembles claims (1) through (5) and the closing application of 17.3 in their printed order to show that an optimal counterexample cannot exist, completing the proof of 17.5 by contradiction.

decls.name: mem_drop_iff
decls.docstring: Read a vertex of a suffix at its original index.

links.rationale: Technical list lemma: reads a vertex of a dropped suffix at its index in the original list.

decls.name: two_first
decls.docstring: The first block has the first two vertices named in the paper.

links.rationale: Names the first two vertices of the X-block as x1 and x2 (the latter used as the second vertex of the final prism configuration).

decls.name: blocks_disjoint
decls.docstring: Disjointness of the two blocks follows from the antipath having no repeated vertex.

links.rationale: X and Y are disjoint, since the antipath list qX++qY built from AntipathBlocks has no repeated vertex.

decls.name: tail_set
decls.docstring: Removing the first vertex leaves exactly the tail of the whole antipath.

links.rationale: Removing x1 from X and taking the union with Y gives exactly the tail of the whole antipath list qX++qY.

decls.name: W_set
decls.docstring: The paper's set `W` is an initial segment of the antipath with `x₁` deleted.

links.rationale: Rewrites the paper's set W as an initial segment (via drop/take) of the concatenated antipath list qX++qY with x1 removed.

decls.name: W_anticonnected
decls.docstring: Both sets used in the smaller counterexample are anticonnected.

links.rationale: Both W and W∪Y are anticonnected, since each is (up to reindexing) an initial or final segment of the induced antipath qX++qY.

decls.name: head_pair_facts
decls.docstring:
Deleting the first two vertices leaves an anticonnected set. The first
vertex is complete to this set, and the second is not.

links.rationale: From an antipath x1,x2,R, derives that the tail R is anticonnected, x1 is complete to R while x2 is not, and x1,x2 are nonadjacent and distinct from every vertex of R.

decls.name: second_missed
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "Choose `s₀` ... minimum such that `p_h` is nonadjacent to `x_{s₀}`.
So `p_j-x₁-...-x_{s₀}-p_h-p_j` is an antihole, and so `s₀` is even.
Hence `x₁-...-x_{s₀}-p_h-z` is an odd antipath ... by 13.6 it has length 3,
that is, `s₀=2`."

links.rationale: Formalizes the choice of s0 (the first x-block vertex nonadjacent to ph) and the antihole/antipath parity argument via 13.6 forcing s0=2, giving x2 (the second vertex of the X-block) as the vertex ph is nonadjacent to.

decls.name: odd_W_edges
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "From the optimality of `P,X,Y`, it follows that `P,W,Y` is not a
counterexample ... and so there are an odd number of `W`-complete edges in `P`."

links.rationale: Formalizes the optimality-based parity conclusion opening the paragraph after claim (4): the number of W-complete edges of P is odd, since P,W,Y is not itself a smaller counterexample.

decls.name: last_not_complete
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "From (5), since `p_h` is adjacent to `x₁`, it follows that `p_h`
is not complete to `X\{x₁}`."

links.rationale: Formalizes the deduction from claim (5) that ph, being adjacent to x1, cannot be X-complete and hence is not complete to X\{x1} either.

decls.name: later_complete
decls.docstring:
PAPER: "There are an odd number [of `W`-complete edges] in the path
`p_h-...-p_n` ... Choose `i,j` ... Hence `j>i`."  Only the later complete
vertex is needed below. Since `p_h` is not complete, its index exceeds `h+1`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the choice of the later W-complete vertex pj (with j strictly after h+1), used to set up the final 2.2 parity argument bounding i-h.

decls.name: EvenRRConfig
decls.docstring:
A counterexample to the parity conclusion of 17.5, with `G`, `X`, `Y`, and
`z` held fixed.

links.rationale: Bundles a counterexample's path data and even complete-edge-count hypothesis, with G, X, Y, z held fixed, used to state and prove printed claim (1).

decls.name: shortest_first_unique
decls.docstring:
Printed claim (1) of 17.5.  The construction of the antipath needed for
17.4 is valid even when `X` and `Y` overlap: take the first `Y`-vertex on an
antipath from the last path vertex into `Y`.

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (1): in a path-length-minimal counterexample, no vertex of P other than p1 is X-complete, using 17.4 to rule out pn-1, then 2.2/2.3 parity and minimality to rule out every other candidate index.

decls.name: Counterexample
decls.docstring:
A full counterexample to 17.5 with the graph and the external vertex held
fixed.  The path data and the even edge count are in `EvenRRConfig`.

links.rationale: Bundles the two anticonnected sets X, Y with an EvenRRConfig core and the remaining hypotheses (anticonnected union, z outside and complete to X∪Y) into a single counterexample structure, with G and z held fixed.

decls.name: IsOptimal
decls.docstring:
The three lexicographic minimality clauses called the optimality of
`P,X,Y` in the paper.  Cardinal minimality is enough for every proper-subset
comparison made in the proof because the vertex type is finite.

links.rationale: Formalizes the paper's named notion of the 'optimality' of P,X,Y as the three lexicographic minimality clauses (path length, then |X∪Y|, then |X|+|Y|); since the vertex type is finite, cardinal minimality suffices for every proper-subset comparison the proof makes.

decls.name: exists_optimal
decls.docstring:
A counterexample has an optimal representative in the order used in the
first paragraph of the proof of 17.5.

links.rationale: Well-ordering argument realizing the paper's 'if possible choose a counterexample P,X,Y such that...': among all counterexamples, one achieving the lexicographically minimal (path length, |X∪Y|, |X|+|Y|) triple exists.

decls.name: first_unique_of_optimal
decls.docstring:
Printed claim (1) for the globally optimal counterexample: its first path
vertex is its only vertex complete to the first side.

links.rationale: Specializes claim (1)'s conclusion (shortest_first_unique) to a globally optimal counterexample, using that optimality in particular implies path-length minimality.

decls.name: swapCounterexample
decls.docstring:
The reversed counterexample with the two anticonnected sides exchanged.
This is the paper's sentence *"In view of (1), there is symmetry between `X`
and `Y`."*

links.rationale: Formalizes the X/Y symmetry noted right after claim (1): reversing the path and exchanging X and Y produces another counterexample, since its Y-complete edge set is empty (pₙ was the unique Y-complete path vertex before reversal, so becomes the unique X-complete one after).

decls.name: swap_isOptimal
decls.docstring:
Reversal and exchanging the two sides preserve the three optimality
measures.

links.rationale: The reversed, X/Y-swapped counterexample preserves all three optimality measures (path length, |X∪Y|, |X|+|Y|) of the original, so optimality transfers across the symmetry.

The Lean formalization of statement 18.1 itself (a source-exact local restatement used by the 18.5 proof): for G in F7 with X, Y disjoint nonempty anticonnected sets complete to each other and a track p1-...-p5 outside X union Y, induced except possibly for the edge p2p5, with X complete to p1, p5 but not to p2, p3, p4, if p1, p3, p4 are all Y-complete then so is p2 or p5. The proof exhibits, via 17.1, a reflection of the triangle {p1,p3,p5} and derives an odd wheel on Y when both p2 and p5 fail to be Y-complete.

decls.name: dropLast_getLast?_eq
decls.docstring: The last vertex of `p.dropLast` is `p[p.length - 2]`.

links.rationale: Pure list-indexing fact: for a list p of length at least 2, the last element of p.dropLast is p[p.length - 2] -- pins down the paper's p_{n-1} as a list index. No single paper sentence corresponds to this bookkeeping step.

decls.name: dropLast_dropLast_getLast?_eq
decls.docstring: The last vertex of `p.dropLast.dropLast` is `p[p.length - 3]`.

links.rationale: Pure list-indexing fact: for a list p of length at least 3, the last element of p.dropLast.dropLast is p[p.length - 3] -- pins down the paper's p_{n-2} as a list index. No single paper sentence corresponds to this bookkeeping step.

decls.name: getElem_mem_take
decls.docstring: Membership of `p[i]` in the prefix `p.take (m + 1)` when `i ≤ m`.

links.rationale: Routine list fact: if i <= m then p[i] lies in the prefix p.take (m + 1). Pure bookkeeping with no paper sentence of its own.

decls.name: xed_eq_take
decls.docstring:
Truncating `p` at its last `X`-complete vertex does not change the set of
`X`-complete edges.

links.rationale: Shows that truncating a path p at its last X-complete vertex leaves the set of X-complete edges of p unchanged -- the silent step that lets 18.2's printed proof read "an even number of its edges are X-complete" off the initial segment p1-...-pi rather than off the whole path P. Infrastructure the proof relies on implicitly, not a quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_max_complete_index
decls.docstring:
**"Choose an `X`-complete vertex `pᵢ` in `P` with `i` maximum."**  Stated with
0-based indices, so the paper's `i` is `m + 1`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the opening move of 18.2's printed proof: since p1 is X-complete, the finite set of indices of X-complete vertices of P is nonempty and so has a maximum m, giving the paper's index i = m + 1 under this file's 0-based indexing.

decls.name: slice_infix
decls.docstring: Every stretch of `p` is a contiguous block of `p`.

decls.name: infix_eq_slice
decls.docstring: A contiguous block of `p` is a stretch `pᵢ-⋯-pⱼ` of it.

decls.name: getElem_congr_idx
decls.docstring:
Transporting an index equality through `List.getElem` without asking `rw` to construct a
dependent motive.

decls.name: not_unique_YComplete
decls.docstring:
If every `Y`-complete vertex of `P` is one fixed vertex `z`, then `P` has at most one
`Y`-complete vertex — contrary to 18.3's hypothesis.

links.rationale: Cardinality helper: if every Y-complete vertex of p equals one fixed vertex z, then p has at most one Y-complete vertex -- contradicting 18.3's hypothesis that at least two vertices of P are Y-complete. Used repeatedly to rule out degenerate placements of the line's endpoints.

decls.name: line_parity
decls.docstring:
**18.3, second conclusion** (repaired; see `FIXES.md` §F7).

*"let `P'` be a maximal subpath of `P` such that none of its internal vertices are `Y`-complete
[and of length `≥ 2`].  Then the length of `P'` has the same parity as the number of ends of
`P'` that belong to `{p₁,pₙ}` and are not `Y`-complete."*

links.rationale: Formalizes 18.3's second conclusion on its own: for a maximal subpath (line) q of P of length at least 2 with no Y-complete internal vertex, the parity of q's length equals the number of q's two ends that lie in {p1, pn} and are not Y-complete. Assembled here from the even case (both ends Y-complete, Thm183LineEvenCase) and the odd case (one end not Y-complete, Thm183LineOddCase / Thm183Lines), including the bookkeeping the printed proof performs silently: identifying a line as a contiguous stretch p_i-...-p_j of P, and showing a non-Y-complete end must be p1 or pn by maximality.

decls.name: thm_18_3_full
decls.docstring:
**18.3**, in exactly the shape of the frozen
`Workspace.Statements.S18.SPGT.thm_18_3` (repaired second conjunct; `FIXES.md` §F7).

links.rationale: The complete Lean formalization of statement 18.3, assembling all three of its conclusions -- P has even length; a line's length parity; the Y-complete-edge-count parity of P -- into exactly the hypothesis/conclusion shape of the frozen Workspace.Statements.S18.SPGT.thm_18_3.

decls.name: YEdgeIdx
decls.docstring:
The set of indices `k` such that the `k`-th and `(k+1)`-st vertices of `p` both exist and
are `Y`-complete.  This is the paper's *"`Y`-complete edge of `P`"*, read off positionally.

links.rationale: Definition: the set of indices k such that the consecutive vertices p[k], p[k+1] both exist and are Y-complete -- the paper's notion of a 'Y-complete edge of P', read off positionally. A bookkeeping redefinition, not itself a paper claim.

decls.name: yEdges_ncard_eq_index_ncard
decls.docstring:
**The `Y`-complete edges of an induced path are exactly its `Y`-complete consecutive
pairs.**  Two vertices of an induced path are adjacent iff their positions differ by one, so
`k ↦ s(pₖ, pₖ₊₁)` is a bijection from `YEdgeIdx` onto the edge set counted by 18.3.

links.rationale: Bridging lemma: on an induced path, two vertices are adjacent exactly when their positions differ by one, so the Y-complete edges of P correspond bijectively to the Y-complete consecutive index pairs. A step the paper's counting argument relies on silently rather than stating.

decls.name: ends_YComplete_ncard
decls.docstring:
*"the number of elements of `{p₁, pₙ}` that are `Y`-complete"*, evaluated.

`VertexComplete` is not decidable, so the two `if`s are elaborated with
`Classical.propDecidable`; downstream callers should discharge any instance mismatch with
`split_ifs` (or `Subsingleton.elim`) rather than by trying to match the instance.

links.rationale: Routine evaluation of the cardinality of {w in {p1, pn} : w is Y-complete} as a sum of two indicator terms. Mechanical arithmetic used to match the shape of 18.3's third conclusion; not a distinct paper sentence.

decls.name: even_pathLength_of_ends_only_XComplete
decls.docstring:
**18.3, first conclusion.**  *"Since `P` is a path of length ≥ 4, and its ends are
`X`-complete and its internal vertices are not, it follows that `P` has even length, by 13.6."*

`hXuniq` is 18.3's hypothesis *"`p₁, pₙ` are the only `X`-complete vertices of `P`"*, and
`hpX` is the half of *"`P` is a path of `G \ (X ∪ Y)`"* that this argument needs.

links.rationale: Formalizes 18.3's first conclusion together with its one-sentence proof: since P is an induced path of length at least 4 whose ends alone are X-complete, 13.6 forces P to have even length -- an odd such path would need either an X-complete edge (impossible, since that would force p1 and pn adjacent) or length exactly 3 (impossible, since n >= 5 gives length >= 4).

decls.name: yFrom
decls.docstring: The number of `Y`-complete edges `{k, k+1}` with `i ≤ k < N - 1`.

decls.name: zL
decls.docstring:
Left boundary correction: `1` exactly when `i` is the left end of the path and that end
is not `Y`-complete.

decls.name: zR
decls.docstring:
Right boundary correction: `1` exactly when `i` is not itself the right end of the path
and that right end is not `Y`-complete.

decls.name: split_count
decls.docstring: Splitting the edge count at an intermediate index.

decls.name: near_count
decls.docstring:
Inside a line there is at most one `Y`-complete edge, and there is one exactly when the
line has length `1` and both its ends are `Y`-complete.

decls.name: key
decls.docstring:
The induction from the right along the T-points.  The extra argument `m` is fuel: it lets
the induction be an ordinary `Nat` induction on an upper bound for `N - 1 - i`.

links.rationale: Pure-arithmetic skeleton of 18.3's closing counting paragraph, abstracted away from graph theory entirely: given indices 0..N-1 with N >= 5, an even total length N-1, a marker predicate c with at least two true indices, and the three parity facts about 'lines' (maximal runs between consecutive marked-or-boundary indices), the number of consecutive marked index pairs has the same parity as the number of the two ends 0, N-1 that are marked. Consumed by Thm183Lines.yEdges_parity, which supplies the graph-theoretic facts about P, X, Y as the three hypotheses.

decls.name: endgame
decls.docstring:
The last three printed sentences of Case A, parameterised by the witness vertex `z`
(which is `p₁` or `pₙ`, per the printed symmetry):

*"Since `pᵢ₊₁, pᵢ₊₂` are not `X`-complete, they are joined by an antipath `Q'` with interior in
`X`.  Since `Q ∪ Q'` is an antihole it follows that `Q'` is odd.  But then
`p₁-pᵢ₊₁-Q'-pᵢ₊₂-p₁` is an odd antihole, a contradiction."*

decls.name: line_even_of_both_ends_YComplete
decls.docstring:
**18.3, "Case A"**: *"So in this case `P'` has even length."*

`P'` is the stretch `pᵢ-⋯-pⱼ` of `P`, of length `j - i ≥ 2`, whose two ends are `Y`-complete
and none of whose internal vertices is.

links.rationale: Formalizes 18.3's proof Case A: a line (a maximal subpath of P none of whose internal vertices is Y-complete) of length at least 2 whose two ends are both Y-complete must itself have even length. Proved by contradiction: an odd such line would force, via 13.6, length exactly 3 and an odd antipath between its two interior vertices with interior in Y, which together with an X-interior antipath to p1 or pn (by symmetry) completes to an odd antihole.

decls.name: line_odd_of_last_end_not_YComplete
decls.docstring:
**18.3, "Case B"**: *"Consequently `P'` is odd, as required."*

`P'` is the line from `p[a]` (the paper's `pᵢ`, the last `Y`-complete vertex of `P`) to the
last vertex `pₙ` of `P`, which is not `Y`-complete.  Its length `p.length - 1 - a` is odd.

links.rationale: Formalizes 18.3's proof Case B for the pn-ended instance singled out by the paper's symmetry remark: the line running from the last Y-complete vertex p[a] to the non-Y-complete end pn has odd length. Proved by contradiction: an even such line would, via 13.7, have length exactly 2, i.e. a = n-2, and yield two even antipaths (p_{n-2}p_{n-1} with interior in X, completed through p1; p_{n-1}p_n with interior in Y, completed through an earlier Y-complete vertex), contradicting 13.7's exclusive parity conclusion.

decls.name: YIdx
decls.docstring: *"`pₖ` is `Y`-complete"*, read off positionally.  Out of range it is false.

links.rationale: Definition: 'p[k] is Y-complete', read off positionally (false when k is out of range). A bookkeeping restatement of Y-completeness as an index predicate, not itself a paper claim.
Trivial unfolding lemma relating the index predicate YIdx to VertexComplete at an in-range index. Pure bookkeeping.

decls.name: getElem_rev
decls.docstring:
*"`pₖ` is `Y`-complete"*, read off positionally.  Out of range it is false. -/
def YIdx (G : SimpleGraph V) (Y : Set V) (p : List V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : k < p.length, VertexComplete G (p[k]'h) Y

theorem yIdx_iff {G : SimpleGraph V} {Y : Set V} {p : List V} {k : ℕ} (hk : k < p.length) :
    YIdx G Y p k ↔ VertexComplete G (p[k]'hk) Y :=
  ⟨fun h => h.2, fun h => ⟨hk, h⟩⟩

decls.name: second_witness
decls.docstring:
If every index at which `c` holds equals a single index `m`, then `c` holds at most once —
contradicting *"at least two vertices of `P` are `Y`-complete"*.

decls.name: yEdges_parity
decls.docstring:
**18.3, third conclusion.**  *"the number of `Y`-complete edges of `P` has the same parity
as the number of elements of `{p₁, pₙ}` that are `Y`-complete."*

Stated in exactly the shape of the third conjunct of the frozen

`Thm183EvenLength`) and `h2` is *"Assume that at least two vertices of `P` are

links.rationale: Formalizes 18.3's third conclusion on its own: the number of Y-complete edges of P has the same parity as the number of elements of {p1, pn} that are Y-complete. Obtained by feeding the graph-theoretic facts about lines -- Case A/B here, with the p1-side case supplied by line_odd_of_first_end_not_YComplete -- into the pure-arithmetic engine Thm183LineCounting.yEdge_parity.

decls.name: EvenRRConfig
decls.docstring:
A path counterexample to the parity conclusion of 17.5, with the two
anticonnected sides and the external complete/anticomplete vertex held fixed.
Packaging this predicate makes the paper's first, path-length minimality clause
usable without hiding any hypothesis.

links.rationale: Bundles the hypotheses of a hypothetical shortest even-length counterexample used inside claim (6) of 18.5's proof: a path with X-complete first vertex, unique Y-complete last vertex, avoiding X, Y and a fixed external vertex z, with an even number of X-complete edges; a data-packaging structure with no single paper sentence of its own.

decls.name: minimal_config_first_unique
decls.docstring:
Claim (1) in the proof of 17.5, specialized to the disjoint one-vertex
extension setting needed by 18.5.  In a shortest even counterexample the first
path vertex is its only `X`-complete vertex.

The distinguished `y₀ ∈ Y` which is not `X`-complete supplies the antipath
needed by 17.4.  In the application it is the adjoined vertex `v`.

links.rationale: Reproves, in the specialized one-vertex-extension setting needed for claim (6) of 18.5, the first structural claim of Theorem 17.5's own proof: in a shortest counterexample path with an even number of X-complete edges, the only X-complete vertex is the path's first vertex.

decls.name: singleton_first_side_absurd
decls.docstring:
The singleton first-side case in claim (3) of the source proof of 17.5.
After minimizing the path and applying `minimal_config_first_unique`, prefixing
the path by `z-a` gives a long odd path between `Y`-complete vertices with no
`Y`-complete internal vertex, contrary to 13.6.

links.rationale: Reproves, in the same specialized setting, the singleton-side case of Theorem 17.5's own proof: prefixing the minimal counterexample path by z-a yields a long odd path between Y-complete ends with no Y-complete interior vertex, contradicting Theorem 13.6.

decls.name: singleton_sides_absurd
decls.docstring:
The smallest cut-vertex instance is already ruled out by triangle catching.
This is the base case for a direct proof of the one-vertex extension bridge.

links.rationale: Rules out the smallest cut-vertex instance of the one-vertex extension bridge directly via triangle catching (Theorem 17.1), as an alternative base case for a future direct proof of claim (6)'s invocation of Theorem 17.5; not reachable from the main theorem in the compiled dependency graph.

decls.name: even_complete_edges_absurd
decls.docstring:
The exact one-sided triple-RR contradiction used in claim (6) of 18.5.

At present the short proof below records that this is precisely the indicated
specialization of 17.5.  The deliberately stronger `A`/`B`/`v` interface is the
standalone target for replacing that last dependency by the source proof.

links.rationale: Formalizes the concluding contradiction of claim (6) of 18.5's proof: a path with an even number of X-complete edges whose Y-complete vertex pa and unique X∪{v}-complete vertex pn would force an odd count by Theorem 17.5, so the parity mismatch is absurd.

Extracts, for a given index window [a,b] of the path P, the corresponding subpath together with proofs that it contains every neighbour of v in P, has no Y-complete vertex in its interior, and satisfies the X-complete endpoint alternative; the single index-window construction underlying every 'the theorem/claim holds' exit used throughout 18.5's proof.

Generic Finset.min'/Finset.max' extraction producing simultaneous minimal and maximal witnesses of a decidable predicate on a range, used to instantiate the index pairs (h,k) and (i,j) chosen at the start of 18.5's proof.
Formalizes the opening parenthetical of 18.5's proof in its degenerate form: when v has no neighbour at all on the path P (so no h, k as in exists_minmax_index exist), the theorem holds trivially.
Purely technical bridge lemma converting a List infix witness into the drop/take slice representation used by the path-manipulation lemmas elsewhere in this file; no paper counterpart.
Purely technical converse bridge lemma showing every drop/take slice of a list is an infix of it; no paper counterpart.

Bundles the structural facts about an optimal pseudowheel P needed throughout 18.5's proof — that P is a path of length at least 7 with even total length, that its X-complete vertices are exactly its two ends, and that it carries at least one Y-complete internal vertex — derived by citing 18.3 and 18.4; a data-packaging convenience shared by the proof's terminal claims rather than a single printed sentence.

decls.name: claim2_witness
decls.docstring:
The positive half of printed claim `(2)` of 18.5: *"If `v` has a neighbour in this set then
the claim holds"*.

Given an index window `[a,b]` of the path `P` whose two ends are, in one order or the other, a
neighbour `P[t]` of `v` and a `Y`-complete vertex `P[r]`, and inside which `P[t]` is the *only*
neighbour of `v` and `P[r]` the *only* `Y`-complete vertex, the path `Q = v-P[t]-⋯-P[r]` is
exactly the object claim `(2)` asks for.  Callers obtain such a window by taking `r` the nearest
`Y`-complete index to a neighbour of `v` and then `t` the nearest neighbour index to `r`, both
searches staying inside the printed range `{p_{i+1}, …, p_{j-1}}`.

links.rationale: Generic constructor building, from an index window [a,b] containing exactly one neighbour of v and exactly one Y-complete vertex at its two ends, the path Q from v to that Y-complete vertex demanded by the positive branch of claim (2); instantiated by claim2_of_neighbour with the nearest such witnesses.

decls.name: window_after
decls.docstring:
The *"for otherwise the conclusion holds"* exit used when every neighbour of `v` in `P` has
index `≥ c` and no `P[t]` with `t > c` is `Y`-complete: take `P' = p_{c+1}-⋯-p_n`.  In printed
claim `(2)` this is *"We may assume `v` has a neighbour in `{p_1, …, p_i}`, for otherwise the
conclusion holds"*, with `c = j`; the `X`-complete clause is free because `p_n ∈ V(P')`.

links.rationale: Formalizes the 'for otherwise the theorem holds' exit in claim (2)'s proof: if every neighbour of v has index at least c and no vertex past index c is Y-complete, the tail subpath p_{c+1}-⋯-p_n already satisfies the theorem's conclusion.

decls.name: window_le
decls.docstring:
The *"then the conclusion holds"* exit used when `v` is **not** `X`-complete and every
neighbour of `v` in `P` has index `≤ c`, no `P[t]` with `1 ≤ t < c` being `Y`-complete: take
`P' = p_{a+1}-⋯-p_{c+1}` where `a` is the least neighbour index.  In printed claim `(2)` this is
*"So `v` has no neighbours in `{p_j, …, p_n}`, and hence `k ≤ i`.  We may therefore assume that
`v` is `X`-complete"*, with `c = i`.  The degenerate case *"(If this is impossible then the
conclusion holds.)"* — `v` has no neighbour in `P` at all — is folded in.

links.rationale: Formalizes the complementary trivial exit of claim (2)'s proof at the point where v is shown to have no neighbours past index i: when v is additionally not X-complete, the initial subpath up to the last neighbour of v already satisfies the theorem's conclusion, which is why the proof may thereafter assume v is X-complete.

decls.name: hole_from_two_neighbours
decls.docstring:
*"Then there is a hole `C` containing `v`, with `C \ v ⊆ P`"* (printed claim `(2)`).

`P[a]` and `P[b]` are neighbours of `v` with no neighbour of `v` strictly between them, so
`v-p_{a+1}-⋯-p_{b+1}-v` closes up.  Callers take `a` the **largest** neighbour index `≤ i` and
`b` the **smallest** neighbour index `≥ j`, which makes the hypothesis `hmid` exactly *"`v` has
no neighbour in `{p_{i+1}, …, p_{j-1}}`"* plus the two extremality choices; the resulting hole
contains `p_i-⋯-p_j`, as the printed proof needs.

links.rationale: Formalizes the hole-construction step in claim (2)'s proof: two neighbours P[a], P[b] of v with no neighbour of v strictly between them close up with v into a hole containing the subpath between them.

decls.name: claim2_of_neighbour
decls.docstring:
Printed claim `(2)` of 18.5, positive branch: *"there is a `Y`-complete vertex in
`{p_{i+1}, …, p_{j-1}}`.  If `v` has a neighbour in this set then the claim holds"*.

`P[t]` is the neighbour of `v` and `P[s]` the `Y`-complete vertex, both with index strictly
between `i` and `j`; the conclusion is exactly the positive branch of printed claim `(2)`.  The `Q` produced
runs from `v` to the `Y`-complete vertex nearest to `P[t]` on the `P[s]` side, entered at the
neighbour of `v` nearest to that vertex — so `v` has exactly one neighbour on `Q \ v` and `Q`
carries exactly one `Y`-complete vertex, its far end.

links.rationale: Formalizes the positive branch of claim (2): given a neighbour of v and a Y-complete vertex both strictly between indices i and j, constructs the path Q from v to the nearest such Y-complete vertex that the claim demands.

decls.name: claim1
decls.docstring:
**Printed claim `(1)` of the proof of 18.5** (`paper/proofs/18_5.md`, published p. 111):

> *"(1) If `v` is both adjacent to `p₁` and `X`-complete then the conclusion holds.*
>
> *For from the optimality of `(X, Y, P)` it follows that `(X, Y ∪ {v}, P)` is not a
> pseudowheel, and so `p₁` is the only `Y ∪ {v}`-complete vertex in `P`.  By 2.11 (with
> `X, Y` replaced by `Y ∪ {v}, X`) we deduce that either there exists `y ∈ Y ∪ {v}`
> nonadjacent to all `p₂, …, p_n`, or there exist nonadjacent `y₁, y₂ ∈ Y ∪ {v}` such that
> `y₁-p₂-⋯-p_n-y₂` is a path.  But `p_i` is `Y`-complete and `3 ≤ i ≤ n − 1`, so the second
> statement does not hold; and the first holds only if `y = v`.  This proves (1)."*

*"the conclusion holds"* is the conclusion of 18.5 itself, i.e. exactly the conclusion of
`Thm185Claim3.claim3` / of the negative branch of printed claim `(2)` — so a caller in the `X`-complete
branch closes with `exact claim1 …` (or `exact Or.inl (claim1 …)` against the
disjunction of printed claim `(2)`).

The hypothesis prefix is the one shared by `Thm185Claim3.claim3`, `Thm185Claim4.claim4` and
`Thm185Final.finalCase`; the two extra hypotheses `hadj`, `hvX` are the printed
*"both adjacent to `p₁` and `X`-complete"*.  The indices `i, j` of the opening paragraph are
**not** parameters: the printed proof re-chooses them internally (*"but `p_i` is `Y`-complete
and `3 ≤ i ≤ n − 1`"*), and they are recoverable from `hopt` through `setup` and
`exists_minmax_index`.

links.rationale: Formalizes printed claim (1) of 18.5's proof: if v is adjacent to p1 and X-complete then the theorem's conclusion holds, established via Theorem 2.11 applied with X, Y replaced by Y∪{v}, X.

This is the Lean formalization of Theorem 18.5 itself: given an optimal pseudowheel (X, Y, P) in G ∈ F7 and a vertex v outside X∪Y∪V(P) that is not Y-complete, there is a subpath P' of P containing every neighbour of v, with no Y-complete interior vertex, and (when v is X-complete) equal to {p1} or reaching pn; proved by case-splitting on whether v is X-complete or adjacent to p1.

In the setting of 18.6's minimal-counterexample argument, shows a counterexample set F cannot have fewer than two vertices by reducing the case |F| ≤ 1 to the single-vertex statement 18.5 (via singleton_good) and the empty case directly; formalizes the sentence 'From 18.5 |F| ≥ 2' in 18.6's proof, but is not reachable from the main theorem in the compiled dependency graph.

decls.name: exists_antipath_to_Y_with_interior_in_X
decls.docstring:
The antipath implicitly chosen before the application of 17.4 in the proof
of 17.5.  If `u` is outside `X ∪ Y`, complete to the nonempty set `Y`, but not
complete to `X`, anticonnectivity of `X ∪ Y` supplies an antipath from `u` to a
vertex of `Y` whose interior lies in `X`.  Choosing the first `Y`-vertex on an
induced antipath is the small point hidden by the paper's notation.

links.rationale: Constructs, for a vertex u outside X∪Y that is Y-complete but not X-complete, an induced antipath from u to some y ∈ Y whose interior lies entirely in X and is nonempty; this is the antipath implicitly chosen before invoking Theorem 17.4 inside the proof of Theorem 17.5, reused here for 18.5's invocations of 17.5.

decls.name: penultimate_not_complete
decls.docstring:
If the last end of a path and a vertex of the other anticonnected side are
adjacent, but both miss the first side, 17.4 says that the penultimate path
vertex cannot be complete to the first side.

links.rationale: Shows the penultimate vertex of a path cannot be X-complete when the path's last vertex pn is adjacent to some y ∈ Y that has a nonneighbour in X, by supplying Theorem 17.4 with an induced antipath from pn to y whose interior lies in X.

decls.name: penultimate_not_adj_of_two_edge_antipath
decls.docstring:
The literal antipath `pₙ-v-y` makes the first interior vertex in 17.4
equal to `v`, so its conclusion is the desired nonadjacency to `v`.

links.rationale: Given the two-edge antipath pn-v-y with v ∈ X and y ∈ Y, shows the penultimate path vertex cannot be adjacent to v, by feeding Theorem 17.4 this antipath, whose sole interior vertex is v.

decls.name: odd_complete_edges_of_complete_ends
decls.docstring:
The parity consequence of 2.2--2.3 used in the first minimality step of
17.5.  The exceptional conclusion of 2.3 says that the two ends are the only
`X`-complete vertices of the ambient path.  If they are adjacent, the complete
edge set is a singleton; if they are nonadjacent, 2.2 contradicts the external
`X`-complete vertex which is anticomplete to the path.

links.rationale: The parity consequence of Theorems 2.2 and 2.3 used in the first minimality step of Theorem 17.5's proof: if the two ends of an odd-length path are the path's only X-complete vertices, the set of X-complete edges of the path has odd cardinality.

decls.name: max_complete_index_even_of_even_edges
decls.docstring:
If the total number of `X`-complete edges is even, then the last
`X`-complete vertex has even zero-based index.  Otherwise its initial segment
has odd length and the preceding lemma makes that same edge set odd.

links.rationale: Shows the zero-based index of the last X-complete vertex on a path must be even whenever the total number of X-complete edges is even, by reducing to odd_complete_edges_of_complete_ends on the initial segment when the index would otherwise be odd.

decls.name: no_even_unique_ends
decls.docstring:
A positive even path cannot have its two ends as the unique complete
vertices for two disjoint complete anticonnected sets when a common complete
vertex is anticomplete to the path.  Indeed, 13.7 reduces the path to three
vertices and supplies an odd antipath through one of the two sets; the common
vertex makes both relevant pairs balanced by 2.6.

links.rationale: Rules out a positive even-length path whose two ends are the unique complete vertices for two disjoint complete anticonnected sets A, B, given a vertex anticomplete to the path but complete to A∪B, via Theorem 13.7's trichotomy and the balanced pairs supplied by Theorem 2.6; not reachable from the main theorem in the compiled dependency graph.

decls.name: odd_of_unique_ends
decls.docstring:
Parity form of `no_even_unique_ends`: a positive path with unique complete
ends for the two sides has odd length.

links.rationale: Parity restatement of no_even_unique_ends: under the same hypotheses, a positive-length path with unique complete ends for the two sides must have odd length; not reachable from the main theorem in the compiled dependency graph.

decls.name: thm_18_6_full
decls.docstring:
**18.6**, in exactly the shape of the frozen
`Workspace.Statements.S18.SPGT.thm_18_6`.

links.rationale: This is the Lean formalization of Theorem 18.6 itself: given an optimal pseudowheel (X, Y, P) in G ∈ F7 and a connected F disjoint from X∪Y∪V(P) with no Y-complete vertex, there is a subpath P' of P containing all attachments of F, with no Y-complete interior vertex, and (when some vertex of F is X-complete) equal to {p1} or reaching pn; proved by contradiction via a minimal counterexample, claim (2), and the closing paragraph's parity contradiction.
