decls.name: exists_uPath
decls.docstring:
The opening sentence of the proof: the minimal subpath exists.  `uₙ` has a neighbour in `A_t`
because the tail `T` ends in `V(C) \ {z, x₀, x₁} ⊆ A₀ ⊆ A_t`, and a *minimal* such initial segment
exists by well-ordering; `uₙ` is then `X_t`-complete by the maximality of `A_t` (otherwise `A_t`
could be enlarged by `uₙ`), and no `uᵢ` is `Y`-complete because they are internal vertices of the
tail `T`.

links.rationale: Constructs the minimal subpath y-u_1-⋯-u_n of T \ z used throughout 22.4's proof (p. 137): un is the first vertex with a neighbour in A_t, whose X_t-completeness (and hence X_1-completeness) follows from the maximality of A_t.

decls.name: uPath_length_even
decls.docstring:
**(2)** PAPER: *"We may assume that `Q` has even length `≥ 4`, and so `n` is even."*

`Q` is the path `z-y-u₁-⋯-uₙ-P-p`, whose ends are `Y`-complete and none of whose internal
vertices is; by (1) `P` is odd, so the parity of `Q` determines the parity of `n`.  The length-3
case is excluded because it makes `u₁` a kite for `(C, Y)`, and 13.6 excludes every other odd
length.

links.rationale: Proves claim (2) of the printed proof of 22.4 (p. 137): Q has even length ≥ 4, so n is even.

decls.name: xt1_adj_dropLast
decls.docstring:
**(3)** PAPER: *"`x_{t+1}` is adjacent to one of `u₁,…,u_{n−1}`."*

Otherwise a path `N` from `x_{t+1}` to `uₙ` with interior in `A_t` closes the hole
`z-y-u₁-⋯-uₙ-N-x_{t+1}-z`; since `n` is even, `N` is even, so `z-x_{t+1}-N-uₙ` is an odd path whose
ends are `X_t`-complete and whose internal vertices are not, while the `X_t`-complete vertex `y`
has no neighbour in its interior — contrary to 2.2.

links.rationale: Proves claim (3) of the printed proof of 22.4 (p. 137): x_{t+1} is adjacent to one of u_1,…,u_{n-1}.

decls.name: no_dropLast_Xt_complete
decls.docstring:
**(7)** PAPER: *"None of `u₁,…,u_{n−1}` is `X_t`-complete."*

Otherwise a path `S` from `x_{t+1}` to the first such vertex `s`, together with the path `R` of
(5) from `x_{t+1}` to a `Y`-complete vertex `r ∈ A_t`, is pushed through 2.2 and 13.7 to force
both `R` and `S` to have length 1; then every `Y`-complete vertex is adjacent to one of
`x_{t+1}, s`, which makes `x_{t+1}` have two adjacent neighbours in `C` of opposite wheel-parity
and at least one other neighbour in `C` — contrary to 16.1, since `x_{t+1}` is not a kite and the
wheel is optimal.

links.rationale: Proves claim (7) of the printed proof of 22.4 (p. 138): none of u_1,…,u_{n-1} is X_t-complete.

decls.name: endgame
decls.docstring:
The final paragraph.  PAPER: *"By (3) we may choose `i` with `1 ≤ i ≤ n−1` minimum such that
`x_{t+1}` is adjacent to `uᵢ`.  By (7), the only `X_t`-complete vertices in the hole
`z-y-u₁-⋯-uᵢ-x_{t+1}-z` are `z, y`, and therefore by (6) this hole has length `≥ 6`.  By 2.10 `X_t`
contains a leap or a hat.  If it contains a leap, … this contradicts 13.6.  So there is a hat,
that is, there exists `x ∈ X_t` with no neighbours in `{u₁,…,uᵢ,x_{t+1}}`.  Then
`A_t ∪ {u₁,…,uₙ,x_{t+1}}` (`= F` say) catches the triangle `{z, y, x}`; … and so `F` contains no
reflection of the triangle.  This contradicts 17.1, and therefore proves 22.4."*

links.rationale: Carries out the endgame of 22.4's proof (p. 138): the least index i with x_{t+1} adjacent to u_i gives a hole of length ≥ 6 whose X_t-leap/hat trichotomy (2.10) is resolved by 13.6 and 17.1, proving 22.4.

decls.name: exists_anticomponent
decls.docstring: Every vertex lies in an anticomponent of `V(G)` — a maximal anticonnected set.

decls.name: no_four_cycle
decls.docstring: A hole of length `≥ 6` contains no four-cycle.

decls.name: exists_path_interior_in
decls.docstring:
The paper's *"there is a path `P` in `G` joining them such that none of its interior
vertices is in …"*: the `G`-analogue of `InducedPathExtraction.exists_antipath_interior_in`.

decls.name: end_adj_interior
decls.docstring: One end of a path with at least three vertices has a neighbour in the interior.

decls.name: exists_interior_set
decls.docstring:
The first paragraph of the printed proof of 23.1: the set `F` (the interior of
the minimal subpath `P'`) together with the four properties 16.2 needs of it, and
the two attachments of `F` in `C` that are nonadjacent and of opposite
wheel-parity.

links.rationale: Proves the body of 23.1's proof (p. 139): builds the connected set F, the interior of a minimal opposite-parity subpath, with the two nonadjacent opposite-parity attachments 22.3 and 16.2 need.

decls.name: edge_position_eq
decls.docstring:
A cyclic edge of a nodup list has a unique cyclic position, even though its ends are
recorded as an unordered pair.

decls.name: layout_opposite
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3), printed p. 139):**
*"Then `c,z` are nonadjacent and have opposite wheel-parity in the wheel `(C,Y)`"*.

Here `c` lies in `A₀ \ {c₂}`.  The four exhaustive `Y`-complete edges make `z` and `c₂`
the two vertices in one parity class, while every other rim vertex lies in the other class.

links.rationale: Step within claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): every c ∈ A_0 \ {c_2} is nonadjacent to z with opposite wheel-parity, since the four Y-complete edges split the rim into the two parity classes.

decls.name: no_neighbour_except_c2
decls.docstring: The first paragraph of claim (3): `y` has no neighbour in `A₀ \ {c₂}`.

links.rationale: The first paragraph of claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): y has no neighbour in A_0 \ {c_2}, taken here as a hypothesis (hnone) to derive the remaining case y not adjacent to c_2.

decls.name: not_adj_c2_gap
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3), printed pp. 139–140):**
*"Next suppose that `y` is adjacent to `c₂`. … But then the hole
`x₀-Q-c₃-c₂-y-z-x₀` is the rim of an odd wheel with hub `Y`, contrary to `G ∈ F₈`.
So `y` is not adjacent to `c₂`."*

links.rationale: Step within claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): if y were adjacent to c_2, the hole x_0-Q-c_3-c_2-y-z-x_0 would be the rim of an odd wheel, contrary to G ∈ F_8, so y is not adjacent to c_2.

decls.name: claim3
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2), claim (3):** `y` is anticomplete to
`A₀ = V(C) \ {z,x₀,x₁}`.

links.rationale: Proves claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): y is anticomplete to A_0 = V(C) \ {z,x_0,x_1}, docstring labelled PAPER (23.2), claim (3).

decls.name: mod_le_self
decls.docstring:
A cyclic index below the length of the cycle is its own residue, and the length itself
has residue `0`.

links.rationale: A cyclic index below the length of the cycle is its own residue, and the length itself has residue 0.

decls.name: mem_rotate_take
decls.docstring: The vertices of the cyclic arc of `C` that starts at position `m` and has `L` vertices.

links.rationale: The vertices of the cyclic arc of C that starts at position m and has L vertices.

decls.name: pos_ne
decls.docstring: Two cyclic positions of a hole carry different vertices when their residues differ.

links.rationale: Two cyclic positions of a hole carry different vertices when their residues differ.

decls.name: prefix_getElem
decls.docstring: Reading a vertex of a prefix of a rotation off the original cycle.

links.rationale: Reading a vertex of a prefix of a rotation off the original cycle.

decls.name: not_mem_arc
decls.docstring: A cyclic position outside the index range of an arc is not a vertex of that arc.

links.rationale: A cyclic position outside the index range of an arc is not a vertex of that arc.

decls.name: arc_even
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (2.3)** applied to an arc of the rim that carries no `Y`-complete edge: the arc has
even length, because some `Y`-complete rim vertex lies outside it.

links.rationale: General fact used in claim (3) of 23.2's proof: by 2.3, an arc of the rim carrying no Y-complete edge has even length, since some Y-complete rim vertex lies outside it.

decls.name: orientation_absurd
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3), printed pp. 139–140), the argument for one arc of `C \ z`.**

`a, z, b` are consecutive on the rim and `f, c₂, e` are consecutive, with the arc `Q` of
`C \ z` running from `f` to `a`.  In the printed orientation `(a,b,e,f) = (x₀,x₁,c₁,c₃)`; the
other orientation is `(x₁,x₀,c₃,c₁)`.

links.rationale: Carries out claim (3)'s argument of 23.2's proof (p. 139-140) for one arc of C \ z, in the printed orientation (a,b,e,f) = (x_0,x_1,c_1,c_3) and its mirror (x_1,x_0,c_3,c_1).

decls.name: not_adj_c2
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3), printed pp. 139–140):** *"So `y` is not adjacent to `c₂`."*

The hypotheses are the ones the printed proof has in hand: the optimal wheel, the configuration
`x₀,z,x₁,c₁,c₂,c₃` of the four `Y`-complete rim edges (claim (1)), the neighbour `y` of `z` on
the path `T`, which is an interior vertex of `T` and so is neither in `Y` nor `Y`-complete, and
the first half of claim (3), that `y` has no neighbour in `A₀ \ {c₂}`.

links.rationale: Restates claim (3)'s conclusion of 23.2's proof (p. 140) from the hypotheses in hand at this point of the printed proof: y is not adjacent to c_2.

decls.name: no_adj_far_end
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3)):** *"Since `x₀-Q-c₃-c₂-y-x₀` is not an odd hole, it follows that
`y` is not adjacent to `x₀`."*

`Q` runs from `c₃` to `x₀`; the cycle of the printed sentence is `Q ++ [y, c₂]`, of length
`pathLength Q + 3`.

links.rationale: Step within claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): since x_0-Q-c_3-c_2-y-x_0 is not an odd hole, y is not adjacent to x_0.

decls.name: odd_wheel_absurd
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (3)):** *"But then the hole `x₀-Q-c₃-c₂-y-z-x₀` is the rim of an odd
wheel with hub `Y`, contrary to `G ∈ F₈`."*

The rim is `[x₀, z, y, c₂] ++ Q.dropLast`, and the odd segment is the single `Y`-complete edge
`x₀z`: its two rim neighbours are `y`, which is not `Y`-complete, and the neighbour of `x₀` on
`Q`, which is not `Y`-complete because `x₀` is and `C` carries only the four listed
`Y`-complete edges.

links.rationale: Step within claim (3) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): the hole x_0-Q-c_3-c_2-y-z-x_0 would be the rim of an odd wheel with hub Y, contrary to G ∈ F_8.

decls.name: exists_odd_antipath
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (4)):** *"Since `y, v₁` are not `Y`-complete, there is an antipath
joining them with interior in `Y`, and it is odd since it can be completed to an antihole via
`v₁-z-v₂-y`."*

Here `u` is the paper's `v₂`, the `Y`-complete neighbour of `v₁` in `A₀`.

links.rationale: Step within claim (4) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): the antipath joining y, v_1 with interior in Y is odd, since it completes to an antihole via v_1-z-v_2-y.

decls.name: every_complete_adj
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (4)):** *"Hence every `Y`-complete vertex is adjacent to one of
`y, v₁`."*

links.rationale: Step within claim (4) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): every Y-complete vertex is adjacent to one of y, v_1.

decls.name: orientation_absurd
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (4), printed p. 140), the argument for one arc of `C \ z`.**

`a, z, b` are consecutive on the rim and `f, c₂, e` are consecutive, with the arc `Q` of
`C \ z` running from `f` to `a`; `y-v₁` are the second and third vertices of the path `T`, and
`u` is the paper's `v₂`, the neighbour of `v₁` in `A₀` assumed `Y`-complete.  In the printed
orientation `(a, z, b, e, c₂, f) = (x₀, z, x₁, c₁, c₂, c₃)`; the other one is
`(x₁, z, x₀, c₃, c₂, c₁)`.

links.rationale: The module's principal result: it formalizes the printed passage of 23.2 quoted in the module header (PDF p. 142).

decls.name: four_neighbours
decls.docstring: Four distinct rim vertices adjacent to `v` make *"at least four neighbours in `C`"*.

decls.name: nbrs_subset
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (4)):** *"By 16.1, there are three consecutive vertices in `C`, all
`Y`-complete and adjacent to `v₁`.  By 22.3, `v₁` has no other neighbours in `C`."*

`e, f` are the two rim neighbours of `c₂`, and `hfedge` is the consequence of claim (1) that
`c₂` is the only `Y`-complete rim neighbour of `f`.

links.rationale: Step within claim (4) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): by 16.1 three consecutive Y-complete rim vertices are adjacent to v_1, and by 22.3 v_1 has no other neighbours on C.

decls.name: claim4
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2), claim (4), printed p. 140:** *"If `n = 1` then no neighbour of `v₁` in `A₀`
is `Y`-complete."*  See `Thm232Claim4Core.orientation_absurd` for the printed argument.

links.rationale: Proves claim (4) of the printed proof of 23.2 (p. 140): if n = 1 then no neighbour of v_1 in A_0 is Y-complete.

decls.name: exists_anticomplete_interior
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2(5), printed p. 141): "Since `G ∈ F₈`,
`(Y,{x₀,x₁},z-y-p₁-...-p_k)` is not a pseudowheel. ... So no other vertices
of the path are `{x₀,x₁}`-complete. By 2.11 ... one of `x₀,x₁` is
nonadjacent to all of `y,p₁,...,p_{k-1}`."

The set `X` stands for the rim pair. The proof works for any nonempty
anticonnected set `X` with the listed completeness properties.

links.rationale: The printed argument of claim (5) of 23.2 (printed p. 141 = PDF p. 143), once its path has been chosen: absence of a pseudowheel (`G ∈ F₈`) identifies the vertices complete to the rim pair, 13.6 makes the path even, and 2.11 then yields a member of the pair with no neighbour in the path interior — the sentence quoted. The Lean statement is proved for an arbitrary nonempty anticonnected `X` in place of the rim pair `{x₀,x₁}`, which is a faithful generalisation of the printed use, and both outcomes of 2.11 are handled (the second via `Thm232Claim5SecondOutcome.last_anticomplete_dropLast`).

decls.name: exists_anticomplete_tail
decls.docstring:
The same conclusion on the interior of `T`, using the inclusion stored
by `Claim5PathData.tailContains`.

links.rationale: The transfer of `exists_anticomplete_interior` from the interior of the constructed path `P` to the interior of `T`, which is the paper's closing sentence of claim (5) (quoted). The inclusion is supplied as the hypothesis `hcontains`, matching `Claim5PathData.tailContains`; the paper derives it from the minimum-length choice of `T` made just before claim (4) (*"By choosing T of minimum length we may assume that none of y, v 1 , . . . , vn−1 have neighbours in A0 "*, printed p. 140), a premise that the project's frozen `Thm232RemainingClaims.claim5_path_gap` does not record.

decls.name: claim4_gap
decls.docstring:
**Remaining gap, PAPER (23.2), claim (4), printed p. 140:**
*"(4) If `n = 1` then no neighbour of `v₁` in `A₀` is `Y`-complete."*

Here `n = 1` means that `T` is the four-vertex path `z-y-v₁-v₂` with `v₂ ∈ A₀`, so `v₁` is the
last interior vertex of `T`.  The printed proof of (4) goes through an antipath between `y` and
`v₁` with interior in `Y`, then 16.1 and 22.3, and ends with the odd hole
`x₀-Q-c₃-v₁-y-x₀`.

links.rationale: Discharges the n = 1 case of claim (4) of 23.2's proof (p. 140), where T is the four-vertex path z-y-v_1-v_2 with v_2 ∈ A_0.

decls.name: exists_claim5_path
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (5), printed p. 140):** the path `z-y-p₁-⋯-p_k`, with every property
its use in claim (5) needs.  `hclaim4` is claim (4).

links.rationale: Constructs the path z-y-p_1-⋯-p_k of claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 140) with every property its use needs, from claim (4).

decls.name: initial_indices
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2(5), printed p. 141): "Since none of `y,v₁,...,v_{n-1}`
have neighbours in `A₀` it follows that
`{y,v₁,...,v_n} ⊆ {y,p₁,...,p_{k-1}}`."

Here `F` is the initial path, including `z` but omitting its rim endpoint.
Its vertices lie outside `A`, and only its last vertex can have a neighbour
in `A`. Any path from its first vertex to `A` inside `F ∪ A` starts with `F`.

links.rationale: Step within claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): since none of y,v_1,...,v_{n-1} have neighbours in A_0, {y,v_1,...,v_n} ⊆ {y,p_1,...,p_{k-1}}.

decls.name: initial_subset
decls.docstring:
The vertex inclusion from the same sentence, without introducing indices
at its call sites.

links.rationale: The vertex-inclusion consequence of claim (5)'s initial-indices sentence, stated without introducing indices at its call sites.

decls.name: last_anticomplete_dropLast
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2(5), printed p. 141): "By 2.11 ... one of `x₀,x₁` is
nonadjacent to all of `y,p₁,...,p_{k-1}`." In the second outcome of 2.11 this
is its last endpoint. The last vertex of `L` is omitted from the conclusion.

links.rationale: Step within claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): in the second outcome of 2.11, one of x_0,x_1 is nonadjacent to all of y,p_1,...,p_{k-1} (its last vertex omitted here).

decls.name: second_outcome_anticomplete
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2(5), printed p. 141): "Since
`{y,v₁,...,v_n} ⊆ {y,p₁,...,p_{k-1}}`, this proves (5)."
The stored inclusion in `P.tail` suffices: the last vertex is `Y`-complete,
whereas the interior of `T` contains no `Y`-complete vertex.

links.rationale: Closes claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): since {y,v_1,...,v_n} ⊆ {y,p_1,...,p_{k-1}} (the stored inclusion in P.tail, whose last vertex is Y-complete while the interior of T is not), this proves (5) -- re-quoted from the docstring's substantive sentence rather than the generic closing phrase 'this proves (5)' alone.

decls.name: triple_neighbours
decls.docstring: Decode a rim triple in either of the orientations allowed by 16.2.

links.rationale: Decodes a rim triple in either of the two orientations 16.2 allows.

decls.name: path_from_attachments
decls.docstring:
The third outcome of 16.2 must go between `p,q`: its ends attach to `F`,
so neither is the anticomplete vertex `x`.  Its middle vertex is therefore `x`.
The first two outcomes are excluded by optimality and anticompleteness.

links.rationale: The third outcome of 16.2 must run between p,q in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof: its ends attach to F so neither is the anticomplete vertex x, forcing x to be its middle vertex.

decls.name: path_from_initial_path
decls.docstring:
Use the initial part of `T` outside the rim.  If it has only `p,q` as
attachments, it is already the required path.  Otherwise 16.2 applies.

links.rationale: Builds the required attachment path from the initial part of T outside the rim, applying 16.2 when it has more than the two attachments p,q.

decls.name: attachment_path
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “there is a path `R` between `z,c₂` with interior
in `F`, and no vertex of `C` has neighbours in the interior of `R` except `z,c₂`.”
The two cases exchange the ends of the complete triples.

links.rationale: Constructs the closing-paragraph path of 23.2's proof (p. 141): R between z,c_2 with interior in F, with no vertex of C adjacent to its interior except z,c_2.

decls.name: pair_segment
decls.docstring:
The complete edge `p-z` is a segment when the vertices immediately before and
after it are not complete to the hub.

links.rationale: The complete edge p-z is a Y-segment when its immediate rim neighbours on both sides are not Y-complete.

decls.name: only_pair
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “Since `(C',Y)` is not an odd wheel, it follows
that `(C',Y)` is not a wheel, and so `x₀,z` are the only `Y`-complete vertices in `C'`.”
Here 2.3 supplies the last implication: an even complete-edge count would provide
a second complete edge disjoint from the isolated edge.

links.rationale: Step in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): since (C',Y) is not an odd wheel it is not a wheel at all, so x_0,z are the only Y-complete vertices of C' (via 2.3).

decls.name: middles_ne
decls.docstring:
The two middle vertices are distinct because their offsets are `1` and `d+1`,
both strictly within the same turn of the rim.

links.rationale: The two middle vertices of the closing-paragraph argument are distinct, since their offsets 1 and d+1 lie strictly within the same turn of the rim.

decls.name: not_both_overlap
decls.docstring:
The two possible end coincidences cannot both hold, since the rim has at least
six vertices.  This is the paper's “and therefore `x₁ ≠ c₁`”.

links.rationale: The two possible end-coincidences of the closing paragraph cannot both hold, since the rim has at least six vertices; this is 23.2's proof's 'and therefore x_1 ≠ c_1' (p. 141).

decls.name: offset_ne
decls.docstring: Different offsets in one turn give different vertices of a hole.

links.rationale: Different offsets within one turn of the rim give different vertices of the hole.

decls.name: outer_ne
decls.docstring:
Apart from the two permitted end coincidences, the ordered triples do not
overlap at an outer vertex.

links.rationale: Apart from the two permitted end-coincidences, the closing paragraph's ordered rim triples do not overlap at an outer vertex.

decls.name: hat_absurd
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “the only neighbour of `x₀` in `F ∪ A₀` is its
neighbour in `S`, say `s`; the only neighbour of `z` in `F ∪ A₀` is `y`; and `s,y`
are nonadjacent, and both nonadjacent to `y₀`, contrary to 17.1.”

links.rationale: Step in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): the catching set F ∪ A_0 has unique neighbours s (of x_0) and y (of z), which are nonadjacent and both nonadjacent to y_0, contradicting 17.1.

decls.name: next_complete
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “We claim that `x₀ = c₃`.”  If the other rim
neighbour of the inactive end is not complete, the auxiliary hole has just two
complete vertices. The hat and leap alternatives of 2.10 both give contradictions.

links.rationale: Proves the closing paragraph's claim x_0 = c_3 (23.2's proof, p. 141): if the other rim neighbour of the inactive end were not complete, 2.10's hat and leap alternatives on the auxiliary hole both give contradictions.

decls.name: leap_absurd
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “A leap would imply there are two vertices in
`Y`, joined by an odd path of length ≥ 5 with interior in `F ∪ A₀`. Hence its
ends are `{x₀,x₁}`-complete, and its internal vertices are not, contrary to 13.6.”

links.rationale: Excludes the leap alternative in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): a leap gives an odd path of length ≥ 5 between two {x_0,x_1}-complete-ended vertices of Y, contrary to 13.6.

decls.name: orientation
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “This proves that `x₀ = c₃`, and therefore
`x₁ ≠ c₁`. By exchanging `x₀,x₁`, we deduce that `x₁` has a neighbour in `F`.”
The four complete edges identify the inactive end once its other neighbour has
been proved complete.

links.rationale: Step in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): this proves x_0 = c_3, hence x_1 ≠ c_1, and by exchanging x_0,x_1 the other end also has a neighbour in F.

decls.name: first_rim_path
decls.docstring:
The paper chooses `T` of minimum length.  For the attachment argument it suffices
to take a path inside the given `T` that first reaches `C \ {z}`.  Its interior is
outside the rim and is a subset of the original interior.

links.rationale: For the closing paragraph's attachment argument, extracts the prefix of T (chosen of minimum length in the paper) that first reaches C \ {z}, with interior a subset of the original interior.

decls.name: end_attaches
decls.docstring: Each end of a path with at least three vertices attaches to its interior.

links.rationale: Each end of a path with at least three vertices attaches to its interior.

decls.name: Region
decls.docstring:
The region used in the closing proof.  Its two prescribed neighbours are `y`
at `z`, and the next rim vertex `s` at the inactive rim neighbour `p`.

links.rationale: The Prop-valued specification of the closing-paragraph region, with prescribed neighbours y at z and the next rim vertex s at the inactive rim neighbour p.

decls.name: region
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “Let `F = {y,v₁,…,v_n}`. ... Let `S` be a path
from `y` to `x₀` with interior in `F ∪ A₀`.”  The original path attaches `F` to
the connected arc `A₀`; inducedness gives the unique neighbour of `z`.

links.rationale: Constructs the closing paragraph's region of 23.2's proof (p. 141): F = {y,v_1,…,v_n} attaches to the connected arc A_0 via the path S from y to x_0.

decls.name: five_distinct
decls.docstring:
The four complete edges form the path `u-p-x-q-v`.  A repeated vertex would
give a triangle or a four-cycle inside the hole.

links.rationale: The four closing-paragraph complete edges form the path u-p-x-q-v with five distinct vertices, since a repeat would give a triangle or a four-cycle inside the hole.

decls.name: triple_shape
decls.docstring:
Every three-vertex path made from the four listed edges contains `x`.  If
neither end is `x`, its ends must be `p,q`.

links.rationale: Every three-vertex path built from the four listed closing-paragraph edges contains x; if neither end is x, its ends must be p,q.

decls.name: exists_configuration
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 139):** *"Since `(C,Y)` is not an odd wheel, there are vertices
`x₀, z, x₁, c₁, c₂, c₃` of `C`, in order, and all distinct except possibly `x₁ = c₁` or
`c₃ = x₀`, such that the `Y`-complete edges in `C` are `x₀z, zx₁, c₁c₂, c₂c₃`."*

links.rationale: The paragraph after step (1) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): since (C,Y) is not an odd wheel, the four Y-complete rim edges lay out the six vertices x_0,z,x_1,c_1,c_2,c_3 in cyclic order.

decls.name: no_wheel_contradiction
decls.docstring: **PAPER (23.2, printed pp. 139–141), steps (3)–(5) and the closing paragraph.**

links.rationale: Carries out steps (3)-(5) and the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (pp. 139-141): from the configuration x_0,z,x_1,c_1,c_2,c_3, the path T=z-y-⋯, and step (2), derives via claim3, claim5, closing_orientation_gap, attachment_path_gap and final_odd_wheel_gap the contradiction refuting the wheel's existence. Siblings Thm212.endgame and Thm224Claims.endgame are linked at this same aggregate-step granularity.

decls.name: closing
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, printed p. 141): “But then the hole formed by the union of `R` and
the path `C \ x₀` is the rim of an odd wheel with hub `Y`, a contradiction.”

We build this hole using `RimSurgery`.  On it, the segment through `z` is the single edge
`z`-`x₁`: the interior of `R` carries no `Y`-complete vertex, `x₀` has been deleted, and the
four `Y`-complete edges of `C` listed in `hexh` leave `x₁` no other `Y`-complete neighbour.
So the new wheel is odd, contrary to the no-odd-wheel clause of `G ∈ F₈`.

links.rationale: Closes 23.2's proof (p. 141): the hole formed from R and C \ x_0 is the rim of an odd wheel with hub Y, the final contradiction, built here via RimSurgery.

decls.name: interior_outside
decls.docstring:
An isolated joining path cannot meet the old rim internally: such a vertex would
have the same two rim neighbours as the deleted vertex, giving a four-cycle in the rim.
This supplies the disjointness needed for the paper's “hole formed by the union”.

links.rationale: An isolated joining path cannot meet the old rim internally: such a vertex would have the same two rim neighbours as the deleted vertex, giving a four-cycle in the rim. This is a Lean-internal disjointness fact (needed to build the closing paragraph's replacement hole) that the paper never argues explicitly -- reverted from an 8-word fragment match.

decls.name: replacement_absurd
decls.docstring:
The paper's last hole is a wheel with hub `Y`, and the segment through `p` is the
single edge `p`-`u`, so the wheel is **odd** — contrary to `G ∈ F₈`.

The vertex `x` is the one the paper deletes, `p, q` are its two neighbours on the old rim
(so the new hole is `(C \ x) ∪ R*`), and `u` is the other neighbour of `p` on the old rim.
`hpNbr` and `huNbr` say that on the old rim the only `Y`-complete neighbours of `p` and `u`
are each other and the deleted `x`, and the interior of the joining path carries no
`Y`-complete vertex, so `p`-`u` is a whole segment of the new hole.  The fourth
`Y`-complete vertex `hfourth` shows that the new hole has `Y`-complete vertices beyond
`p, u`, which is what an odd wheel forbids.

links.rationale: Re-anchored to the closing sentence of 23.2's proof (p. 141): the replacement hole D, built by RimSurgery from two disjoint complete edges avoiding the deleted vertex x, is a wheel with hub Y that violates hmin -- the same closing contradiction Thm232Final.closing reaches (via common_end_absurd) for the specific rim configuration. This entry was previously quoted with the proof's opening minimality choice (p. 139) rather than the closing contradiction it actually discharges; it has no caller in the finished proof chain (Thm232Final.closing uses common_end_absurd instead), so it stands as a generic/uncalled alternate route to the same conclusion.

decls.name: rimNeighbours_of_two
decls.docstring: Two distinct neighbours on a hole are its two rim neighbours.

links.rationale: Two distinct neighbours on a hole are its two rim neighbours.

decls.name: common_end_absurd
decls.docstring:
When the two complete triples meet at an end, deleting that end leaves the
two other complete edges disjoint.  The hole has at least six vertices, so those
edges cannot meet to form a four-cycle with the deleted end.

`hedgeY` is the layout of the four `Y`-complete edges of the old rim established before the
closing paragraph of 23.2: they are `x`-`p`, `p`-`u`, `v`-`q` and `q`-`x`.

links.rationale: When the closing paragraph's two complete triples meet at an end, deleting that end leaves the other two complete edges disjoint, since the hole has at least six vertices.

decls.name: no_three_cyc_adj
decls.docstring:
In the cyclic order on `{0, …, n−1}` with `n ≥ 4`, three distinct positions cannot be
pairwise cyclically consecutive.

decls.name: exists_pos_of_yEdge
decls.docstring: Every `Y`-complete edge of a hole occurs at one of its cyclic positions.

links.rationale: Every Y-complete edge of a hole occurs at one of its cyclic positions.

decls.name: pos_eq_of_getElem?
decls.docstring: Reading a cyclic position off a `getElem?` equation.

decls.name: exists_disjoint_yEdges
decls.docstring:
A hole with at least three `Y`-complete edges carries two **disjoint** `Y`-complete
edges — the last clause of `IsWheel`.

links.rationale: A hole with at least three Y-complete edges carries two disjoint Y-complete edges, the last clause IsWheel requires.

decls.name: isWheel_of_three_yEdges
decls.docstring:
A hole of length `≥ 6`, disjoint from a nonempty anticonnected `Y` and carrying at least
three `Y`-complete edges, **is** the rim of a wheel with hub `Y`.

links.rationale: A hole of length ≥ 6, disjoint from a nonempty anticonnected Y and carrying at least three Y-complete edges, is the rim of a wheel with hub Y.

decls.name: three_le_yEdgeCount
decls.docstring:
The rim of a wheel that carries two `Y`-complete edges meeting in a common vertex carries
at least **three** `Y`-complete edges: the wheel's own two `Y`-complete edges are disjoint, so
the two pairs of edges cannot coincide.

links.rationale: The rim of a wheel with two Y-complete edges meeting at a common vertex carries at least three Y-complete edges, since the wheel's own disjoint pair cannot coincide with them.

decls.name: exactly_four_yEdges
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 139), step (1):** *"Exactly 4 edges of `C` are `Y`-complete."*

`hmin` is the second half of the opening sentence of the proof — *"choose an optimal wheel
`(C,Y)` such that `C` contains as few `Y`-complete edges as possible"* — in the form delivered
by `OptimalWheelChoice.exists_optimal_wheel`.

links.rationale: Proves step (1) of the printed proof of 23.2 (p. 139): exactly 4 edges of C are Y-complete.

decls.name: exists_min_clean_path
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 140):** *"By choosing `T` of minimum length we may assume that
none of `y, v₁, …, v_{n−1}` have neighbours in `A₀`."*

links.rationale: Step within claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 140): choosing T of minimum length, none of y,v_1,…,v_{n-1} have neighbours in A_0.

decls.name: not_adj_both
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 139), step (2):** *"`y` is not adjacent to both `x₀`, `x₁`."*

`T = z :: y :: R` is the path of `G \ {x₀,x₁}` from `z` to `A₀ = V(C) \ {z,x₀,x₁}` produced by
the previous sentence, and `y` is the neighbour of `z` on it.  Were `y` adjacent to both `x₀`
and `x₁`, `T` would be a tail for `z` with respect to `(C,Y)`, contrary to 22.5.

links.rationale: Proves step (2) of the printed proof of 23.2 (p. 140): y is not adjacent to both x_0, x_1, else the path T would be a tail for z, contrary to 22.5.

decls.name: impossible
decls.docstring:
PAPER (23.2, step (3), use of 16.1): a vertex outside an optimal wheel cannot have two
nonadjacent rim-neighbours of opposite wheel-parity.

links.rationale: General fact used at step (3) of 23.2's proof, via 16.1: a vertex outside an optimal wheel cannot have two nonadjacent rim-neighbours of opposite wheel-parity.

decls.name: exists_clean_path
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 139):** *"Since `G` does not admit a skew partition, there is a
path `T` of `G \ {x₀,x₁}` from `z` to `A₀`, such that no vertex in its interior is in `Y` or
`Y`-complete.  Let `y` be the neighbour of `z` in `T`."*

The statement carries **the three `Y`-completeness facts and the minimality clause that the
printed proof has in hand at this point** — the printed sentence is the second half of a
paragraph whose first half says *"the `Y`-complete edges in `C` are `x₀z, zx₁, c₁c₂, c₂c₃`"*
(so `x₀`, `z`, `x₁` are `Y`-complete, by `EdgeComplete`), and the minimality of the number of
`Y`-complete rim edges is the second half of the opening sentence of the proof.  Without them
the statement is not the paper's: nothing would force `T` to avoid `x₀, x₁`, and nothing would
supply a vertex outside the separator `Y ∪ {Y`-complete`}`.

The bridge *"`G` does not admit a skew partition"* is **15.1** (`thm_15_1`: a graph in `F₆`
admitting a skew partition admits a balanced one), exactly as the printed proof of 23.4 spells
out for the identical step.

links.rationale: Step (2) of 23.2's proof (p. 139-140): since G admits no skew partition, the path T of G \ {x_0,x_1} from z to A_0 exists with clean interior; y is its neighbour of z.

decls.name: Claim5PathData
decls.docstring: The data about `z-y-p₁-⋯-p_k` used in the proof of claim (5).

links.rationale: The Prop-valued bundle of data about the path z-y-p_1-⋯-p_k used in the proof of claim (5) of 23.2.

decls.name: claim5_path_gap
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claims (4)–(5), printed p. 140):**
*"Let `P` be a path `y-p₁-⋯-p_k` from `y` to some `Y`-complete vertex `p_k ∈ A₀`, with
interior in `A₀ ∪ {v₁,…,v_n}`, such that `p_k` is the only `Y`-complete vertex in `P`. …
From (4), `k ≥ 3`."*

The structure uses the path with `z` prepended.  Its `tailContains` field is the printed
inclusion `{y,v₁,…,v_n} ⊆ {y,p₁,…,p_{k-1}}`.

links.rationale: Step within claims (4)-(5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): constructs the path P = y-p_1-⋯-p_k to the first Y-complete vertex p_k ∈ A_0, so that k ≥ 3 by (4).

decls.name: claim5_path_even
decls.docstring:
The path supplied for claim (5) has even length.  This is the printed parenthetical
*"and therefore has even length by 13.6"*: if its length were odd, 13.6 would either give a
`Y`-complete edge, although only its nonadjacent ends are `Y`-complete, or say its length is
three, although it has length at least four.

links.rationale: The path supplied for claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141) has even length, the printed parenthetical 'and therefore has even length by 13.6'.

decls.name: claim5_second_alternative_gap
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, claim (5), printed p. 140):** *"By 2.11 … it follows that one of `x₀, x₁`
is nonadjacent to all of `y, p₁, …, p_{k-1}`."*

In the second outcome of 2.11 the path is `a-y-p₁-⋯-p_k-b` with `{a,b} = {x₀,x₁}`, and the
vertex with that property is `b`: by inducedness its only neighbour on `y-p₁-⋯-p_k` is `p_k`,
which is `Y`-complete, whereas no vertex of the interior of `T` is.  (The earlier `False`
conclusion here was stronger than the paper's, which never excludes the second outcome.)

links.rationale: Step within claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): in the second outcome of 2.11, one of x_0,x_1 is nonadjacent to all of y,p_1,…,p_{k-1}.

decls.name: claim5
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2), claim (5):** one of `x₀,x₁` has no neighbours in the interior of `T`,
which is the paper's set `{y,v₁,…,v_n}`.

links.rationale: Proves claim (5) of 23.2's proof (p. 141): one of x_0,x_1 has no neighbours in the interior of T, the paper's set {y,v_1,…,v_n}.

decls.name: EndgameContext
decls.docstring:
The full collection of hypotheses available after claim (3) in the proof of 23.2.  Keeping
them together ensures that each closing gap below states the corresponding paper sentence in
its real context.

links.rationale: The full collection of hypotheses available after claim (3) in 23.2's proof, kept together so each closing gap states its paper sentence in context.

decls.name: closing_orientation_gap
decls.docstring:
**Remaining gap, PAPER (23.2, first half of the closing paragraph, printed pp. 140–141):**
if `x₀` has no neighbour in `F`, the path `S`, 2.10, 13.6, and 17.1 force `x₀ = c₃`.
After exchanging `x₀,x₁`, the other side has an attachment in `F`.  The second disjunct is the
same statement with the two sides exchanged.

links.rationale: Remaining gap in the first half of the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): if x_0 has no neighbour in F, the path S with 2.10, 13.6 and 17.1 force x_0 = c_3; exchanging x_0,x_1 gives the symmetric disjunct, matching the printed sentence 'By exchanging x_0, x_1, we deduce that x_1 has a neighbour in F.'

decls.name: attachment_path_gap
decls.docstring:
**Remaining gap, PAPER (23.2, closing paragraph, printed p. 141):**
*"There are therefore two attachments of `F` in `C` with opposite wheel-parity, and two that
are nonadjacent. By (1), 16.2, 22.3 and the optimality of the wheel … there is a path `R`
between `z,c₂` with interior in `F`, and no vertex of `C` has neighbours in the interior of
`R` except `z,c₂`."*

links.rationale: Step in the closing paragraph of 23.2's proof (p. 141): there are two attachments of F in C with opposite wheel-parity and two that are nonadjacent, giving (by (1), 16.2, 22.3 and optimality) the path R between z,c_2.

decls.name: final_odd_wheel_gap
decls.docstring:
**Remaining gap, PAPER (23.2, final sentence, printed p. 141):**
*"But then the hole formed by the union of `R` and the path `C \ x₀` is the rim of an odd
wheel with hub `Y`, a contradiction."*

The two alternatives record which symmetric rim vertex is deleted.

links.rationale: Closes 23.2's proof (p. 141) from either symmetric alternative: the hole formed by R and C \ x_0 (or its mirror) is the rim of an odd wheel with hub Y. This is a thin wrapper that adapts the EndgameContext-based interface and calls Thm232Final.closing directly, which does the actual RimSurgery work for this same printed sentence at 0.95 -- a packaged/duplicate form, not an independent anchor.

decls.name: not_complete_to_pair
decls.docstring:
No rim vertex other than `z` has both `x₀` and `x₁` as neighbours: on a hole of length at
least six, the two neighbours of `x₀` are `z` and the vertex at cyclic position `-1`, while
those of `x₁` are `z` and the vertex at cyclic position `3`.

links.rationale: No rim vertex other than z is adjacent to both x_0 and x_1: on a hole of length ≥ 6, their neighbour sets meet only at z.

decls.name: a0_connected
decls.docstring:
The set `A₀ = V(C) \ {z, x₀, x₁}` is the vertex set of the arc of `C` running from the
successor of `x₁` to the predecessor of `x₀`, hence is connected.

links.rationale: A_0 = V(C) \ {z, x_0, x_1} is the vertex set of the rim arc from the successor of x_1 to the predecessor of x_0, hence connected.

decls.name: exists_yEdge_layout
decls.docstring:
**PAPER (23.2, printed p. 139):** *"Since `(C,Y)` is not an odd wheel, there are vertices
`x₀, z, x₁, c₁, c₂, c₃` of `C`, in order, and all distinct except possibly `x₁ = c₁` or
`c₃ = x₀`, such that the `Y`-complete edges in `C` are `x₀z, zx₁, c₁c₂, c₂c₃`."*

On cyclic positions: the `Y`-complete edges of the rim are exactly the ones at positions
`k, k+1, k+d, k+d+1`, with `2 ≤ d` and `d + 2 ≤ |C|`.

links.rationale: The paragraph after step (1) of 23.2's proof (p. 140), on cyclic positions: the four Y-complete rim edges sit at positions k,k+1,k+d,k+d+1 with 2 ≤ d and d+2 ≤ |C|. This positional encoding is the input Thm232Configuration.exists_configuration builds on to name the six vertices themselves as the paper's sentence does; that entry is the printed step at 0.95, so this is kept as the packaged/duplicate positional form.

decls.name: descent
decls.docstring:
The descent step of 23.3, as printed: apply 22.2 to the configuration
`(z,A₀), x₀,…,x_s, y` and read off the new configuration `(y,A₀), x₀,…,x_r, z`,
whose height `r` satisfies `1 ≤ r < s`.

links.rationale: The descent step of 23.3's proof (p. 141): 22.2 applied to (z,A_0), x_0,…,x_s, y produces the smaller configuration (y,A_0), x_0,…,x_r, z with 1 ≤ r < s, contradicting the minimality of s.

decls.name: gidx
decls.docstring: Rewriting the *index* of a `getElem` is a motive error; this is the usable form.

decls.name: legs_even
decls.docstring: *"their union violates (1)"* — for a single pair of legs.

decls.name: case1_refute
decls.docstring: **Case 1 of the printed proof of 24.4 is impossible.**

links.rationale: Refutes case 1 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 144): two of P_1,P_2,P_3 always share length parity, and their union violates claim (1).

decls.name: path_self_singleton
decls.docstring: A path whose two named ends coincide is a single vertex.

decls.name: connectedSet_empty
decls.docstring: The empty set is connected.

decls.name: connectedSet_leg
decls.docstring: A path minus its last vertex is a connected set.

decls.name: connected_attach
decls.docstring: Attaching a possibly-empty connected set to a connected set.

decls.name: exists_pred_neighbour
decls.docstring: The last-but-one vertex of a nondegenerate path.

decls.name: leg_nonempty
decls.docstring: A path minus its last vertex is nonempty only if the path is nondegenerate.

decls.name: connectedSet_triple
decls.docstring: Three vertices, two of which are joined to the first, form a connected set.

decls.name: isPathFrom_tailSlice
decls.docstring: The tail of a path, as a slice (so that `PathBasics.mem_slice_iff` decodes membership).

decls.name: antihole_witness
decls.docstring:
*"… can be completed to an antihole via `z`"*: a single `X`-complete vertex non-adjacent to
both ends closes an antipath with interior in `X` into an antihole.

decls.name: antihole_two_antipaths
decls.docstring:
*"Since `Q ∪ R` is an antihole …"*: two antipaths with the same ends, one with interior in
`Ys` and one with interior in `Xs`, where `Xs` is complete to `Ys`, close into an antihole.

decls.name: middle_of_antipath
decls.docstring:
*"let `xᵢ` be the middle vertex of `Qᵢ`"*: an antipath of length `2` with interior in `Xs`
has a single interior vertex, which lies in `Xs` and is nonadjacent to both ends.

decls.name: degenerate_case
decls.docstring:
*"If `P₁, P₂, P₃` all have length 0, then the union of `Q₁, Q₂, Q₃` is an antihole of
length `> 4`, a contradiction."*

decls.name: core_case
decls.docstring:
The main body of the printed argument, once the paper's *"we may assume that `P₁` has
length `> 0`"* has fixed an index `a` with `v a ≠ u a`; `b` and `c` are the other two.

decls.name: case2_refute
decls.docstring:
**Refutation of the second case of the trichotomy in the proof of 24.4** (printed p. 144).

*"Now suppose the second holds, and for `i = 1,2,3` let `uᵢ, vᵢ, Pᵢ` be as in the second
case. … This is contrary to 17.1."*

links.rationale: Refutes case 2 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 145): the connected catching set built from P_1,P_2,P_3,x_1,x_2,x_3 contains no reflection of the triangle {u_1,u_2,u_3}, contrary to 17.1.

decls.name: gidx
decls.docstring: Rewriting the *index* of a `getElem` is a motive error; this is the usable form.

decls.name: path_mem_dec
decls.docstring: Every vertex of a path is one of its two ends or an interior vertex.

decls.name: antipath_pair
decls.docstring:
The printed step *"`p_k,p_{k+1}` are joined by an antipath with interior in `X₁`, and by
another with interior in `X₂`, and the union of these is an antihole; so they both have
length 2.  Hence there exist `xᵢ ∈ Xᵢ` nonadjacent to both `p_k,p_{k+1}`."*

Stated asymmetrically (it produces the vertex of `Y`); apply it twice, once with `(Y,Z)` and
once with `(Z,Y)`.

decls.name: second_yEdge
decls.docstring:
If a hole `C` disjoint from an anticonnected `Y` has three distinct `Y`-complete
vertices and at least one `Y`-complete edge, then it has a **second** `Y`-complete edge:
2.3's first alternative (an even number of `Y`-complete edges) must hold, since its second
alternative allows only two `Y`-complete vertices.

decls.name: three_consecutive_absurd
decls.docstring:
The `F₁₀` clause of `InF11`, in the shape a caller with three *listed* consecutive
vertices can use: no vertex of `Y` may be adjacent to three consecutive vertices of a hole of
length `≥ 6`, so a hole cannot carry three consecutive `Y`-complete vertices.

decls.name: case3_refute
decls.docstring: **Case 3 of the printed proof of 24.4 is impossible.**

links.rationale: Refutes case 3 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 145): the path P between v_1, v_2 through an X_3-complete vertex is shown impossible via 24.2, an antipath argument, and a hole of length ≥ 6.

decls.name: gidx
decls.docstring: Rewriting the *index* of a `getElem` is a motive error; this is the usable form.

decls.name: chop
decls.docstring:
**Deleting the last vertex of a path leaves a path.**

Stated with an explicit membership decoder so that no `slice` expression escapes into
the caller's goal, and so that the caller can read off the index of any vertex of the
truncated path.  Degenerate case included: a two-vertex path truncates to a
one-vertex path.

This is the shape every *"`p₁-Q-pₙ-⋯`"* concatenation in §24 needs, since gluing two
paths that share an endpoint means dropping that endpoint from one of them.

links.rationale: Deletes the last vertex of a path, leaving a path; used for every p_1-Q-p_n-⋯ concatenation in section 24.

decls.name: even_length_of_unique_ends
decls.docstring:
**Claim (1) of the printed proof of 24.4.**

`G ∈ F₁₁`; `X, Y` are disjoint nonempty anticonnected sets complete to each other;
`p` is a path of `G` with distinct ends `p₁, pₙ` such that `p₁` is the **unique**
`X`-complete vertex of `p` and `pₙ` is the **unique** `Y`-complete vertex of `p`.
Then the *number of vertices* of `p` is even.

(The paper's `n` is `p.length`; its `X₁, X₂` are `X, Y` here, so that the statement
can be applied to any of the three pairs drawn from `X₁, X₂, X₃`.)

links.rationale: Proves claim (1) of the printed proof of 24.4 (p. 144): a path with unique X-complete first vertex and unique Y-complete last vertex has an even number of vertices.

decls.name: Spider
decls.docstring:
**Case 1 of the trichotomy — a spider with centre `u`.**

*"there is a unique `Nᵢ`-vertex `vᵢ ∈ F`; there is a vertex `u ∈ F` different from
`v₁,v₂,v₃`, and three paths `P₁,P₂,P₃` in `F`, all of length `≥ 1`, such that each
`Pᵢ` is from `vᵢ` to `u`, and for `i ≠ j`, `V(Pᵢ \ u)` is disjoint from
`V(Pⱼ \ u)` and there is no edge between them."*

*"all of length `≥ 1`"* is not a separate conjunct: it follows from `u ≠ v i`
together with `IsPathFrom G (P i) (v i) u`.

links.rationale: The Prop-valued specification of case 1 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 144): a spider with centre u and three legs P_1,P_2,P_3 to the v_i.

decls.name: TriangleLegs
decls.docstring:
**Case 2 of the trichotomy — three legs hanging off a triangle.**

*"there is a unique `Nᵢ`-vertex `vᵢ ∈ F`; there are three paths `P₁,P₂,P₃` in `F`,
where each `Pᵢ` is from `vᵢ` to some `uᵢ` say, possibly of length 0; and for
`i ≠ j`, `V(Pᵢ)` is disjoint from `V(Pⱼ)` and the only edge between `V(Pᵢ),V(Pⱼ)`
is `uᵢuⱼ`."*

Note that *"the only edge … **is** `uᵢuⱼ`"* asserts in particular that `uᵢuⱼ` **is**
an edge, so `{u₁,u₂,u₃}` is a triangle; that is recovered from the last conjunct
by instantiating it at `a := u i`, `b := u j`.

links.rationale: The Prop-valued specification of case 2 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 144): three legs P_1,P_2,P_3 from the v_i to u_i, pairwise disjoint except for the single edge u_iu_j.

decls.name: ThroughPath
decls.docstring:
**Case 3 of the trichotomy — a single path through the third terminal.**

*"for `i = 1,2` there is a unique `Nᵢ`-vertex `vᵢ ∈ F`, and there is a path `P` in
`F` between `v₁,v₂` containing at least one `N₃`-vertex."*

The paper's *"up to symmetry"* is the explicit choice of which two of the three
indices play the roles of `1, 2`; here that is the triple `i, j, k` of pairwise
distinct elements of `Fin 3`.

links.rationale: The Prop-valued specification of case 3 of the trichotomy in 24.4's proof (p. 144): a single path P between v_1,v_2 containing an X_3-complete vertex.
The minimal connected set F ⊆ V(G)\(X_1∪X_2∪X_3) with an X_i-complete vertex for each i, from whose minimality the trichotomy of 24.4's proof (p. 144) is read off.

Undocumented auxiliary; its quote was attributed from elsewhere (spillover) and has been removed. Step within 24.5's proof (p. 145): 15.2 produces the path Q from z to p_1 with clean interior, with the extra alternative that Q ⊆ {z,p_1,…,p_n} when z has a neighbour among p_2,…,p_n.

decls.name: glue_antihole

`Gᶜ` means anticomplete).

`G`-complete to the interior (so `Gᶜ`-anticomplete to it).

between different marked edges has opposite-coloured ends, then at least one marked edge has
both ends in the connected set.  This is the first consequence of the auxiliary graph `K`: if
each edge had only one end in the component, two of the three ends would have the same colour.

decls.name: sixTerminalCore
decls.docstring:
PAPER (5.7 (4), printed p. 24), after the equal-colour parity step:

> *"Also, by (3) it follows that `a₃` is not adjacent in `K` to both `b₁` and `b₂`, and
> five similar statements. Since there is a component of `K` containing an end of each of
> `x₁,x₂,x₃`, we may assume that `a₁b₃,b₂a₃,a₃b₃ ∈ E(K)` ... But then the tracks
> `b₁-a₁-P₁-b₃`, `P₄`, and the one-edge track made by `x₃`, violate (3)."*

This lemma isolates the remaining six-terminal graph argument.  `hpair` is the preceding
sentence already proved by `endpointCleanConnection_different_color`: every endpoint-clean
connection between two marked edges has differently coloured ends.  `hclaim3` is printed claim
(3).  The conclusion is precisely the contradiction constructed in the quoted passage.

decls.name: endgame
decls.docstring:
**GAP LEMMA.**  The final paragraph of the printed proof of 5.7 (4), quoted in full in the
module docstring above.  `A` is a *maximal* connected subgraph of `H \ X` (`hmaximal`), the
three marked edges `x i, x j, x k` are pairwise disjoint edges of `H` in `X`, with ends `a`
and `b` as in `hs`, and `K` has the edges `a k b k`, `a k b j`, `a i b k` and no other edge at
`a k` or at `b k`.  The conclusion is the contradiction with claim (3) that the paragraph
constructs.

decls.name: cycle_config_at_interior_edge
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER (5.8 (7), printed p. 28): *"There is a cycle in `H` using the
branch between `u₁` and `v₁`, and using `u₂` and not `v₂` (since `J \ v₂` is
2-connected).  There correspond two paths in `L(H)`, say `P` and `Q`, from
`N_{u₁}` and `N_{v₁}` respectively to `N_{u₂}`, disjoint from each other, and
there is a third path `R` say from `p₁` to `N_{u₂}` via `F` and a subpath of
`R_{u₂v₂}`.  There are no edges between these paths except within the triangle
`T` formed by their ends in `N_{u₂}`."*

This is the version used when a vertex `w` of the first rung is to be deleted:
the hole is listed with `w` first, and `P`, `Q` are the two arcs obtained by
`Thm58BranchBranchCut.link_of_hole_cut`.  The hypothesis on `w` says that its
edge of `H` is internal to the branch, which is what keeps `w` away from the two
cycle edges at `u₂`; `R` is listed from its end in `N_{u₂}` towards `F`, and
stops just before `p₁`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (7) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: starTrackLink_singleton_star_at_branch_end
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"Hence in `L(H)` there are three
vertex-disjoint paths, from `N_{v₁}`, `N_{v₂}`, `N_u` respectively to `N_w`, and there are no
edges between them except in the triangle `T` formed by their ends in `N_w`.  If `pₙ` has a
unique neighbour (say `r`) in `R_{v₁v₂}`, then `r` can be linked onto the triangle `T`."*

This is the case the printed proof does not separate: every neighbour of `p₁` in the star at
`u = c` is an edge of `H` from `c` to a vertex of the branch, so the third path meets the first
two on the branch and the three paths above are not vertex-disjoint.  The link is then built at
`w := v₁` instead, from the branch truncated just before `r`, the one-edge track `c v₁`, and
the return track `D` continued along the branch past `r`; the triangle is listed so that its
first two vertices are the edge `c v₁` and the edge of `D` at `v₁`, neither of which meets `r`.
That construction needs `r` to be an internal edge of the branch; when `r` is the edge of the
branch at `v₁`, the whole attachment set of `F` lies in `N_{v₁}` and is local, contrary to the
hypothesis of 5.8.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: starTrackLink_singleton_of_host
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"Hence in `L(H)` there are three
vertex-disjoint paths, from `N_{v₁}`, `N_{v₂}`, `N_u` respectively to `N_w`, and there are no
edges between them except in the triangle `T` formed by their ends in `N_w`.  If `pₙ` has a
unique neighbour (say `r`) in `R_{v₁v₂}`, then `r` can be linked onto the triangle `T`."*

The two arcs of the return track `D` out of `w` and the minimal track `S` back to `c` are the
three tracks; each is extended, along the branch towards `r` from either side, or through the
star at `c` and then along `P` to `pₙ`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: starTrackLink_separated_star_at_branch_end
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"If `pₙ` has two nonadjacent neighbours in
`R_{v₁v₂}`, then `pₙ` can be linked onto the triangle `T`, contrary to 2.4."*

This is the case the printed proof does not separate: every neighbour of `p₁` in the star at
`u = c` is an edge of `H` from `c` to a vertex of the branch, so the path *"from `N_u`"* meets
the other two on the branch and the three paths are not vertex-disjoint.  Rebuilding the link
at a branch vertex, as in `starTrackLink_singleton_star_at_branch_end`, is not available here,
because the conclusion asks for a `w` off the branch.  The escape is instead a parity count:
with `i < j` the two indices of the branch edges at the two neighbours of `pₙ`, the branch
together with `P` closes into three holes of `G` — through the two branch edges and through the
return track `D` — whose lengths force `i + j` to be odd and `j - i` to be even at the same
time, contrary to `Berge G`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.docstring:

`R_{v₁v₂}`, then `pₙ` can be linked onto the triangle `T`, contrary to 2.4."*

Same three tracks as `starTrackLink_singleton_of_host`; only the extensions change, because the
two branch directions are now attached to `pₙ` directly at its two nonadjacent neighbours `r`
and `s`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_starTrackLink_singleton
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"Choose a cycle `C₁` of `H` using the
branch between `v₁` and `v₂` and not using `u`, and choose a minimal track `S` in
`H \ {v₁,v₂}` between `u` and `V(C₁)`.  Let the ends of `S` be `u` and `w` say.  Hence in
`L(H)` there are three vertex-disjoint paths, from `N_{v₁}`, `N_{v₂}`, `N_u` respectively to
`N_w`, and there are no edges between them except in the triangle `T` formed by their ends in
`N_w`.  If `pₙ` has a unique neighbour (say `r`) in `R_{v₁v₂}`, then `r` can be linked onto the
triangle `T`."*

The two arcs of `C₁` out of `w` are extended along the branch towards `r` from either side,
and the track `S` is extended through the star at `c` and then along `P`, so that `r` — whose
neighbours are the two branch vertices next to it and `pₙ` — has a neighbour on each of the
three paths.  The last two conjuncts record that the triangle can be ordered so that its first
two vertices are nonneighbours of `r`; only the edge of the branch at a common end of the
branch and of an arc could be adjacent to a vertex of the triangle.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_starTrackLink_separated
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"If `pₙ` has two nonadjacent neighbours in
`R_{v₁v₂}`, then `pₙ` can be linked onto the triangle `T`, contrary to 2.4."*

The cycle, the minimal track and the two arcs are the same as in
`exists_starTrackLink_singleton`; only the extensions change, because now the two branch
directions are attached to `pₙ` directly at its two nonadjacent neighbours `r` and `s`.
The vertex `w` is not on the branch between `v₁` and `v₂`, which is what
`starTrackLink_not_adj_apex` turns into the nonadjacency required by 2.4.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: branch_end_absurd
decls.docstring:
**The branch-end case of 5.8 (6) cannot occur.**

Assume every neighbour of `p₁` in the star `N_u` at `u = c` is an edge of `H` from `c` to a
vertex of the branch.  Such a vertex is an end `v₁` or `v₂` of the branch, by
`eq_end_of_adj_star`.  If `pₙ` sees a branch edge that is not the branch edge at that end, then
`branch_end_false` (or `branch_end_false_right`) produces two holes of different parity.
Otherwise every attachment of `F` is an edge of `H` at that end, so the attachments are local,
contrary to the hypothesis of 5.8 — unless the branch has length `1` and `c` is joined to both
its ends, which is a triangle of the bipartite graph `H`.

decls.name: exists_mixedSectors
decls.docstring:
**The two sectors of 5.8 (6).**  The rung of the cycle `C₂` of the paper is a hole `L` of
`G` inside the appearance (`Thm58StarBranchMixedHole.exists_mixed_hole`, the one remaining gap
of claim (6)).  Cutting `L` at the vertex `a` — the `A`-end of its unique edge in `N(u)` — and
at the edge `rs` leaves exactly the two arcs the link needs: one runs from a neighbour of `a`
to `r`, the other from the other neighbour of `a` to `s`.  Both arcs are induced paths because
`L` is a hole, they are disjoint and their only cross edge is `rs` for the same reason, and no
vertex of either is adjacent to `p₁` because `a` carried the only edge of `N(u)` on `L`.

links.rationale: Produces the two sectors (pieces of the path) of the quoted sentence, from the hole that the cycle C2 induces in G.

decls.name: exists_mixed_hole
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"In `H` there is a cycle `C₂` using the
branch between `v₁` and `v₂`, and using an edge in `A` and an edge in `B`.  (To see this,
divide `u` into two adjacent vertices, one incident with the edges in `A` and the other with
those in `B`, and use Menger's theorem to deduce that there are two vertex-disjoint paths
between these two vertices and `{v₁,v₂}`.)  Hence in `G`, there is a path between `N_{v₁}`
and `N_{v₂}` using a unique edge of `N(u)`, and that edge is between a vertex `a ∈ A` and
some vertex in `B`."*

The rung of that cycle `C₂` is a hole `L` of `G` contained in the appearance.  Reading it
from the `A`-end `a` of its unique edge in `N(u)`, the vertex `a` is `L[0]`, no other vertex
of `L` is adjacent to `p₁` (that is what *"a unique edge of `N(u)`"* says, since the only
edges from `p₁` into the appearance land in `N(u)`), and the two neighbours `r`, `s` of `pₙ`
are the consecutive pair `L[k]`, `L[k+1]` on the branch part of the cycle.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_mixed_track
decls.docstring:
**The cycle `C₂` of 5.8 (6).**  PAPER, proof of 5.8 (6), printed p. 28: *"In `H` there is a
cycle `C₂` using the branch between `v₁` and `v₂`, and using an edge in `A` and an edge in `B`.
(To see this, divide `u` into two adjacent vertices, one incident with the edges in `A` and the
other with those in `B`, and use Menger's theorem to deduce that there are two vertex-disjoint
paths between these two vertices and `{v₁,v₂}`.)"*

Here `u` is the star vertex `c` and `Av` is the set `A`; `v₁`, `v₂` are the two ends of the
branch `q`.  The cycle `C₂` is returned as the branch `Q` (that is `q`, read in whichever
direction makes the `A`-edge the one on the `w₁` side) together with the complementary track
`D`, which runs from `w₁` to `w₂` through `c`, arriving along an edge `c xA` into `A` and
leaving along an edge `c xB` into `B`, and which meets the branch only at `w₁` and `w₂`.

links.rationale: The cycle `C₂` of 5.8 (6). Discharges the quoted step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (6).

decls.name: exists_twoTrackCompletion
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (2), printed p. 26: *"Let `Q` be the path between `r₂` and `s₁`
with interior in `F ∪ V(R_{uv} \ {r₁})`. ... Consequently there is a track of `H` from `u` to
`v` with first edge `s₁`; and hence there is a path `S₁` of `L(H)` from `s₁` to `r₂`,
vertex-disjoint from `V(R_{uv}) ∪ N_u` except for its ends.  Indeed, if we delete from `H` both
the vertex `w` and all edges incident with `u` except `s₂`, the graph remains connected; so
there is a path `S₂` of `L(H)` between `s₂` and `r₂`, vertex-disjoint from
`R_{uv} ∪ N_u ∪ V(R_{uw}) ∪ N_w` except for its ends.  Now `S₁` and `S₂` have the same parity
since `H` is bipartite."*

`Q` is the interior of `r₂-Q-s₁`: it starts at the neighbour `y₀` of `t = r₂` on the branch and
ends at the neighbour `y₁ = p₁` of `s₁` in `F`.  The equal parity of `S₁` and `S₂` is the
bipartiteness of `H` read through
`BipartiteClosedWalkEven.even_trackLength_iff`: both tracks join `u` to `v`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (2) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_crossTrack
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (4), printed p. 27: *"There is a cycle in `J` of length `≥ 4`
using the edge `v₁v₂`, and so there is a path in `L(H)` of length `≥ 2` from `A₁` to `A₂` with
no internal vertex in `N_{v₁} ∪ V(R_{v₁v₂}) ∪ N_{v₂}`."*

The path of `L(H)` is the rung of a track `Q` of `H` from `v₁` to `v₂` that shares no edge with
the branch: the cycle of `J` of length `≥ 4` through `v₁v₂` is a cycle of `H` through the
branch, and `Q` is the rest of that cycle.  *"Length `≥ 2"`* is `4 ≤ Q.length`, and
*"from `A₁` to `A₂`"* is the two adjacencies, `A₁` being the set of vertices of
`N_{v₁} \ {r₁}` adjacent to `p₁` and `A₂` the set of vertices of `N_{v₂} \ {r₂}` adjacent to
`p₂`.  Both `B₁` and `B₂` are empty here (`hB₁`, `hB₂`), so the first edge of any such track
is automatically a neighbour of `p₁` and its last edge one of `p₂`.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (4) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_tracks
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (4), printed p. 27: *"There is a path `S₁` from `A₁` to `A₂` with
no vertex in `N_{v₁} ∪ N_{v₂} ∪ V(R_{v₁v₂})` except for its ends.  Suppose that there is no
vertex `w ∈ V(J)` with `A₁ ∪ A₂ ⊆ N_w`.  Then we can apply 5.6 to the graph obtained from `H`
by deleting the edges and internal vertices of the branch between `v₁` and `v₂`.  We deduce
(possibly after exchanging `v₁` and `v₂`) that there is a path `S₂` of `L(H)` with first vertex
in `A₁`, second vertex in `B₁`, last vertex in `A₂`, and otherwise disjoint from
`N_{v₁} ∪ N_{v₂} ∪ V(R_{v₁v₂})`."*

The two paths are the rungs of two tracks of `H`, exactly as in claim (3), and *"no vertex in
`V(R_{v₁v₂})`"* is the disjointness of the two tracks from the edges of the branch.  The
disjunction is the paper's *"possibly after exchanging `v₁` and `v₂`"*.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (4) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: covered_holes
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (4), printed p. 27, the final paragraph: *"Consequently there is
a vertex `w ∈ V(J)` with `A₁ ∪ A₂ ⊆ N_w`.  Since `H` is bipartite, and there is a 2-edge track
of `H` between `v₁, v₂` (via `w`), it follows that the branch of `H` with ends `v₁, v₂` has
even length, and therefore `R_{v₁v₂}` has odd length, and in particular `r₁ ≠ r₂`.  Since
`|N_{vᵢ} ∩ N_w| ≤ 1` (since `J` is simple) it follows that `|Aᵢ| = 1`, `Aᵢ = {aᵢ}` say, for
`i = 1, 2`.  Since `X` is not local it is not a subset of `N_w` and so there is a vertex of
`R_{v₁v₂}` in `X`.  Since `Xᵢ ⊆ N_{vᵢ}` for `i = 1, 2`, no internal vertex of `R_{v₁v₂}` is in
`X`, so we may assume that `r₁ ∈ X`.  Since `r₁ ∉ N_{v₂}` it follows that `r₁ ∉ X₂`, and hence
`p₁` is the only vertex in `F` adjacent to `r₁`.  Now the hole `p₁-⋯-pₙ-a₂-a₁-p₁` is even, and
so `n` is even.  If we delete the vertex `v₂` and the edge `a₁` from `H`, what remains is still
connected, and so contains a track from `w` to `v₁`.  Hence there is a path `T` in `L(H)` from
some `a₃ ∈ N(w)` to `r₁`, disjoint from `N_{v₂} ∪ a₁`.  But `T` can be completed to a hole via
`r₁-R_{v₁v₂}-r₂-a₂-a₃` and via `r₁-p₁-⋯-pₙ-a₂-a₃`, and these two completions have different
parity, a contradiction."*

The two completions of the last sentence are the two holes of different parity below.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (4) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.docstring:
PAPER: *"Since `X` is not local it is not a subset of `N_w` and so there is a vertex of
`R_{v₁v₂}` in `X`.  Since `Xᵢ ⊆ N_{vᵢ}` for `i = 1, 2`, no internal vertex of `R_{v₁v₂}` is in
`X`, so we may assume that `r₁ ∈ X`.  Since `r₁ ∉ N_{v₂}` it follows that `r₁ ∉ X₂`, and hence
`p₁` is the only vertex in `F` adjacent to `r₁`."*

decls.name: covered_endgame
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (4), printed p. 27, the final paragraph from its third sentence
on: *"Since `X` is not local it is not a subset of `N_w` and so there is a vertex of
`R_{v₁v₂}` in `X`.  Since `Xᵢ ⊆ N_{vᵢ}` for `i = 1, 2`, no internal vertex of `R_{v₁v₂}` is in
`X`, so we may assume that `r₁ ∈ X`.  Since `r₁ ∉ N_{v₂}` it follows that `r₁ ∉ X₂`, and hence
`p₁` is the only vertex in `F` adjacent to `r₁`.  Now the hole `p₁-⋯-pₙ-a₂-a₁-p₁` is even, and
so `n` is even.  If we delete the vertex `v₂` and the edge `a₁` from `H`, what remains is still
connected, and so contains a track from `w` to `v₁`.  Hence there is a path `T` in `L(H)` from
some `a₃ ∈ N(w)` to `r₁`, disjoint from `N_{v₂} ∪ a₁`.  But `T` can be completed to a hole via
`r₁-R_{v₁v₂}-r₂-a₂-a₃` and via `r₁-p₁-⋯-pₙ-a₂-a₃`, and these two completions have different
parity, a contradiction."*

The two sentences before this one are proved in `Thm58StarStarAdjacentGap.covered_holes`, and
they are exactly the hypotheses `hw₁`, `hw₂`, `hs₁`, `hs₂`, `hsing₁`, `hsing₂` below: the
covering vertex `w` of `V(J)` is a common neighbour of the two star vertices whose two edges to
them are off the branch, and `Aᵢ` is the single vertex `vᵢw` of `L(H)`.  Since the argument
ends in *"a contradiction"*, the conclusion is the pair of holes of different parity that 5.8
is looking for.

theorem connectedSet_diff {H : SimpleGraph W} {X D : Set W} {b : W}
    (hbX : b ∈ X) (hbD : b ∉ D)
    (hexit : ∀ z ∈ D, ∀ y ∈ X, y ∉ D → H.Adj z y → y = b)
    (hX : ConnectedSet H X) : ConnectedSet H (X \ D) := by
  intro u v
  have hu : (u : W) ∈ X \ D := u.2
  have hv : (v : W) ∈ X \ D := v.2
  obtain ⟨h1, h2, hr⟩ :=
    rchIn_diff hbX hbD hexit hu.2 hv.2 ⟨hu.1, hv.1, hX ⟨(u : W), hu.1⟩ ⟨(v : W), hv.1⟩⟩
  exact hr

decls.name: incidentEdges_del
decls.docstring:
A connected set of `H` all of whose vertices survive, and no two of whose vertices are
joined by a deleted edge, is a connected set of the deleted graph. -/
theorem connectedSet_del {T : Set ↥S} {Y : Set W}
    (hYT : ∀ x : W, x ∈ Y ↔ ∃ hx : x ∈ S, (⟨x, hx⟩ : ↥S) ∈ T)
    (hE : ∀ x ∈ Y, ∀ y ∈ Y, s(x, y) ∉ E)
    (hconn : ConnectedSet H Y) :
    ConnectedSet (del H E S) T := by
  classical
  intro u v
  set GB := (del H E S).induce T with hGB
  have hmemY : ∀ w : ↥T, ((w : ↥S) : W) ∈ Y := fun w => (hYT _).mpr ⟨(w : ↥S).2, w.2⟩
  let f : ↥Y → ↥T := fun x =>
    ⟨⟨(x : W), ((hYT (x : W)).mp x.2).choose⟩, ((hYT (x : W)).mp x.2).choose_spec⟩
  have hf : ∀ {x y : ↥Y}, (H.induce Y).Adj x y → GB.Adj (f x) (f y) := by
    intro x y hxy
    have hadj : H.Adj (x : W) (y : W) := hxy
    refine del_adj.mpr ⟨hadj, hE _ x.2 _ y.2⟩
  have hmap : GB.Reachable (f ⟨((u : ↥S) : W), hmemY u⟩) (f ⟨((v : ↥S) : W), hmemY v⟩) :=
    (hconn ⟨((u : ↥S) : W), hmemY u⟩ ⟨((v : ↥S) : W), hmemY v⟩).map
      (⟨f, hf⟩ : (H.induce Y) →g GB)
  have hu : f ⟨((u : ↥S) : W), hmemY u⟩ = u := Subtype.ext (Subtype.ext rfl)
  have hv : f ⟨((v : ↥S) : W), hmemY v⟩ = v := Subtype.ext (Subtype.ext rfl)
  rwa [hu, hv] at hmap

theorem incidentEdges_del {c : W} (hc : c ∈ S) :
    incidentEdges (del H E S) ⟨c, hc⟩
      = Sym2.map Subtype.val ⁻¹' (incidentEdges H c \ E) := by
  ext e
  induction e using Sym2.ind with
  | _ x y =>
    simp only [incidentEdges, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_preimage, Set.mem_diff,
      Sym2.map_mk, SimpleGraph.mem_edgeSet]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hadj, hmem⟩
      rw [del_adj] at hadj
      refine ⟨⟨hadj.1, ?_⟩, hadj.2⟩
      rcases Sym2.mem_iff.mp hmem with h | h
      · exact h ▸ Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _
      · exact h ▸ Sym2.mem_mk_right _ _
    · rintro ⟨⟨hadj, hmem⟩, hE⟩
      refine ⟨del_adj.mpr ⟨hadj, hE⟩, ?_⟩
      rcases Sym2.mem_iff.mp hmem with h | h
      · exact (Subtype.ext h : (⟨c, hc⟩ : ↥S) = x) ▸ Sym2.mem_mk_left _ _
      · exact (Subtype.ext h : (⟨c, hc⟩ : ↥S) = y) ▸ Sym2.mem_mk_right _ _

decls.name: nonadjacent_parity_gap
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 claim (3), printed p. 26: *"Certainly `A₁` and `A₂` are both
nonempty, so there is a track in `H` from `v₁` to `v₂` with end-edges in `A₁` and `A₂`
respectively.  Hence there is a path `S₁` in `L(H)` from `A₁` to `A₂`, vertex-disjoint from
`N_{v₁} ∪ N_{v₂}` except for its ends. ...  Hence we can apply 5.6, and we deduce (possibly
after exchanging `v₁` and `v₂`) that there is a path `S₂` in `L(H)` with first vertex in `A₁`,
second vertex in `B₁`, last vertex in `A₂`, and otherwise disjoint from `N_{v₁} ∪ N_{v₂}`.
Since `H` is bipartite, `S₁` and `S₂` have opposite parity; but they can both be completed via
`F`, a contradiction."*

The hypothesis is that at least one of `B₁`, `B₂` is nonempty; the conclusion is the pair of
holes of different parity that the last sentence produces.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (3) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: adjacent_both_complete_parity_gap
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 claim (4), printed p. 27: *"Suppose that both `B₁` and `B₂` are
empty.  There is a cycle in `J` of length ≥ 4 using the edge `v₁v₂`, and so there is a path in
`L(H)` of length ≥ 2 from `A₁` to `A₂` with no internal vertex in
`N_{v₁} ∪ V(R_{v₁v₂}) ∪ N_{v₂}`.  The union of this path with `R_{v₁v₂}` induces a hole, and so
does its union with `F`, and therefore these two paths have lengths of the same parity."*

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (4) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: adjacent_parity_gap
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 claim (4), printed p. 27: *"So we may assume that at least one of
`B₁`, `B₂` is nonempty. ...  Since `H` is bipartite, `S₁` and `S₂` have opposite parity; but
they can both be completed via `F`, a contradiction.  Consequently there is a vertex
`w ∈ V(J)` with `A₁ ∪ A₂ ⊆ N_w`. ...  But `T` can be completed to a hole via
`r₁-R_{v₁v₂}-r₂-a₂-a₃` and via `r₁-p₁-⋯-pₙ-a₂-a₃`, and these two completions have different
parity, a contradiction."*

Both branches of that argument end in two holes of different parity, which is the conclusion
below.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (4) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

decls.name: exists_tracks
decls.docstring:
GAP — PAPER, proof of 5.8 (3), printed p. 26: *"Certainly `A₁` and `A₂` are both nonempty,
so there is a track in `H` from `v₁` to `v₂` with end-edges in `A₁` and `A₂` respectively. ...
Since `X = A₁ ∪ A₂` is not local, there is no `w ∈ V(J)` with `A₁ ∪ A₂ ⊆ N_w`.  Hence we can
apply 5.6, and we deduce (possibly after exchanging `v₁` and `v₂`) that there is a path `S₂` in
`L(H)` with first vertex in `A₁`, second vertex in `B₁`, last vertex in `A₂`."*

`A₁` is the set of vertices of `N_{v₁}` adjacent to `p₁` and `B₁ = N_{v₁} \ A₁`, and `A₂` is
the set of vertices of `N_{v₂}` adjacent to `p₂`, so *"end-edges in `A₁` and `A₂`"* is the pair
of adjacencies asked of the first track, and the three conditions on the first three vertices
of the path `S₂` of 5.6 are the conditions on the first two edges and the last edge of the
second track (the path given by 5.6 has second vertex in `B₁`, hence second vertex `c₁`, which
is why the second track passes through `c₁` at its second vertex).  The two tracks avoid no
edges here, so the edge set to be avoided is empty.  The disjunction is the paper's *"possibly
after exchanging `v₁` and `v₂`"*: 5.6 gives its track at either of the two stars.

links.rationale: Fills an implicit step of the paper's proof of 5.8, case (3) that the printed argument leaves to the reader, via the quoted sentence.

because `b` has degree `≥ 3`; and the branches exist because `H` is a subdivision of `J`.

The nine vertices are the cells of `L(K₃,₃)`. In the complement, the shear
`(i,j) ↦ (i+j,i+2j)` again gives `L(K₃,₃)`. Remove the vertex `w (2,2)` and replace its
edge by the path `Q`. The two pairs in `hattach` are exactly the remaining edges at its two
ends. The new branch has `Q.length` edges, which is odd and at least three. The omitted
vertex `w (2,2)` is adjacent to the other two edges at each end and witnesses overshadowing.

Only this explicit line-graph edge replacement remains open. No conclusion of 6.1 or
minimal-counterexample hypothesis is assumed here.

theorem apply_edge (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) (edge : I ≃ H.edgeSet) (w : I → V)
