decls.name: rung_mem_strip
decls.docstring: Every vertex of a rung lies in `V(S) = A ∪ B ∪ C`.

decls.name: banister_rung_edges
decls.docstring: The only edges between a banister `a₀-R₀-b₀` and a rung `a-R-b` are `a₀a` and `b₀b`.

decls.name: rung_odd_of_banister_odd
decls.docstring:
**The paper's fourth sentence**: *"For any rung `a`-`R`-`b`, the hole
`a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀`-`b`-`R`-`a`-`a₀` has even length, and so `R` is odd."*

The printed cycle is the list `R₀ ++ R.reverse`.

decls.name: banister_odd
decls.docstring:
**The paper's first three sentences**: *"Let `a₁`-`R₁`-`b₁`, `a₂`-`R₂`-`b₂` be a step.
Then these three paths form a prism, and it is not an even prism by hypothesis.  In
particular `R₀` has odd length, by 7.2."*

decls.name: thm_11_3
decls.docstring:
**11.3** (printed p. 65), introduced by *"We remark:"*

PAPER: *"Let `G` be Berge, containing no even prism, let `S = (A, C, B)` be a step-connected
strip in `G`, and let `a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀` be a banister.  Then every rung of the strip has odd
length, and so does `R₀`."*

This is the **published** form of 11.3.  The arXiv v1 draft stops at *"every rung of the strip
has odd length"*, which is strictly weaker than the form its own 11.4 cites (*"By 11.3 `R₀`
and every rung has odd length"*); both proofs in fact derive the assertion about `R₀`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 11.3 (printed on PDF page 67).

decls.name: thm_11_4
decls.docstring:
**11.4** (printed p. 66)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, such that there is no appearance of `K₄` in `G` and no even
prism in `G`.  Let `S = (A, C, B)` be a step-connected strip in `G`.  Let
`F ⊆ V(G) \ (A ∪ B ∪ C)` be connected, such that there are no edges between `F` and
`A ∪ B ∪ C`.  There is no anticonnected set `Q ⊆ V(G) \ (A ∪ B ∪ C ∪ F)` such that:*

* *some right-star has a neighbour in `F` and a nonneighbour in `Q`,*
* *some vertex in `B` has a nonneighbour in `Q`,*
* *some left-star with a neighbour in `F` is `Q`-complete,*
* *every vertex in `Q` has a neighbour in `F`,*
* *every vertex in `Q` has a neighbour in `A ∪ B ∪ C`, and*
* *no vertex in `Q` is a left-star."*

The six bullets are listed in the printed order.  No banister is assumed.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 11.4 (printed on PDF page 67).

decls.name: rung_swap
decls.docstring: A rung read backwards is a rung of the reversed strip.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: reverses a rung of the strip `(A,C,B)` into a rung of the reversed strip `(B,C,A)`, part of the left/right-exchange bookkeeping the printed proof invokes but does not spell out.

decls.name: step_swap
decls.docstring: A step read backwards is a step of the reversed strip.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: reverses a step of the strip `(A,C,B)` into a step of the reversed strip `(B,C,A)`, extending `rung_swap` to pairs of rungs for the same exchange.

decls.name: union3_comm
decls.docstring: `V(S)` does not see the order of the two ends of the strip.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: records `A ∪ B ∪ C = B ∪ A ∪ C`, so the strip's vertex set `V(S)` is unchanged by exchanging the two ends `A` and `B`.

decls.name: stepConnected_swap
decls.docstring: A step-connected strip stays step-connected when its two ends are exchanged.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: shows a step-connected strip `(A,C,B)` remains step-connected as `(B,C,A)`, the structural fact behind the proof's repeated appeal to ‘possibly exchanging left and right’.

decls.name: isLeftStar_swap
decls.docstring: Left-stars of `(A, C, B)` are exactly the right-stars of `(B, C, A)`.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: left-stars of the strip `(A,C,B)` are exactly the right-stars of the exchanged strip `(B,C,A)`, one half of the left/right-exchange bookkeeping.

decls.name: isRightStar_swap
decls.docstring: Right-stars of `(A, C, B)` are exactly the left-stars of `(B, C, A)`.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: right-stars of the strip `(A,C,B)` are exactly the left-stars of the exchanged strip `(B,C,A)`, the other half of the left/right-exchange bookkeeping.

decls.name: oneBreaker_swap
decls.docstring:
A 1-breaker of `(A, C, B)` becomes a 1-breaker of the exchanged strip `(B, C, A)` once
the two asymmetric bullets of the definition are supplied in their right-star form.  Those
two are exactly what the paper's claim (2) provides, which is why the paper can only say
*"all hypotheses of the theorem are true with 'left' and 'right' exchanged"* after (2).

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: turns a 1-breaker `(A,C,B,F,Q)` into a 1-breaker of the exchanged strip `(B,C,A,F,Q)` once the two asymmetric hypotheses are supplied in right-star form, formalizing the proof's step (2) remark that ‘all hypotheses of the theorem are true with left and right exchanged’.

decls.name: exists_cross_edge
decls.docstring: A connected set has an edge leaving any nonempty proper subset.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: a general fact about connected sets — any nonempty proper subset has an edge leaving it — used to derive contradictions from the maximality of `F` and `Q`.

decls.name: exists_anticomponent_containing
decls.docstring: An anticonnected subset of `N` is contained in an anticomponent of `N`.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: an anticonnected subset of `N` is contained in a single anticomponent of `N`, producing the anticomponent `N₁ ⊇ Q` that claim (3) of the proof works with.

decls.name: rung_mem_strip
decls.docstring: Every vertex of a rung lies in `V(S) = A ∪ B ∪ C`.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: every vertex of a rung of the strip lies in `V(S) = A ∪ B ∪ C`, a basic containment fact used throughout the strip bookkeeping.

decls.name: exists_nonneighbour_in_B
decls.docstring:
**"Since the strip is step-connected, every vertex in `A` has a nonneighbour in `B`."**
(printed p. 67, in the proof of (7)).  Every vertex of `A` is the `A`-end of a rung of some
step, and the `B`-end of the other rung of that step is a nonneighbour of it.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: proves the parenthetical of the proof's claim (7) — since the strip is step-connected, every vertex of `A` has a nonneighbour in `B` — which the proof uses to conclude `B₁ ≠ B` and hence `B₂` nonempty.

decls.name: getElem_eq_index
decls.docstring: Two entries of a list at equal indices agree.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: a trivial list-indexing fact (equal indices give equal entries) used as a rewriting step in the path-interior bookkeeping of `interior_ends` and `mem_interior_iff_index`.

decls.name: isPathList_three
decls.docstring:
A three-element list with the two consecutive edges present and the end pair absent
is a path.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: certifies that a three-vertex list with its two consecutive edges present and its end pair absent forms an induced path, used to assemble short paths in the proof's case analysis.

decls.name: mem_interior_iff_index
decls.docstring: Interior membership, indexed.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: characterizes membership in a path's interior by list index, the technical bridge between the paper's path notation and the Lean list representation used by `interior_ends`.

decls.name: interior_ends
decls.docstring:
In an induced path `u-P-w` on at least three vertices, `u` is adjacent to exactly one
interior vertex (the first) and `w` to exactly one (the last).  This is the paper's *"`p₁-P-p₂`
with `V(P)` minimal"*: minimality is inducedness.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: in an induced path `u`-`P`-`w` of length ≥ 2, each end is adjacent to exactly one interior vertex, formalizing the paper's device of taking `V(P)` minimal to isolate the first and last interior vertices of banisters and rungs.

decls.name: path_avoid
decls.docstring:
The routine avoidance bookkeeping for a path built through `F`: its ends lie outside
`V(S)` and differ from the excluded star `z`, and its interior lies in `F`.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: routine avoidance bookkeeping for a path built through `F` — its ends lie outside `V(S)` and differ from an excluded vertex `z`, and its interior lies in `F` — used when assembling banisters and cross paths.

decls.name: len_ge_two
decls.docstring: A path with two distinct ends has at least two vertices.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: a path with two distinct ends has at least two vertices, a basic length fact used to justify splitting rungs into a head and a nonempty tail.

decls.name: rung_tail
decls.docstring: A rung with its `A`-end removed: a path inside `B ∪ C` containing the `B`-end.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: strips the `A`-end off a rung to leave a path inside `B ∪ C` containing the rung's `B`-end, the key step in proving `B ∪ C` connected for claim (3).

decls.name: bc_connected
decls.docstring:
**"`B ∪ C` is connected (because every vertex of `B ∪ C` is in a step and the strip is
step-connected)"** — printed p. 66, in the proof of (3).

The component `K` of `B ∪ C` containing a fixed vertex of `B` absorbs all of `B` (any
partition of `B` is crossed by a stepped edge) and then all of `C` (each vertex of `C` lies
on a rung, whose `A`-end-deleted tail is a connected subset of `B ∪ C` meeting `B`).

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: proves the parenthetical of the proof's claim (3) — `B ∪ C` is connected because every vertex of `B ∪ C` lies on a step and the strip is step-connected — which feeds into 2.7.1 to balance `(F, N₁)`.

decls.name: star_notMem_F
decls.docstring: A left- or right-star is never in `F`: it has a neighbour in `V(S)`, and `F` has none.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: a left- or right-star cannot lie in `F`, since it has a neighbour in `V(S)` while `F` is anticomplete to `V(S)`.

decls.name: banister_through_F
decls.docstring:
**The banister the paper uses without comment**: a 1-breaker supplies a left-star and a
right-star each with a neighbour in the connected set `F`, and `F` is anticomplete to `V(S)`,
so a path between them with interior in `F` is a banister.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: builds the banister between the left-star `a₀` and right-star `b₀` that a 1-breaker guarantees, with interior contained in `F`, the object the printed proof works with from the outset without naming it.

decls.name: core
decls.docstring:
The body of the printed proof of 11.5, for a 1-breaker `(S, F, Q)` chosen with
`|F| + |Q|` maximum *"(possibly exchanging "left" and "right")"*, in a graph that admits no
balanced skew partition.  The paper's claims (1)-(9) are the `have`s below, in order.

links.rationale: Auxiliary lemma for 11.5: the full body of the printed proof, run for a maximal 1-breaker `(S,F,Q)` in a graph admitting no balanced skew partition, deriving `False` through the paper's claims (1)-(9) in order; `thm_11_5` obtains the maximal 1-breaker by extremal choice and calls this lemma to close the contradiction.

decls.name: thm_11_5
decls.docstring:
**11.5** (printed p. 66)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, such that there is no appearance of `K₄` in `G` and no even
prism in `G`.  If there is a 1-breaker in `G` then `G` admits a balanced skew partition."*

A 1-breaker is a triple `(S, F, Q)` with `S = (A, C, B)`, so *"there is a 1-breaker in `G`"*
is the existence of five sets `A, C, B, F, Q` with `IsOneBreaker G A C B F Q`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 11.5 (printed on PDF page 68).

decls.name: thm_12_1
decls.docstring:
**12.1** (printed p. 69)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, such that there is no appearance of `K₄` in `G`, no even
prism in `G`, and no 1-breaker in `G`.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a maximal
staircase in `G`, and let `v ∈ V(G) \ V(K)`.  Then exactly one of the following holds:*

*1. `v` is minor; and in that case, either `v` is a left-star or `v` is not `A`-complete, and
either `v` is a right-star or `v` is not `B`-complete.*

*2. `v` is major; and in that case, it is either left- or right-diagonal or central.*

*3. `v` is a left-star with a neighbour in `R₀ \ a₀`, or a right-star with a neighbour in
`R₀ \ b₀`."*

Notes on the transcription.

* This is the **published** form of case 1.  The arXiv v1 draft reads only *"`v` is minor"*;
  the published version adds the clause about `A`- and `B`-completeness, and rewrites the
  proof of 12.1(4) accordingly.
* *"and in that case, …"* in cases 1 and 2 is part of the alternative, so each of those
  alternatives is the conjunction of the type of `v` with the extra conclusion.
* *"exactly one of the following holds"* is `∃! i : Fin 3, ![·, ·, ·] i`, the three
  alternatives being listed in the printed order.  (This is provably equivalent to
  `(P₁ ∨ P₂ ∨ P₃) ∧ ¬(P₁ ∧ P₂) ∧ ¬(P₁ ∧ P₃) ∧ ¬(P₂ ∧ P₃)`.)

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 12.1 (printed on PDF page 71).

decls.name: thm_12_2
decls.docstring:
**12.2** (printed p. 71)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, such that there is no appearance of `K₄` in `G`, no even
prism in `G`, and no 1-breaker in `G`.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a maximal
staircase in `G`, and let `F ⊆ V(G) \ V(K)` be connected, such that its set of attachments in
`V(K)` is not local with respect to `K`.  Then `F` contains either:*

*1. a major vertex, or*

*2. a banister `u`-`R`-`v`, such that there are no edges between `V(R)` and `V(R₀)`, or*

*3. (up to symmetry) a path `u`-`R`-`v`, where `u` is a left-star, `v` has a neighbour in
`R₀ \ a₀`, and there are no edges between `V(R \ u)` and `V(S)`."*

Notes on the transcription.

* *"`F` contains …"* means that all the vertices of the object lie in `F`.
* *"up to symmetry"*: the only symmetry of the hypotheses is the reversal of the strip, which
  interchanges `A` with `B`, `a₀` with `b₀`, and left-stars with right-stars (`V(S)`, `V(K)`
  and `V(R₀)` are unchanged).  So alternative 3 is stated as the two-way disjunction of the
  printed alternative and its mirror image, exactly as for 10.3.
* `V(R \ u)` is the set of vertices of `R` other than `u` (`u` being an end of `R`).

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 12.2 (printed on PDF page 73).

decls.name: banister_of_swapped
decls.docstring:
Transport a banister obtained after exchanging the two ends of the staircase back to the
published orientation.

decls.name: thm_12_3
decls.docstring:
**12.3** (printed p. 73), introduced by *"The previous result can be strengthened as
follows."*

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, such that there is no appearance of `K₄` in `G`, no even
prism in `G`, and no 1-breaker in `G`.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a maximal
staircase in `G`, and let `F ⊆ V(G) \ V(S)` be connected, containing a left-star and with an
attachment in `B ∪ C`.  (Note that `F` may intersect `V(R₀)`.)  Then `F` contains either a
major vertex or a banister."*

Notes on the transcription.

* Here `F` avoids `V(S) = A ∪ B ∪ C` only — **not** `V(K)`; the parenthetical *"(Note that `F`
  may intersect `V(R₀)`.)"* is a remark pointing this out, and so is deliberately not a
  hypothesis.
* *"with an attachment in `B ∪ C`"*: some vertex of `B ∪ C` has a neighbour in `F`, i.e. the
  set of attachments of `F` in `B ∪ C` is nonempty.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 12.3 (printed on PDF page 74).

decls.name: thm_12_4
decls.docstring:
**12.4** (printed p. 74)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, containing no appearance of `K₄`, no even prism, and no
1-breaker.  If there is a 2-breaker in `G` then `G` admits a balanced skew partition."*

A 2-breaker is a pair `(K, Q)` with `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)`, so *"there is a
2-breaker in `G`"* is the existence of the staircase data together with the set `Q`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 12.4 (printed on PDF page 76).

decls.name: thm_12_5
decls.docstring:
**12.5** (printed p. 77)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be a Berge graph, containing no appearance of `K₄`, no even prism, no
1-breaker and no 2-breaker.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a strongly maximal
staircase in `G`.  Let `q₁`-`⋯`-`q_k` be an antipath such that `q₂, …, q_{k-1}` are both left-
and right-diagonal, and `q₁` is left- and not right-diagonal, and `q_k` is right- and not
left-diagonal.  Then `q₁` is a left-star and `q_k` is a right-star."*

The antipath `q₁-⋯-q_k` is the list `q` of its vertices in order, with ends `q₁` and `q_k`;
`q₂, …, q_{k-1}` is its interior `SPGT.interior q`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 12.5 (printed on PDF page 78).

decls.name: thm_13_1
decls.docstring:
**13.1** (printed pp. 79–80)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be Berge, containing no appearance of `K₄`, no even prism, no 1-breaker and
no 2-breaker.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a strongly maximal staircase in `G`,
and let `x₁, …, x_t` be a right-sequence.  Let `b` be a right-star, and let `a`-`R`-`b` be a
`b`-optimal banister.  Let `a`-`w₁`-`⋯`-`w_n` be the trajectory of `a`.  Then `n` is odd, and
either:*

*• `b` is the unique vertex of `R` which is `{w₁, …, w_n}`-complete, or*

*• `R` has length 1, and there exists some even `m` with `1 ≤ m < n` such that
`a`-`w₁`-`⋯`-`w_m`-`b` is an antipath."*

Notes on the transcription.

* *"the trajectory of `a`"* is the second of the section's two `trajectory` notions (the one
  for a general vertex, printed p. 79), which produces the antipath `a`-`w₁`-`⋯`-`w_n`
  **including** its first vertex `a`; so the trajectory is the list `a :: w` with
  `w = [w₁, …, w_n]`, and the paper's `n` is `w.length`.
* `{w₁, …, w_n}` is `{u | u ∈ w}`, and *"`b` is the unique vertex of `R` which is
  `{w₁, …, w_n}`-complete"* is: a vertex of `R` is `{w₁, …, w_n}`-complete exactly when it is
  `b` (`b` is a vertex of `R`, being one of its ends).
* `a`-`w₁`-`⋯`-`w_m`-`b` is the list `a :: (w.take m ++ [b])`, since `w.take m` is
  `[w₁, …, w_m]`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.1 (printed on PDF page 81).

decls.name: thm_13_2
decls.docstring:
**13.2** (printed p. 80)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be Berge, containing no appearance of `K₄`, no even prism, no 1-breaker and
no 2-breaker.  Let `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)` be a strongly maximal staircase in `G`,
and let `x₁, …, x_t` be a right-sequence.  Then `x₁, …, x_t` are all adjacent to `a₀`."*

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.2 (printed on PDF page 83).

decls.name: thm_13_3
decls.docstring:
**13.3** (printed p. 83)

PAPER: *"Let `G` be Berge, containing no appearance of `K₄`, no even prism, no 1-breaker and
no 2-breaker.  Suppose that there is a 3-breaker in `G`; then `G` admits a balanced skew
partition."*

A 3-breaker is a pair `(K, x)` with `K = (S = (A, C, B), a₀`-`R₀`-`b₀)`, so *"there is a
3-breaker in `G`"* existentially quantifies the six pieces of staircase data together with the
vertex `x`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.3 (printed on PDF page 85).
The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.4 (printed on PDF page 86).

decls.name: bipartite_of_no_adj
decls.docstring:
A graph with no edges at all is 2-colourable, hence bipartite.  (Used twice below:
`G` complete makes `Ḡ` edgeless, and `Ḡ` complete makes `G` edgeless.)

decls.name: thm_13_5
decls.docstring:
**13.5** (printed p. 86), introduced by *"The remainder of the paper is basically a proof
of the following."*

PAPER: *"If `G` is recalcitrant then either `G` or `Ḡ` is bipartite."*

Followed by *"Clearly any counterexample to 1.3 is recalcitrant, so 13.5 will imply 1.3."*
*Recalcitrant* is the four-bullet notion defined immediately before the statement and
transcribed in `Workspace.Types.LongOddPrism`; *bipartite* is Mathlib's
`SimpleGraph.IsBipartite`, and the paper's `Ḡ` is `Gᶜ`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.5 (printed on PDF page 88).

decls.name: formPrism_mk
decls.docstring:
Assembling a long prism from its presenting data: six vertices forming the two
triangles `{a0, a1, a2}`, `{b0, b1, b2}`, the three paths `P₁, P₂, P₃` with
`Pᵢ` running from `aᵢ` to `bᵢ`, the nine disjointness conditions between the two
triangles, the three "only edges between `V(Pᵢ)` and `V(Pⱼ)`" conditions, and the
witness that one of the three paths has length `> 1`.

This is pure bookkeeping for `Workspace.Types.Prisms.SPGT.IsLongPrism`; it exists
only so that the `Fin 3`-indexed packaging does not clutter the proof of 13.6.

decls.name: thm_13_6
decls.docstring:
**13.6** (printed p. 86), introduced by *"It turns out that for such graphs, there is a
useful strengthening of 2.1 — the second alternative of that theorem can no longer hold."*

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₅`, and let `P` be a path in `G` with odd length.  Let
`X ⊆ V(G) \ V(P)` be anticonnected, such that both ends of `P` are `X`-complete.  Then
either:*

*1. some edge of `P` is `X`-complete, or*

*2. `P` has length 3 and there is an odd antipath joining the internal vertices of `P` with
interior in `X`."*

Notes on the transcription.

* This is the **published** hypothesis `X ⊆ V(G) \ V(P)`; the arXiv draft has the weaker
  `X ⊆ V(G)`.  Since `V(G)` is the whole vertex type, `X ⊆ V(G) \ V(P)` is
  `X ⊆ {v | v ∈ P}ᶜ`.
* *"some edge of `P` is `X`-complete"* is the existence of two vertices `u, v` of `P` with
  `uv` an `X`-complete edge (`EdgeComplete`, which contains `G.Adj u v`); since `P` is
  induced, its edges are exactly the adjacent pairs of its vertices.
* `P` having length 3 means it has exactly four vertices, so its interior is a two-element
  list `[c, d]`, and *"an odd antipath joining the internal vertices of `P` with interior in
  `X`"* is an antipath from `c` to `d` of odd length all of whose internal vertices lie in
  `X`.  (The two alternatives are the first and third alternatives of 2.1; the second — the
  existence of a leap in `X` — is what this strengthening removes.)

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 13.6 (printed on PDF page 88).

decls.name: alt_absurd
decls.docstring:
The paper's *"But the ends of `P'` are `Y ∪ {p₁}`-complete, and its internal
vertices are not, contrary to 13.6"*: the first two alternatives of 2.9 cannot
occur under the hypotheses of 13.7.

Stated for the first alternative only; the second is obtained by applying this
  lemma to `P.reverse` with `X` and `Y` interchanged.

decls.name: thm_13_7
decls.docstring:
**13.7** (printed p. 86), introduced by *"There is an analogous strengthening of 2.9, as
follows."*

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₅`, and let `X, Y` be disjoint nonempty anticonnected subsets of `V(G)`,
complete to each other.  Let `P` be a path in `G` with even length `> 0`, with vertices
`p₁, …, p_n` in order, such that `p₁` is the unique `X`-complete vertex of `P` and `p_n` is the
unique `Y`-complete vertex of `P`.  Then `P` has length 2 and there is an antipath `Q` between
`p₂` and `p₃` with interior in `X`, and an antipath `R` between `p₁` and `p₂` with interior in
`Y`, and exactly one of `Q, R` has odd length."*

Notes on the transcription.

* The printed hypothesis is *"a path in `G`"* — verified against the PDF — whereas the
  corresponding hypothesis of 2.9, which this statement strengthens, is *"a path in
  `G \ (X ∪ Y)`"*.  The literal printed hypothesis is what is formalized: no disjointness of
  `V(P)` from `X ∪ Y` is assumed here.
* *"with vertices `p₁, …, p_n` in order"* names the first and last vertices of the list, via
  `head?` and `getLast?`.
* *"`p₁` is the unique `X`-complete vertex of `P`"* is: a vertex of `P` is `X`-complete
  exactly when it is `p₁`; likewise for `p_n` and `Y`.
* Since `P` has length 2 it has exactly three vertices `p₁, p₂, p₃ = p_n`, so it is the list
  `[p₁, c, p_n]` with `c = p₂`; `Q` then joins `p₂` and `p₃`, and `R` joins `p₁` and `p₂`.
* *"exactly one of `Q, R` has odd length"* is `Xor'`.

decls.name: maximalCube_swap'
decls.docstring:
The `(A,B,C,D) ↦ (B,A,D,C)` symmetry of a cube preserves maximality.  This is the symmetry
that lets the printed proof say *"So we may assume that `X` meets both `A` and `D`"* after having
disposed of the four `X ⊆ …` cases.

decls.name: thm_14_1
decls.docstring:
**14.1** (printed pp. 87–88)

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₅`.  Let `(A, B, C, D)` be a maximal cube in `G`, forming `K`, let
`v ∈ V(G) \ V(K)`, and let `X` be the set of neighbours of `v` in `V(K)`.  Then either*

*• `X` is a subset of one of `A ∪ B`, `C ∪ D`, `A ∪ C`, `B ∪ D`, and `X ∩ (A ∪ C)` is complete
to `X ∩ (B ∪ D)`, or*

*• `X` includes one of `A ∪ B`, `C ∪ D`, `A ∪ D`, `B ∪ C`, and `(A ∪ D) \ X` is anticomplete
to `(B ∪ C) \ X`."*

The two cases are stated in the printed order, and the paper names them immediately
afterwards: *"Say a vertex `v ∈ V(G) \ V(K)` is minor if the first case of 14.1 applies to it,
and major if the second case applies."*  So the first disjunct below is
`DoubleDiamond.SPGT.MinorForCube G A B C D v` and the second is `MajorForCube G A B C D v`,
each with its `v ∉ V(K)` conjunct removed (that conjunct is the hypothesis `hv` here); they
are written out in full so that the statement reproduces the printed text without appealing to
notions whose definition refers back to 14.1 itself.

`V(K)` is `A ∪ B ∪ C ∪ D` and `X` is `G.neighborSet v ∩ (A ∪ B ∪ C ∪ D)`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 14.1 (printed on PDF page 89).

decls.name: thm_14_2
decls.docstring:
**14.2** (printed p. 88)

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₅`.  Let `(A, B, C, D)` be a maximal cube in `G`, forming `K`, let
`F ⊆ V(G) \ V(K)` be a connected set of minor vertices, and let `X` be the set of attachments
of `F` in `V(K)`.  Then `X` is a subset of one of `A ∪ B`, `C ∪ D`, `A ∪ C`, `B ∪ D`.
Moreover, `X ∩ (A ∪ C)` is complete to `X ∩ (B ∪ D)`."*

Notes on the transcription.

* *"a connected set of minor vertices"*: `F` is connected (`ConnectedSet`) and every vertex of
  `F` is minor with respect to the maximal cube (`MinorForCube`, printed p. 88).
* *"the set of attachments of `F` in `V(K)`"* is `attachments G F (A ∪ B ∪ C ∪ D)` — the
  vertices of `V(K)` having a neighbour in `F` (printed p. 20).
* The *"Moreover"* sentence is part of the statement, so the conclusion is the conjunction of
  the two sentences.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 14.2 (printed on PDF page 90).

decls.name: thm_14_3
decls.docstring:
**14.3** (printed p. 91), introduced by *"The main result of this section is 1.8.6, which
we restate, the following:"*

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₅`.  If `G` contains a double diamond as an induced subgraph, then either
one of `G, Ḡ` admits a proper 2-join, or `G` admits a balanced skew partition.  In particular,
every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₆`."*

This is one of the twelve main steps of the proof of 1.3: it discharges 1.8.6.

Notes on the transcription.

* This is the **published** form: *"one of `G, Ḡ` admits a **proper** 2-join"* (the arXiv
  draft says *"a 2-join"*).
* A double diamond is the eight-vertex graph of printed p. 87; *"`G` contains a double diamond
  as an induced subgraph"* is the existence of eight vertices of `G` realising exactly that
  adjacency pattern (`IsDoubleDiamond`).
* The final sentence *"In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₆`"* is genuine
  mathematical content — unlike the *"In particular, 1.8.k holds"* sentences elsewhere in the
  paper, which merely name a step of the outline — so it is formalized too, but **not** here:
  it speaks about **all** graphs, not about `G`, and the paper asserts it outright, so making
  it a conjunct under this theorem's hypotheses (`G ∈ F₅` and `G` contains a double diamond)
  would assert it only if those hypotheses are satisfiable.  It is therefore the separate,
  hypothesis-free theorem `thm_14_3_recalcitrant` below.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 14.3 (printed on PDF page 93).

decls.name: thm_14_3_recalcitrant
decls.docstring:
**14.3**, final sentence (printed p. 91) — the closing corollary of 14.3, stated on its own
because the paper asserts it of *every* recalcitrant graph, under no hypothesis.

PAPER: *"In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₆`."*

`G` here is an arbitrary finite graph (it is unrelated to the `G ∈ F₅` of `thm_14_3`);
*recalcitrant* is the four-bullet notion of §13.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 14.3 (printed on PDF page 93). This module carries the closing hypothesis-free sentence of that statement.

decls.name: thm_15_1
decls.docstring:
**15.1** (printed p. 92)

PAPER: *"If `G ∈ F₆` admits a skew partition, then `G` admits a balanced skew partition."*

Together with 1.5 (*"if `G` is a minimum imperfect graph, then `G` admits no balanced skew
partition"*) this is the paper's form of Chvátal's skew partition conjecture: no minimum
imperfect graph admits a skew partition.

decls.name: walk_stays
decls.docstring: If no edge of `H` leaves `E` inside `D`, a walk of `H|D` starting in `E` stays in `E`.

decls.name: not_anticonnected_of_meets
decls.docstring:
The paper's *"`Ḡ` is not connected"*, in the form used throughout the proof: if `S` is
complete to `T` and `D ⊆ S ∪ T` meets both `S` and `T`, then `D` is not anticonnected —
a `Ḡ`-walk inside `D` that starts in `S` can never leave `S`.

decls.name: pair_not_connected
decls.docstring: Two distinct nonadjacent vertices do not form a connected set.

decls.name: anticonn_pair
decls.docstring: Two distinct nonadjacent vertices do form an *anti*connected set.

decls.name: anticonn_compl_pair
decls.docstring:
The paper's *"Then `({x,y}, V(G) \ {x,y})` is not a skew partition, and so `G \ {x,y}`
is anticonnected."*

decls.name: side_eq_pair
decls.docstring:
The paper's *"Hence `k = 2` and `B₁ = {x,y}`"*: if `(S,T)` is a complete pair covering
`V(G)` and `x, y ∈ S` are distinct and nonadjacent, then `S = {x,y}`.  (The anticonnected
set `V(G) \ {x,y}` contains all of `T`, so by `not_anticonnected_of_meets` it can contain
no further vertex of `S`.)

decls.name: isAnticomponent_side
decls.docstring:
Each side of a complete pair covering `V(G)` is, if anticonnected, an anticomponent of
`V(G)` — i.e. one of the paper's `Bᵢ`.

decls.name: exists_nonadj_of_anticonn
decls.docstring:
An anticonnected set with more than one vertex contains two distinct nonadjacent
vertices — this is the paper's *"we may assume that some `Bᵢ` … has cardinality `> 1`.
Choose `x, y ∈ B₁`, nonadjacent."*

decls.name: bullet_one
decls.docstring:
The whole content of the first bullet of 15.2, stated symmetrically in the two sides
so that it can be applied whichever side of `(X,Y)` the nonadjacent pair happens to lie in.

decls.name: thm_15_2
decls.docstring:
**15.2** (printed p. 93)

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₆`, and assume that `G` admits no balanced skew partition.  Let
`X, Y ⊆ V(G)` be nonempty, disjoint, and complete to each other.*

*• If `X ∪ Y = V(G)`, then either `G` is complete, or `Ḡ` has exactly two components, both
with `≤ 2` vertices (and hence `|V(G)| ≤ 4`).*

*• If `X ∪ Y ≠ V(G)`, then `V(G) \ (X ∪ Y)` is connected, and if in addition `|X| > 1`, then
every vertex in `X` has a neighbour in `V(G) \ (X ∪ Y)`."*

Transcription notes.

* The two bullets are two implications with a common set of hypotheses, so the conclusion is
  their conjunction.
* *"`G` is complete"* is: every two distinct vertices of `G` are adjacent.
* *"`Ḡ` has exactly two components"*: the components of `Ḡ` are the maximal connected subsets
  of `V(Ḡ)`, i.e. the *anticomponents* of `V(G)` in the sense of `Core`
  (`IsAnticomponent G Set.univ ·`).  *"Exactly two"* is rendered by exhibiting two distinct
  ones and requiring every one to be one of the two.  (`pdftotext` drops the overline on `Ḡ`
  here; the rendered page, the arXiv source and the printed proof — which argues about *"the
  anticomponents of `G`"* — all confirm `Ḡ`.)
* *"both with `≤ 2` vertices"* is the cardinality bound on every component of `Ḡ`.
* The parenthetical *"(and hence `|V(G)| ≤ 4`)"* is flagged by the authors as a consequence,
  not as a further alternative, so it is **not** a conjunct.
* *"`|X| > 1`"* is `X.Nontrivial`, and *"has a neighbour in `S`"* is `∃ z ∈ S, G.Adj x z`.

The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 15.3 (printed on PDF page 95).

decls.name: block_connected
decls.docstring: A cyclically-free block of consecutive vertices of a path is a connected set.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 15.4 (printed on PDF page 96).
The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 15.5 (printed on PDF page 96).

decls.name: odd_antihole_absurd
decls.docstring:
*"`w-u-R-v-w` is an odd antihole"*: an odd antipath `R` whose two ends are nonadjacent to
`w`, while every internal vertex of `R` is adjacent to `w`, closes into an antihole of odd
length.

decls.name: odd_antihole_absurd_two
decls.docstring:
*"`t-s-u-R-v-t` is an odd antihole"*: an even antipath `R` with an extra vertex attached at
each end, the two extra vertices being nonadjacent to each other.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 15.6 (printed on PDF page 96).

decls.name: no_tri_arith157
decls.docstring:
A cycle of length `≥ 4` has no triangle: three pairwise distinct indices cannot be
pairwise cyclically consecutive.

decls.name: hole_no_triangle
decls.docstring:
**No triangle on a hole.**  Used twice: on `C` in `G` (three vertices of a hole are
never pairwise adjacent) and on `D` in `Gᶜ` (three vertices of an antihole are never
pairwise non-adjacent).

decls.name: exists_rotate_adj_pair
decls.docstring:
Two adjacent vertices of a hole can be rotated to positions `0` and `1` (in one of
the two orders).

decls.name: antipath_through
decls.docstring:
Deleting a vertex `z` from a hole leaves a path joining the two neighbours `a`, `b`
of `z` on the hole, whose interior consists of vertices of the hole distinct from `z`
and non-adjacent to `z`.

decls.name: core
decls.docstring:
The printed proof, once the numbering has been fixed: `a = p₁`, `b = p₂` are the
adjacent pair at the front of the hole `C`, and `z = p_k` is the third shared vertex.

decls.name: key
decls.docstring: `core` with the numbering of the hole `C` still to be chosen.

decls.name: thm_15_7
decls.docstring:
**15.7** (printed p. 95)

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₆`.  Let `C` be a hole of length `> 4` and `D` an antihole of length `> 4`.
Then `|V(C) ∩ V(D)| ≤ 2`."*

Transcription notes.

* The hole `C` and the antihole `D` are given as the lists of their vertices in cyclic order;
  `V(C)` is `{w | w ∈ C}` and the *length* of either is its number of vertices,
  `holeLength = List.length`.
* `|V(C) ∩ V(D)|` is `Set.ncard` of the intersection (honest here: the ambient vertex type is
  a `Fintype`).

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 15.7 (printed on PDF page 97).
The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 16.1 (printed on PDF page 98).

decls.name: thm_16_2
decls.docstring:
**16.2** (printed p. 98)

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₆`, and let `(C,Y)` be a wheel in `G`.  Let `F ⊆ V(G) \ (V(C) ∪ Y)` be
connected, such that no vertex in `F` is `Y`-complete.  Let `X ⊆ V(C)` be the set of
attachments of `F` in `C`.  Suppose that there exist vertices in `X` with opposite
wheel-parity, and there are two vertices in `X` that are nonadjacent.  Then either:*

*• there is a vertex `v ∈ F` such that `(C, Y ∪ {v})` is a wheel, or*

*• there is a vertex `v ∈ F` with at least four neighbours in `C`, and a 3-vertex path
`p₁-p₂-p₃` in `C`, such that `p₁, p₂, p₃` are all `Y ∪ {v}`-complete, and every other
neighbour of `v` in `C` has the same wheel-parity as `p₁`, or*

*• we can number the vertices of `C` as `p₁, …, pₙ` in order, such that `p₁, p₂, p₃` are all
`Y`-complete, and there is a path `p₁-f₁-⋯-f_k-p₃` with interior in `F`, such that there are
no edges between `{f₁, …, f_k}` and `{p₄, …, pₙ}`."*

This is the **published** third bullet (the arXiv draft's version of it is ill-formed; see the
module docstring).

Transcription notes.

* *"`X ⊆ V(C)` is the set of attachments of `F` in `C`"* is `X = attachments G F {u | u ∈ C}`,
  the printed-p.-20 notion: the vertices of `C` with a neighbour in `F`.
* *"there exist vertices in `X` with opposite wheel-parity"* and *"there are two vertices in
  `X` that are nonadjacent"* are two separate hypotheses, as printed (the second pair need not
  be the first pair).
* In the third bullet the numbering of `C` is captured by naming a cyclically consecutive
  triple `p₁, p₂, p₃` of the rim; `{p₄, …, pₙ}` is then the set of vertices of `C` other than
  `p₁, p₂, p₃`, and `{f₁, …, f_k}` is `SPGT.interior P` for the path `P = p₁-f₁-⋯-f_k-p₃`.
* The three alternatives appear in the order printed.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 16.2 (printed on PDF page 100).

decls.name: thm_16_3
decls.docstring:
**16.3** (printed p. 101) — the main result of Section 16; it is statement 7 of 1.8
(*"for every `G ∈ F₆`, either `G` admits a balanced skew partition, or `G ∈ F₇`"*), restated,
and is one of the twelve main steps of the proof of 1.3.

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₆`.  If there is an odd wheel in `G` then `G` admits a balanced skew
partition.  In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₇`."*

Transcription notes.

* *"there is an odd wheel in `G`"* is `∃ C Y, IsOddWheel G C Y`: a wheel `(C,Y)` of `G` — `C`
  a hole of length `≥ 6`, `Y` a non-null anticonnected set disjoint from `C`, with two disjoint
  `Y`-complete edges of `C` — some `Y`-segment of whose rim has odd length.
* The closing sentence *"In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₇`"* is part of
  the statement, and is formalized — but **not** here.  It quantifies over **all** finite
  graphs, not just over `G`, and the paper asserts it outright, so putting it under this
  theorem's hypothesis `G ∈ F₆` would assert it only if that hypothesis is satisfiable.  It is
  the separate, hypothesis-free theorem `thm_16_3_recalcitrant` below.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 16.3 (printed on PDF page 103).

decls.name: thm_16_3_recalcitrant
decls.docstring:
**16.3**, final sentence (printed p. 101) — the closing corollary of 16.3, stated on its own
because the paper asserts it of *every* recalcitrant graph, under no hypothesis.

PAPER: *"In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₇`."*

`G` here is an arbitrary finite graph (unrelated to the `G ∈ F₆` of `thm_16_3`); *recalcitrant*
is the four-bullet notion of §13.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 16.3 (printed on PDF page 103). This module carries the closing hypothesis-free sentence of that statement.

decls.name: thm_17_1
decls.docstring:
**17.1** (printed p. 102).

PAPER: *"Let `A` be a triangle in a graph `G ∈ F₇`, and let `F ⊆ V(G) \ A` catch
`A`.  Then either `F` contains a reflection of `A`, or some vertex of `F` has
`≥ 2` neighbours in `A`."*

Encoding notes.

* *"`F ⊆ V(G) \ A`"* is `F ⊆ Aᶜ`.  (`Catches` already contains `Disjoint F A`, so
  this hypothesis is redundant; it is kept because the paper prints it.)
* *"`F` contains a reflection of `A`"*: a reflection of `A` is a triangle
  `{b₁,b₂,b₃}` matched vertex-by-vertex with `A = {a₁,a₂,a₃}`
  (`IsReflectionOfTriangle`), and *contains* means `{b₁,b₂,b₃} ⊆ F`.
* *"some vertex of `F` has `≥ 2` neighbours in `A`"* is
  `2 ≤ (G.neighborSet f ∩ A).ncard` for some `f ∈ F`; the set is a subset of the
  three-element set `A`, so its `ncard` is its genuine cardinality.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.1 (printed on PDF page 104).

decls.name: thm_17_2
decls.docstring:
**17.2** (printed p. 104).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `F,Y ⊆ V(G)` be disjoint, such that `F` is
connected and `Y` is anticonnected.  Let `a₀,b₀ ∈ V(G) \ (F ∪ Y)` and `a,b ∈ F`
such that `a`-`a₀`-`b₀`-`b` is a 3-edge path in `G`.  Suppose that:*

* *`a₀,b₀` are both `Y`-complete, and `a,b` are not `Y`-complete,*
* *the only neighbours of `a₀,b₀` in `F` are `a` and `b` respectively,*
* *`F \ {a}` and `F \ {b}` are both connected.*

*Then either:*

*1. there is a vertex in `Y` with no neighbour in `F`, or*

*2. there are two nonadjacent vertices `y₁,y₂ ∈ Y`, such that `a` is the only
neighbour of `y₁` in `F`, and `b` is the only neighbour of `y₂` in `F`."*

Encoding notes.

* *"`a`-`a₀`-`b₀`-`b` is a 3-edge path in `G`"* is `IsPathList G [a, a₀, b₀, b]`:
  paths of the paper are induced, and a four-vertex list has length `3`.
* *"the only neighbours of `a₀` in `F` are `a`"* is the set equality
  `{f ∈ F | G.Adj a₀ f} = {a}`, and likewise for `b₀`, `y₁`, `y₂`.
* *"there is a vertex in `Y` with no neighbour in `F`"* is
  `∃ y ∈ Y, VertexAnticomplete G y F`.
* *"two nonadjacent vertices `y₁,y₂ ∈ Y`"* is `∃ y₁ ∈ Y, ∃ y₂ ∈ Y, ¬ G.Adj y₁ y₂`;
  their distinctness is not stated separately by the paper (and follows, since
  `a ≠ b`).

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.2 (printed on PDF page 105).

decls.name: thm_17_3
decls.docstring:
**17.3** (printed p. 105).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `F,Y ⊆ V(G)` be disjoint, such that `F` is
connected and `Y` is anticonnected.  Let `a₀,b₀ ∈ V(G) \ (F ∪ Y)` and `a,b ∈ F`
such that `a`-`a₀`-`b₀`-`b` is a 3-edge path in `G`.  Suppose that:*

* *`a₀,b₀` are both `Y`-complete, and `a,b` are not `Y`-complete,*
* *the only neighbours of `a₀,b₀` in `F` are `a` and `b` respectively,*
* *`F \ {a}` is connected.*

*Then there is a vertex `y ∈ Y` with no neighbour in `F \ {a}`."*

(Introduced by: *"The following is a variant of 17.2, not so symmetrical, but more
useful."*  Note that only `F \ {a}` — not also `F \ {b}` — is assumed connected.)

Same encoding as 17.2; *"no neighbour in `F \ {a}`"* is
`VertexAnticomplete G y (F \ {a})`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.3 (printed on PDF page 106).

decls.name: thm_17_4
decls.docstring:
**17.4** (printed p. 105).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇` and let `P` be a path in `G` with length `> 1`, with
vertices `p₁,…,pₙ` in order.  Let `X,Y ⊆ V(G) \ V(P)` be anticonnected sets, such
that `X ∪ Y` is anticonnected, `p₁` is `X`-complete, and `pₙ` is the unique
`Y`-complete vertex in `P`.  (Note that `X,Y` need not be disjoint.)  Let
`z ∈ V(G) \ (X ∪ Y ∪ V(P))`, complete to `X ∪ Y` and with no neighbours in `P`.
Assume that `pₙ` is not `X`-complete.  Let `pₙ`-`x₁`-`⋯`-`x_k`-`y` be an antipath
with interior in `X` from `pₙ` to some `y ∈ Y`.  Then `pₙ₋₁` is nonadjacent to
`x₁`."*

(Introduced by: *"The next result is just a technical lemma for use in proving the
main result of this section, which is 17.5."*)

Encoding notes.

* The antipath is the list `q` with `IsAntipathFrom G q pₙ y` and interior in `X`.
  The paper names its vertices `pₙ, x₁, …, x_k, y`, so `x₁` is the vertex right
  after `pₙ`, i.e. the *first interior vertex*:
  `(SPGT.interior q).head? = some x₁`.  This also records that the list of
  `x`'s is non-empty (`k ≥ 1`), which the paper's notation presupposes — without
  it the "antipath" could be the single edge `pₙ`-`y`, in which case there is no
  `x₁` at all.
* `pₙ₋₁` is written `pn1`, pinned by `p.dropLast.getLast? = some pn1`.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.4 (printed on PDF page 107).

decls.name: thm_17_5
decls.docstring:
**17.5** — the main result of Section 17 (printed p. 105).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇` and let `P` be an odd path in `G` with length `> 1`, with
vertices `p₁,…,pₙ` in order.  Let `X,Y ⊆ V(G) \ V(P)` be anticonnected sets, such
that `X ∪ Y` is anticonnected, `p₁` is `X`-complete, and `pₙ` is the unique
`Y`-complete vertex in `P`.  (Note that `X,Y` need not be disjoint.)  Let
`z ∈ V(G) \ (X ∪ Y ∪ V(P))`, complete to `X ∪ Y` and with no neighbours in `P`.
Then an odd number of edges of `P` are `X`-complete."*

(Preceded by: *"… Incidentally, unlike 2.9, what we are going to prove here is not
true for general Berge graphs — we need the hypothesis that `G ∈ F₇`."*)

Note that, unlike 17.4, this statement does **not** assume that `pₙ` fails to be
`X`-complete.  For the edge-counting convention see the module docstring.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 17.5 (printed on PDF page 107).

decls.name: thm_18_2
decls.docstring:
**18.2** (printed p. 110).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `X,Y` be disjoint nonempty anticonnected subsets of
`V(G)`, complete to each other.  Let `P` be a path in `G` with even length `> 0`,
with vertices `p₁,…,pₙ` in order, such that `p₁` is `X`-complete, `pₙ` is not
`X`-complete and `pₙ` is the unique `Y`-complete vertex of `P`.  Suppose that
there is a `Y`-complete vertex in `G` nonadjacent to both `pₙ₋₁,pₙ₋₂`.  Then
either:*

* *there is an odd number of `X`-complete edges in `P`, or*

* *`n = 3` and there is an odd antipath joining `pₙ₋₁` and `pₙ` with interior in
  `X`."*

(Introduced by: *"There is a reformulation of 13.7 that we sometimes need:"*)

Encoding notes.

* `P` is a path **in `G`** here — the paper does *not* write "in `G \ (X ∪ Y)`" in
  this statement, and that is transcribed as printed.
* Even length `> 0` forces `n ≥ 3`, so `pₙ₋₁` and `pₙ₋₂` exist; they are `pn1` and
  `pn2`.
* *"`n = 3`"* is `p.length = 3` (`n` is the number of vertices).

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.2 (printed on PDF page 111).

decls.name: thm_18_3
decls.docstring:
**18.3** (printed p. 110).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `X,Y` be disjoint nonempty anticonnected subsets of
`V(G)`, complete to each other.  Let `P` be a path `p₁`-`⋯`-`pₙ` of `G \ (X ∪ Y)`,
where `n ≥ 5`, such that `p₁,pₙ` are the only `X`-complete vertices of `P`.  Then
`P` has even length.  Assume that at least two vertices of `P` are `Y`-complete,
and let `P'` be a maximal subpath of `P` such that none of its internal vertices
are `Y`-complete.  Then the length of `P'` has the same parity as the number of
ends of `P'` that belong to `{p₁,pₙ}` and are not `Y`-complete.  Moreover, the
number of `Y`-complete edges of `P` has the same parity as the number of elements
of `{p₁,pₙ}` that are `Y`-complete."*

(Introduced by: *"We need the following extension of 2.3."*)

Encoding notes.

* The statement has three conclusions.  The first, *"`P` has even length"*, is
  unconditional.  The other two live under the sentence *"Assume that at least two
  vertices of `P` are `Y`-complete"*, whose scope extends through the closing
  *"Moreover …"* sentence; they are therefore the two conjuncts of an implication.
* *"a maximal subpath `P'` of `P` such that none of its internal vertices are
  `Y`-complete"* is universally quantified: `q` is a contiguous block of `p`
  (`q <:+: p`), it is a path with ends `a,b` (`IsPathFrom G q a b`), no vertex of
  `SPGT.interior q` is `Y`-complete, and `q` is maximal — every contiguous block
  `r` of `p` with the same property that contains `q` equals `q`.
* *"the number of ends of `P'` that belong to `{p₁,pₙ}` and are not `Y`-complete"*
  is the cardinality of `{w | (w = a ∨ w = b) ∧ (w = p₁ ∨ w = pₙ) ∧ ¬ w is
  Y-complete}`; taking a *set* of vertices makes a length-`0` subpath (where
  `a = b`) count once, as it should.
* For the edge-counting convention see the module docstring.

**ERRATUM (see `FIXES.md` §F7).**  The printed sentence

> *"let `P'` be a maximal subpath of `P` such that none of its internal vertices are
> `Y`-complete.  Then the length of `P'` has the same parity as the number of ends of `P'` that
> belong to `{p₁,pₙ}` and are not `Y`-complete."*

is **false as printed**, for lines of length `1`.  If `pᵢpᵢ₊₁` is a `Y`-complete edge of `P`
with `1 < i` and `i + 1 < n`, then `q = pᵢ-pᵢ₊₁` is a maximal subpath with no `Y`-complete
internal vertex (it has no internal vertex at all, and neither one-step extension is admissible,
since it would make `pᵢ` resp. `pᵢ₊₁` an internal `Y`-complete vertex).  Its length is `1`,
while the number of its ends that lie in `{p₁,pₙ}` **and are not `Y`-complete** is `0` — both
its ends are `Y`-complete.  The printed claim would read `1 ≡ 0 (mod 2)`.  Read literally it
forces `P` to have no `Y`-complete edge at all, contradicting 18.3's own closing paragraph
(*"`y` … the number of `Y`-complete edges in `P`"*) and 18.4 (*"`P` contains an odd number, at
least 3, of `Y`-complete edges"*).  The machine-checked refutation is
`ProofAttempts/thm_18_3/Claim2_Refutation.lean`.

The missing side condition is supplied by the paper's own proof, which carries it throughout:

> *"Let `P'` be a line of length `≥ 2`, and assume first that both ends of `P'` are
> `Y`-complete."*

and whose recap of the case analysis reads *"a line has odd length if and only if **either it
has length 1**, or one of its ends is one of `p₁, pₙ` and is not `Y`-complete."*  The second
conjunct below therefore carries the extra hypothesis `2 ≤ pathLength q`, which is exactly the
scope of the printed argument.  Conjuncts 1 and 3 are untouched; the closing counting paragraph
of 18.3 — and hence 18.4, the only consumer — uses the length-`1` case through its own recap,
not through this conjunct.

erratum.title: Theorem 18.3, second conclusion: the parity clause fails for lines of length 1
erratum.problem: The second conclusion of 18.3 (p. 110) says that for every maximal subpath P′ of P with no Y-complete internal vertex, the length of P′ has the same parity as the number of ends of P′ in {p₁, pₙ} that are not Y-complete. A Y-complete edge pᵢpᵢ₊₁ of P is such a maximal subpath: it has no internal vertex, length 1, and no end in {p₁, pₙ} that fails to be Y-complete, so the clause demands 1 ≡ 0. Read literally the sentence therefore forces P to have no Y-complete edge, which contradicts the third conclusion of 18.3 and the paper's own use of it in 18.4 ("P contains an odd number of Y-complete edges"). The paper's proof carries the side condition "let P′ be a line of length ≥ 2", and its recap states the correct trichotomy including "either it has length 1"; the alternative was dropped when the recap became the statement.
erratum.fix: The formalized 18.3 adds the side condition 2 ≤ length of the subpath to the second conclusion, exactly the condition the printed proof uses. The only consumer, 18.5, applies the conclusion with index ≥ 3, so the paper's own uses are unaffected.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.3 (printed on PDF page 112).

decls.name: thm_18_4
decls.docstring:
**18.4** (printed p. 111).

PAPER: *"Let `(X,Y,P)` be a pseudowheel in a graph `G ∈ F₇`, where `P` is
`p₁`-`⋯`-`pₙ`.  Then `P` contains an odd number, at least `3`, of `Y`-complete
edges, and `P` has length `≥ 6`."*

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.4 (printed on PDF page 113).

decls.name: thm_18_5
decls.docstring:
**18.5** (printed p. 111).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `(X,Y,P)` be an optimal pseudowheel in `G`, where
`P` is `p₁`-`⋯`-`pₙ`.  Let `v ∈ V(G) \ (X ∪ Y ∪ V(P))`, not `Y`-complete.  Then
there is a subpath `P'` of `P` such that*

* *`V(P')` contains all the neighbours of `v` in `P`,*

* *there is no `Y`-complete vertex in the interior of `P'`, and*

* *if `v` is `X`-complete, then either `V(P') = {p₁}`, or `pₙ ∈ V(P')`."*

Encoding notes.

* `p₁` and `pₙ` are the first and last vertices of `P`, named by `hhead`/`hlast`.
* *"a subpath `P'` of `P`"* is a contiguous block `q <:+: P` which is a path
  (`IsPathList G q`, so in particular non-null — the empty list is not a path of
  the paper).

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.5 (printed on PDF page 113).

decls.name: thm_18_6
decls.docstring:
**18.6** (printed p. 114).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`, and let `(X,Y,P)` be an optimal pseudowheel in `G`, where
`P` is `p₁`-`⋯`-`pₙ`.  Let `F ⊆ V(G) \ (X ∪ Y ∪ V(P))` be connected, such that no
vertex in `F` is `Y`-complete.  Then there is a subpath `P'` of `P` such that*

* *`V(P')` contains all the attachments of `F` in `P`,*

* *there is no `Y`-complete vertex in the interior of `P'`, and*

* *if some vertex of `F` is `X`-complete then either `V(P') = {p₁}` or
  `pₙ ∈ V(P')`."*

*"The attachments of `F` in `P`"* is `attachments G F {w | w ∈ P}` — the vertices
of `P` having a neighbour in `F` (§5, printed p. 20).  Otherwise the encoding is
that of 18.5.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.6 (printed on PDF page 116).

decls.name: shrink
decls.docstring:
The engine behind *"from the minimality of `F`"*: given a connected `F`, a vertex
`v ∈ F` and another vertex `w ∈ F`, the component `D` of `F \ {v}` containing `w` is a
strictly smaller connected set that still reaches `w`, and — because `F` is connected —
some vertex of `D` is adjacent to `v`.

decls.name: exists_optimal

An infix sits at a fixed offset inside the ambient list. -/
private theorem infix_getElem {α : Type*} {q P : List α} (h : q <:+: P) :
    ∃ r : ℕ, r + q.length ≤ P.length ∧
      ∀ (k : ℕ) (hk : k < q.length) (hk' : r + k < P.length), (P[r + k]'hk') = q[k]'hk := by
  obtain ⟨s, t, hst⟩ := h
  subst hst
  refine ⟨s.length, by simp [List.length_append], ?_⟩
  intro k hk hk'
  rw [List.getElem_append_left (by simp only [List.length_append]; omega),
    List.getElem_append_right (by omega)]
  simp

decls.name: thm_18_7
decls.docstring:
**18.7** — the main result of Section 18 (printed p. 115).

Preceded by: *"Now we come to the main result of this section, 1.8.8, which we
restate, the following."*

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₇`.  If it contains a pseudowheel then it admits a balanced
skew partition.  In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₈`."*

This is the eighth of the twelve main steps of the proof of 1.2: it discharges
statement 8 of theorem 1.8 (printed p. 7), *"For every `G ∈ F₇`, either `G` admits
a balanced skew partition, or `G ∈ F₈`."*

Encoding notes.

* Both sentences are part of the statement; they are formalized as two theorems.
* **This** theorem is the first sentence, with its own hypothesis `G ∈ F₇`: if
  `G ∈ F₇` and `G` contains a pseudowheel (i.e. some triple `(X,Y,P)` is a
  pseudowheel in `G`), then `G` admits a balanced skew partition.
* The closing *"In particular"* sentence is `thm_18_7_recalcitrant` below.  It is
  deliberately **not** placed under the hypothesis `G ∈ F₇`, nor under any other:
  the paper asserts it of every recalcitrant graph.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.7 (printed on PDF page 117).

decls.name: thm_18_7_recalcitrant
decls.docstring:
**18.7**, final sentence (printed p. 115) — the closing corollary of 18.7,
stated on its own because the paper asserts it of *every* recalcitrant graph,
under no hypothesis.

PAPER: *"In particular, every recalcitrant graph belongs to `F₈`."*

Encoding notes.

* `G` is an arbitrary finite graph, unrelated to the `G ∈ F₇` of `thm_18_7`;
  *recalcitrant* is the four-bullet notion of §13.
* This sentence is genuinely stronger than the first, and is the form the rest of
  the paper uses.  `F₈` requires that **neither** `G` **nor** `Ḡ` contain a
  pseudowheel, whereas the first sentence produces a balanced skew partition only
  from a pseudowheel *in `G`*; the bridge is that recalcitrance is closed under
  complementation and excludes balanced skew partitions.

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 18.7 (printed on PDF page 117). This module carries the closing hypothesis-free sentence of that statement.

decls.name: thm_19_1
decls.docstring:
**19.1** (printed p. 117).

PAPER: *"Let `G ∈ F₈`, let `(z,A₀)` be a frame, and let `x₀,…,x_{t+1}` be a wheel
system with hub `Y`, and with `t ≥ 1`.  Define `Aᵢ, Xᵢ` as usual, and assume that
at most one member of `Y` has no neighbour in `A₁`.  Suppose that for all `r` with
`1 ≤ r ≤ t`, if `x₀,x₁,…,x_r,x_{t+1}` is a wheel system, then every member of `Y`
has a neighbour in `A_r ∪ {x_{t+1}}`.  Then there is a wheel with hub `Y`."*

19.1 is the only statement of Sections 19–20 about `F₈`; everything else is about
`F₇`.  It is stated here but proved only at the end of Section 21 (*"The proof of
19.1 is completed in section 21."*); its three cases are 19.2, 20.1 and 21.2.

Encoding notes.

* *"`x₀,…,x_{t+1}` is a wheel system with hub `Y`"* is
  `IsHubForWheelSystem G z A₀ x (t + 1) Y`, i.e. the wheel system has **height
  `t + 1`**; `t ≥ 1` is stated separately, exactly as printed.  The hub condition
  already carries `Y` nonempty and anticonnected, `Y ⊆ V(G) \ (A₀ ∪ {z})`, and
  `z, x₀,…,x_t` all `Y`-complete with `x_{t+1}` not.
* *"at most one member of `Y` has no neighbour in `A₁`"* is
  `{y ∈ Y | VertexAnticomplete G y A₁}.Subsingleton`.
* *"`x₀,x₁,…,x_r,x_{t+1}` is a wheel system"*: this is the sequence of height
  `r + 1` whose `j`-th term is `x j` for `j ≤ r` and whose last term is
  `x (t+1)`, i.e. `fun j => if j ≤ r then x j else x (t + 1)`.  (At `r = t` this
  is the given system again, so the hypothesis is not vacuous.)
* `A_r` in the conclusion of that implication is the `A_r` of the **given** wheel
  system, `wheelSystemA G z A₀ x r` — as the paper's *"Define `Aᵢ, Xᵢ` as usual"*
  prescribes.  (It agrees with the `A_r` of the truncated system, since the two
  systems have the same `X_r`.)

links.rationale: The Lean statement of the paper's numbered result 19.1 (printed on PDF page 119).
